sections.title: Predicted 2026 Moed C — full mock exam
sections.blurb: The single most likely problem for each slot, in the 2026 format (4 T/F × 7 = 28, then four written problems). Take it as a timed 3-hour paper with your two A4 sheets, then mark it honestly. No single problem here is above about 6% likely, so do the alternates too.

items.src: T/F block, \(4 \times 7 = 28\) pts. (a) ellipsoid on the primal-dual polyhedron, the flipped twin of 2026B-1a (LP deck slide 80); (b) Schwartz-Zippel with \(|S| = d\) (chain 2023B-c, 2024C-b, 2025B-a, 2026A-b); (c) zero traces imply \(A^n = 0\) (chain 2024B-d, 2026A-c, 2026B-c; Horn-Johnson 2.4.P10); (d) spectral gap implies \(O(\log n)\) diameter (recitation 4; re-skin of 2023B-1d).
items.stem:
Problem 1 (\(4 \times 7 = 28\) points)

For each of the following statements, write whether they are true or false, and briefly explain your answer.

parts.summary: If the ellipsoid method is run on the combined primal-dual polyhedron P' and its center lies in P', the primal part of the center is optimal (True).
parts.q:
Let \((P)\) be the linear program: minimize \(c^T x\) subject to \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\), and let \((D)\) be its dual: maximize \(b^T y\) subject to \(A^T y \le c\). Assume that both \((P)\) and \((D)\) are feasible. Suppose we run the ellipsoid algorithm, as in class, on the polyhedron

\[P' = \{(x,y) \mid c^T x \le b^T y,\ Ax = b,\ x \ge 0,\ A^T y \le c\}.\]

If the center \((x,y)\) of the current ellipsoid lies in \(P'\), then \(x\) is an optimal solution of \((P)\).
parts.basis:
Block as a whole. The 4 T/F items worth 7 points each (28 in total) were the format of both 2026A and 2026B, and the format stays fixed within a year: probability about 0.85. Expected exact or near hits in this block: about 0.18. Expected sub-topic hits: about 0.9.

  • Same slide, other half. 2026B-1a ('if the center of the current ellipsoid is a feasible solution of the LP, then it is necessarily an optimal solution', False) was built from the LP deck's ellipsoid slides. Slide 80 of the same deck, 'Reducing Feasibility to Optimization', gives the true version: 'Step 3: Find optimum by running the ellipsoid algorithm on \(P' = \{(x,y) \mid c^T x \le b^T y, Ax = b, x \ge 0, A^T y \le c\}\). By strong duality, if (P) and (D) are feasible, there exist feasible solutions whose objective are equal. This step will return them.' Slide 85 adds 'At step \(k\): if \(q_k \in P\), return \(q_k\).' Recitations 7-9 say 'We use the Strong Duality theorem to reduce from optimal solution to feasibility.'
  • In a Moed C, slot (a) takes the topic of that year's Moed B. 2024C-1a (the number of vertices) took the topic of 2024B-1b (the vertex test). 2025C-1a (roots of unity) took the topic of 2025B-1a. Each later sitting reused at least one T/F sub-topic from the sitting before it (6 of 6). Slot (a) held an LP item in 7 of 10 exams, including both 2026 papers.
  • Answers flip along a chain. Schwartz-Zippel went F, T, F, F and isolation went T, T, F. Volk comes back to a slide claim and reverses the answer. This is the True counterpart of 2026B-1a (which was False by design): 'feasible implies optimal' does hold for a center in \(P'\), but not for a center in the LP's own feasible region. The mined digest gives this exact twin its top ranking (L4, F5).

Probability. Ellipsoid sub-topic in the 2026C T/F block: about 0.22. This item or a near copy: about 0.06.
parts.sol:
True. If \((x,y) \in P'\), then \(Ax = b\) and \(x \ge 0\), so \(x\) is a feasible solution of \((P)\). Also \(A^T y \le c\), so \(y\) is a feasible solution of \((D)\). By weak duality, every feasible solution \(x'\) of \((P)\) satisfies \(c^T x' \ge b^T y\). Together with the constraint \(c^T x \le b^T y\) of \(P'\),

\[c^T x \le b^T y \le c^T x' \quad \text{for every feasible solution } x' \text{ of } (P),\]

so \(x\) is optimal for \((P)\). In fact \(c^T x = b^T y\), so \(y\) is optimal for \((D)\) as well. This is Step 3 of the reduction from optimization to feasibility that we saw in class. When both programs are feasible, strong duality gives \(P' \neq \emptyset\), so the ellipsoid algorithm on \(P'\) returns an optimal pair (as on slide 80; strictly speaking, \(P'\) has no interior, since it lies in the hyperplane \(c^T x = b^T y\), so one writes \(P' = \{z \mid Cz \le d\}\) and runs the algorithm on the slightly relaxed system \(Cz \le d + 2^{-L'} \mathbf{1}\) of Problem Set 4, Question 1. The statement is about a center that lies in \(P'\), so this does not change the answer).

Compare 2026B-1a (False): there the algorithm runs on the feasible region of the LP alone, and a feasible center need not be optimal. For example, for max \(x\) subject to \(0 \le x \le 1\), the starting center \(0\) is feasible but not optimal. The extra constraint \(c^T x \le b^T y\) is what makes the difference.
parts.srcline: Volk, LP lecture deck, slide 80 'Reducing Feasibility to Optimization', Step 3 (LP lecture deck), and slide 85 'Ellipsoid Method Overview', 'At step \(k\): if \(q_k \in P\)... return \(q_k\)'. Also the 'Ellipsoid Method' slide of recitations 7-9. This is 2026B-1a with the answer flipped.

parts.summary: A nonzero degree-d polynomial need not have a non-root in S^n when S has exactly d elements (False).
parts.q: Let \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) be a non-zero polynomial over \(\mathbb{Q}\) of degree \(d \ge 1\), and let \(S \subseteq \mathbb{Q}\) be a set of size \(|S| = d\). Then there exist \(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in S\) such that \(f(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n) \neq 0\).
parts.basis:
• The longest T/F chain in the bank. Schwartz-Zippel was a T/F item in 4 of 10 exams: 2023B-1c (F: a non-zero polynomial in 5 variables that vanishes on all integers), 2024C-1b (T: a non-root in \(\{1, \ldots, d+1\}^n\)), 2025B-1a (F: roots of unity of order \(m\), with \(\deg f \le m-1\)) and 2026A-1b (F: an arbitrary set \(S \subseteq \mathbb{Q}^n\) of size 100). Each one is a one-line twist on the slide bound \(\Pr[f(\alpha) = 0] \le \frac{d}{|S|}\): 2023B-1c applies it over the integers, 2024C-1b and 2025B-1a apply it to a specific set larger than the degree, and 2026A-1b drops the product-set hypothesis. 2024C-1b is the key sentence of the official 2023B-1c solution, restated as an item.
  • Moed C re-skins old bank items in slots (b) and (c). 2024C-b and 2024C-c re-skinned 2023B-c and 2023A-c. 2025C-b and 2025C-c re-skinned 2023A-d and 2023A-b. Changing the constant from \(d+1\) to \(d\) is his 'swap a constant' trap (2023A-c, 2023B-d, 2024C-b, 2025B-a). The T/F research ranks 'Schwartz-Zippel with \(|S| = d\)' as the top reused twist.
  • Textbook pair. Jukna, Extremal Combinatorics, Exercise 16.4 is the \(d+1\) statement ('If S a subset of F that has d+1 elements, then any nonzero polynomial of local degree d has a nonzero point in \(S^n\)'). Exercise 16.3 asks to show that the bound is tight, with a product of linear factors as the hint.
  • Why the False goes here. 11 of the 40 past items were False, and 3 of those sat in slot (b). The randomized unit has 5 False out of 15. Items (a), (c) and (d) are all True, so (b) carries the False.

Probability. Schwartz-Zippel appears in the block: about 0.18. This item: about 0.04. The answer key 3T/1F with the False in (b): about 0.18.
parts.sol:
False. Write \(S = \{s_1, \ldots, s_d\}\) and take

\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \prod_{j=1}^{d} (x_1 - s_j).\]

This is a non-zero polynomial of degree exactly \(d\). For every \(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in S\) we have \(\alpha_1 = s_j\) for some \(j\), so the factor \(x_1 - s_j\) vanishes and \(f(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n) = 0\). The Schwartz-Zippel lemma only gives \(\Pr[f(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n) = 0] \le \frac{d}{|S|} = 1\), which says nothing. With \(|S| \ge d+1\) the bound is at most \(\frac{d}{d+1} < 1\) and the statement becomes true, as in 2024C-1b.
parts.srcline: Volk, Randomized lecture deck, slide 38 'Schwartz Zippel Lemma' (Randomized lecture deck). A re-skin of 2024C-1b (the \(\{1, \ldots, d+1\}\) version, True; 2024C official solution P1(b)), which is itself the key step of the official 2023B-1c solution. Textbook pair: Jukna, Extremal Combinatorics, 2nd ed., Exercises 16.3-16.4, p.235.

parts.summary: If the traces of A, A^2, ..., A^n are all zero, then A^n = 0, by Newton's identities and Cayley-Hamilton (True).
parts.q: Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\). If \(\mathrm{trace}(A^i) = 0\) for every \(i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}\), then \(A^n = 0\).
parts.basis:
• The only T/F sub-topic in both 2026 papers. 2026A-1c (\(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i^n = \mathrm{trace}(A^n)\) by repeated squaring, True) and 2026B-1c (equal \(\mathrm{trace}(A^i)\) for \(i \le n\) implies the same eigenvalues, True) both come from the Algebraic deck slides 'Eigenvalues of Powers', 'Power sum polynomials' and 'Newton's identities' (slides 58-60). The chain continues 2024B-1d. Algebraic T/F items were True in 8 of 9 cases.
  • The next sentence of the same textbook problem. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Problem 2.4.P10: 'Show that \(A, B \in M_n\) have the same characteristic polynomials, and hence the same eigenvalues, if and only if \(\mathrm{tr}\, A^k = \mathrm{tr}\, B^k\) for all \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, n\). Deduce that \(A\) is nilpotent if and only if \(\mathrm{tr}\, A^k = 0\) for all \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, n\).' 2026B-1c is the first sentence, and this item is the second. Prasolov, Problems and Theorems in Linear Algebra, Theorem 24.2.1, states the same fact.
  • An unused lecture claim closes the argument. Cayley-Hamilton (slides 68-69, used there for matrix inversion) has never been examined. Here it gives the conclusion in one line.
  • Competing outcome. A topic that was a T/F item in both A and B became a free-response problem in C twice: lattices in 2024 and spectral graphs in 2025. In 2026, traces and Newton's identities are that topic, so they may move to a free-response problem instead of this block.

Probability. Trace/Newton sub-topic in the block: about 0.30, the highest of the four. This item: about 0.05.
parts.sol:
True. Let \(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n \in \mathbb{C}\) be the eigenvalues of \(A\), with algebraic multiplicities. As we've seen in class, the eigenvalues of \(A^i\) are \(\lambda_1^i, \ldots, \lambda_n^i\). So the power sums are \(p_i(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n) = \mathrm{trace}(A^i) = 0\) for \(1 \le i \le n\). By Newton's identities,

\[k e_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} (-1)^{i-1} e_{k-i} p_i \qquad (1 \le k \le n),\]

so by induction on \(k\), \(e_1 = e_2 = \cdots = e_n = 0\). Dividing by \(k\) is allowed over \(\mathbb{R}\). Hence the characteristic polynomial of \(A\) is

\[\det(xI - A) = \prod_{j=1}^{n} (x - \lambda_j) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k e_k x^{n-k} = x^n,\]

and by the Cayley-Hamilton theorem \(A^n = 0\). A shorter route: as we have seen in class, by Newton's identities, \(\mathrm{trace}(A), \ldots, \mathrm{trace}(A^n)\) determine the characteristic polynomial of \(A\) (Algebraic deck slides 59-63; this is also the argument of the official 2026B-1c solution). The zero matrix has the same traces of powers, so \(A\) has the same characteristic polynomial as the zero matrix, namely \(\det(xI - A) = x^n\), and Cayley-Hamilton gives \(A^n = 0\).

Sister trap: the conclusion '\(A = 0\)' would be false. The matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) has \(\mathrm{trace}(A) = \mathrm{trace}(A^2) = 0\), but \(A \neq 0\).
parts.srcline: Volk, Algebraic lecture deck, slides 58-60 ('Eigenvalues of Powers', 'Power sum polynomials', 'Newton's identities') and slide 68 (Cayley-Hamilton, 'Matrix Inversion'), which follow Kozen Lecture 31 (Algebraic lecture deck). Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed. (2013), Problem 2.4.P10, second sentence, p.126. Prasolov, Theorem 24.2.1. The sibling of 2026B-1c.

parts.summary: If the lazy walk matrix of a regular graph has second eigenvalue at most 0.9, the graph has logarithmic diameter (True).
parts.q: There exists a constant \(C\) (that doesn't depend on \(n\) or \(d\)) such that the following holds. Let \(G\) be an undirected connected \(d\)-regular graph on \(n \ge 2\) vertices, let \(A\) be its normalized adjacency matrix, and let \(B = \frac{1}{2} I + \frac{1}{2} A\). If the second largest eigenvalue of \(B\) is at most \(0.9\), then the diameter of \(G\) is at most \(C \log n\).
parts.basis:
• A rested topic. Random walks and spectral facts were examined in 2023B-1d, 2025A-1d and 2025B-1d (all in slot (d), all True) and in 2025C-P3 (lazy walk). Neither 2026 paper had one. Every Moed C so far added 1-2 class topics that its year's A and B skipped. Slot (d) has been True in 9 of 10 exams.
  • The 2026 recitation 4 works through exactly this claim. Slides 13-16: '2. Claim: If \(\lambda_2 < 0.9\) then the diameter of \(G\) is \(O(\log n)\)', using the lazy walk \(B = \frac{1}{2} I + \frac{1}{2} A\), with the two-cliques counterexample to the converse. The recitation's first claim (the multiplicity of eigenvalue 1 equals the number of components) is 2025A-1d. The second claim has never been an exam item. The 2026 recitations rework past exam items (2023B-1c, 2023B-1d, 2024B-P4 and others), so their other claims are likely exam material too.
  • A re-skin of 2023B-1d. That item said: if all eigenvalues except the largest are at most \(\frac{1}{2}\) in absolute value, a walk from \(s\) reaches \(t\) within \(C \log n\) steps with probability at least \(\frac{1}{2n}\) (True). Its official solution is one line ('using the same analysis we saw in class'). Here the constant is \(0.9\) and the conclusion is about the diameter. The sister trap, 'diameter \(O(\log n)\) implies a constant spectral gap', is False by the recitation's two-cliques example.

Probability. A spectral or random-walk item in the block: about 0.20. This item: about 0.03.
parts.sol:
True. Let \(1 = \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_n \ge 0\) be the eigenvalues of \(B\), with \(\lambda_2 \le 0.9\). Fix vertices \(s, t\), and let \(e_s\) be the vector that is \(1\) in coordinate \(s\) and \(0\) elsewhere. As we've seen in class,

\[\left\| B^k e_s - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1} \right\|_2 \le \lambda_2^k.\]

Take \(k = \lceil 10 \ln n \rceil\) (for \(n \ge 2\)). Since \(\ln 0.9 \le -0.105\), we get \(\lambda_2^k \le 0.9^{10 \ln n} = n^{10 \ln 0.9} \le n^{-1.05} < \frac{1}{n}\). So every coordinate satisfies \(\left| (B^k e_s)_t - \frac{1}{n} \right| < \frac{1}{n}\), which means \((B^k e_s)_t > 0\) for every vertex \(t\). In words, a lazy random walk of \(k\) steps from \(s\) reaches \(t\) with positive probability. Removing the steps where the walk stays in place leaves a walk from \(s\) to \(t\) in \(G\) of length at most \(k\). So \(\mathrm{dist}(s,t) \le \lceil 10 \ln n \rceil\) for all \(s, t\). Since \(1 \le \log_2 n = \frac{\ln n}{\ln 2} < 1.45 \ln n\) for \(n \ge 2\),

\[\mathrm{diam}(G) \le \lceil 10 \ln n \rceil \le 10 \ln n + 1 < 12 \ln n \le 12 \log_2 n,\]

so the statement holds with \(C = 12\) (whether \(\log\) is to base \(2\) or \(e\)).

Note: the converse is false (recitation 4). Let \(\mu_2\) be the second largest eigenvalue of the normalized adjacency matrix \(A\); the second largest eigenvalue of \(B\) is then \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \mu_2\). Let \(m = \frac{n}{2}\). Take two cliques of size \(m\), delete an edge \(\{u_1, u_2\}\) inside the first and an edge \(\{v_1, v_2\}\) inside the second, and add the edges \(\{u_1, v_1\}\) and \(\{u_2, v_2\}\). The result is \((m-1)\)-regular with diameter 3. The vector \(x\) that is \(1\) on the first clique and \(-1\) on the second is orthogonal to \(\mathbf{1}\), so writing it in the orthonormal eigenbasis of \(A\) with \(v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \mathbf{1}\) (as in class) gives \(x^T A x \le \mu_2 \|x\|^2\). A direct count gives \(x^T A x = \frac{2(m(m-1) - 4)}{m-1}\) and \(\|x\|^2 = 2m\), so \(\mu_2 \ge 1 - \frac{4}{m(m-1)} = 1 - o(1)\). Hence the second largest eigenvalue of \(B\) is at least \(1 - \frac{2}{m(m-1)} > 0.9\) once \(m \ge 6\), while the diameter is \(3\).
parts.srcline: Recitation 4 (2026), slides 13-16, 'Claim: If \(\lambda_2 < 0.9\) then the diameter of \(G\) is \(O(\log n)\)' (recitation 4). The bound \(\| B^k p_0 - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1} \|_2 \le \lambda_2^k\) is on Randomized deck slides 73-78 ('Calculating the error', 'Bounding the error'). A re-skin of 2023B-1d.

parts.summary: Count the 4-cycles of a bipartite graph in O(n^omega) time by computing AA^T and summing (B_uv choose 2) over unordered pairs of left vertices.
parts.q:
Problem 2 (16 points)

Let \(G = (L \cup R, E)\) be a bipartite graph such that \(|L| = |R| = n\). A 4-cycle in \(G\) is a set \(\{u, v, w, z\}\) of four distinct vertices with \(u, v \in L\) and \(w, z \in R\) such that \((u,w), (v,w), (u,z), (v,z)\) are all edges of \(G\).

Find an algorithm that runs in time \(O(n^{\omega})\) and, given \(G\), computes the number of 4-cycles in \(G\).
parts.basis:
Lineage. 2026B-P2 (18 pts) asked for \(|N_{u,v}|\) for every pair \(u, v \in L\) in time \(O(n^{\omega})\). Its official solution is one line: compute \(AA^{T}\) (2026B official solution). This problem keeps the same preamble, "Let \(G = (L \cup R, E)\) be a bipartite graph such that \(|L| = |R| = n\)", and adds one counting step. 2025C-P2 continued 2025B-P2 in the same way, with the same set-cover preamble and dual rounding added.

Pattern. In Volk's exams (2023A-2026B), written matrix-multiplication problems have appeared only in Moed B/C: 2023B-P5 (transitive closure), 2024B-P4 (diameter), 2024C-P2 (Boolean product) and 2026B-P2 (common neighbours). His Moed A papers used the topic only as T/F items (2023A-1d, 2025A-1c, 2026A-1c). The rule does not hold before him: the pre-Volk 2018A Moed A paper asked for Strassen's recurrence in P1(a) (catalog 2018A-p1-a). In 2024, the Moed C algebraic problem (2024C-P2) was a sibling of the Moed B one (2024B-P4) from the same Zwick slides, but it used a different trick. In both Moed C papers so far, about two thirds of the points re-skinned earlier templates (2024C: 64 pts; 2025C: 68 pts).

Source adjacency. The Zwick TAU pool produced 2023B-P5, 2024B-P4 and 2024C-P2. It also contains the unused exercise "Give an \(O(n^{\omega})\)-time algorithm for finding a simple 4-cycle" (Advanced Algorithms 2016, Problem Set 1, Ex 1.3(b)). This is the same as the slide "Exercise 1... b) a simple quadrangle". The pool also has the slide "A graph G contains a \(C_k\) iff \(\mathrm{Tr}(A^k) \neq 0\) ?". Volk's own homework counts triangles as \(\mathrm{tr}(A^3)/6\) (Spring-2024 Problem Set 2, Problem 4: 2025 homework 2 solution, catalog id hw2025s2-p4; the folder is named 2025). Its solution first notes that \((A^2)_{i,j}\) counts the paths of length 2 from \(i\) to \(j\), but it never computes common-neighbour counts for each pair. 2026B-P2 is plausibly a bipartite re-skin of the Algebraic deck's 'Adjacency Matrix' \(A^2\) slide and this homework (the research findings: PLAUSIBLE, unverified). The research findings also lists 2024B-P4 as a candidate parent, and the source-pool analysis credits the \(A^2\) step to the Zwick Matrix-Graph slides. Whatever its parent, counting 4-cycles from \(|N_{u,v}|\) is the next step.

Against. The mined-source digest scores this candidate L3/F5 (the mined-exercise list), but it calls a close variant "possible but unlikely right after B". The reason is that 2026B-P2 already used the \(AA^{T}\) idea, and in 2024 the Moed C sibling switched tricks. For this reason the solution also covers the sibling problems (squaring, Seidel diameter, witnesses) and the trace/characteristic-polynomial promotion variant.

Probability. This problem or a near variant (detecting or counting 4-cycles or \(K_{2,2}\), per-vertex counts, general graphs via \(A^2\) or \(\mathrm{tr}(A^4)\)): 0.05. Any matrix-multiplication graph-counting problem at P2: 0.25. Any algebraic or PIT problem at P2: 0.62. PIT at P2 has never happened (about 0.10). FFT at P2 is about 0.13, spread over several instances. Even at 0.05, this is still the single most likely P2 instance.
parts.sol:
Algorithm. Let \(A\) be the \(n \times n\) biadjacency matrix of \(G\). Its rows are indexed by the vertices of \(L\) and its columns by the vertices of \(R\), and \(A_{u,w} = 1\) if \((u,w) \in E\) and \(0\) otherwise. Compute \(B = AA^{T}\) using fast matrix multiplication and output \[ \sum_{u < v} \binom{B_{u,v}}{2} = \sum_{u < v} \frac{B_{u,v}(B_{u,v}-1)}{2}, \] where the sum runs over all unordered pairs of distinct vertices \(u, v \in L\) (fix any order on \(L\)).

Step 1: the entries of \(B\). For distinct \(u, v \in L\), let \(N_{u,v} \subseteq R\) be the set of common neighbours of \(u\) and \(v\). Then \[ (AA^{T})_{u,v} = \sum_{w \in R} A_{u,w} (A^{T})_{w,v} = \sum_{w \in R} A_{u,w} A_{v,w} = |N_{u,v}|, \] since \(A_{u,w} A_{v,w} = 1\) if \(w\) is a common neighbour of \(u\) and \(v\) and \(0\) otherwise. (This is the identity from Moed B, Problem 2. It takes one line, so write it out.)

Step 2: every 4-cycle is counted exactly once. Claim: the number of 4-cycles in \(G\) equals \(\sum_{u < v} \binom{|N_{u,v}|}{2}\).

Proof. Let \(P\) be the set of pairs \((\{u,v\}, \{w,z\})\) such that \(\{u,v\} \subseteq L\) has two elements and \(\{w,z\} \subseteq N_{u,v}\) has two elements. For a fixed \(\{u,v\}\) there are exactly \(\binom{|N_{u,v}|}{2}\) ways to choose \(\{w,z\}\), so \(|P| = \sum_{u < v} \binom{|N_{u,v}|}{2}\). We show that \(S \mapsto (S \cap L, S \cap R)\) is a bijection from the set of 4-cycles onto \(P\).

  • It maps into \(P\) and is one-to-one. Let \(S = \{u,v,w,z\}\) be a 4-cycle. By definition \(S \cap L = \{u,v\}\) and \(S \cap R = \{w,z\}\), each with exactly two elements. Each of \(w, z\) is adjacent to both \(u\) and \(v\), so \(\{w,z\} \subseteq N_{u,v}\). Since \(S = (S \cap L) \cup (S \cap R)\), different 4-cycles have different images.
  • It is onto. Let \((\{u,v\}, \{w,z\}) \in P\). The four vertices are distinct because \(u \neq v\), \(w \neq z\) and \(L \cap R = \emptyset\). The edges \((u,w), (v,w), (u,z), (v,z)\) are all in \(E\) because \(w, z \in N_{u,v}\). So \(\{u,v,w,z\}\) is a 4-cycle, and its image is \((\{u,v\}, \{w,z\})\).

Hence the number of 4-cycles is \(|P|\). By Step 1, \(B_{u,v} = |N_{u,v}|\), so the algorithm outputs exactly the number of 4-cycles. \(\square\)

Bipartiteness is what makes each 4-cycle count once. The cycle alternates between the sides, so its two vertices in \(L\) are opposite each other. A 4-cycle therefore has exactly one opposite pair inside \(L\), and we only sum over pairs in \(L\). Watch for two mistakes. Summing over ordered pairs \((u,v)\) counts every 4-cycle twice. Including the diagonal adds \(\sum_{u \in L} \binom{\deg(u)}{2}\), because \(B_{u,u} = \deg(u)\), and those terms are not 4-cycles.

Running time. Building \(A\) and \(A^{T}\) takes \(O(n^2)\) time. Computing \(B = AA^{T}\) is one product of two \(n \times n\) matrices. As we have seen in class, this takes \(O(n^{\omega})\) time (for example \(O(n^{\log_2 7})\) with Strassen's algorithm). There are \(\binom{n}{2} = O(n^2)\) pairs, and each term \(B_{u,v}(B_{u,v}-1)/2\) takes \(O(1)\) arithmetic operations on \(O(\log n)\)-bit integers: \(0 \le B_{u,v} \le n\), and the answer is at most \(\binom{n}{2}^{2} < n^4\). The total is \(O(n^{\omega} + n^2) = O(n^{\omega})\), since \(\omega \ge 2\).

Sanity check. For \(G = K_{n,n}\), \(B_{u,v} = n\) for all \(u \neq v\), so the output is \(\binom{n}{2} \cdot \binom{n}{2}\). This is correct, since any two vertices of \(L\) together with any two vertices of \(R\) form a 4-cycle. For a single 4-cycle plus isolated vertices, exactly one pair has \(B_{u,v} = 2\) and the output is \(\binom{2}{2} = 1\).

Where the points are (estimated weighting; no official rubric exists for this mock): the product \(AA^{T}\) with its entry identity; the no-double-counting argument (unordered pairs, diagonal excluded, "choose 2" rather than \(B_{u,v}^2\)); and the \(O(n^{\omega})\) running-time analysis.

Variants with the same idea (practise these).

  • Detect a 4-cycle and output one. \(G\) has a 4-cycle if and only if \(B_{u,v} \ge 2\) for some \(u \neq v\). Scan the off-diagonal entries of \(B\) in \(O(n^2)\). For such a pair, scan rows \(u\) and \(v\) of \(A\) in \(O(n)\) and take the first two \(w\) with \(A_{u,w} = A_{v,w} = 1\). The total is \(O(n^{\omega})\).
  • 4-cycles through a given vertex \(u \in L\). The vertex \(u\) must be one of the two \(L\)-vertices, so the count is \(\sum_{v \in L,\, v \neq u} \binom{B_{u,v}}{2}\). Only row \(u\) of \(B\) is needed. It equals the vector-matrix product of row \(u\) of \(A\) with \(A^{T}\), so \(O(n^2)\) time is enough. For a vertex of \(R\), use \(A^{T}A\) instead. Summing the per-vertex counts over all \(u \in L\) gives twice the total.
  • A general undirected graph with adjacency matrix \(A\), \(m\) edges and degrees \(d_v\): \[ \#C_4 = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{u < v} \binom{(A^2)_{u,v}}{2} = \frac{\mathrm{tr}(A^4) - 2\sum_{v} d_v^2 + 2m}{8}. \] The factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) is needed because a 4-cycle \(a,b,c,d\) has two opposite pairs, \(\{a,c\}\) and \(\{b,d\}\), and is counted once for each. For the trace form, sort the closed walks of length 4 into three kinds. A walk around a 4-cycle gives 8 walks per cycle (4 starting points times 2 directions). A walk \(v,a,v,b,v\) gives \(d_v^2\) walks from \(v\). A walk \(v,a,b,a,v\) with \(b \neq v\) gives \(\sum_{a \sim v} (d_a - 1)\) walks from \(v\). Summing over \(v\) gives \(\mathrm{tr}(A^4) = 8\,\#C_4 + 2\sum_v d_v^2 - 2m\). Both formulas were checked by brute force on random graphs.
  • Triangles. The number of triangles is \(\mathrm{tr}(A^3)/6\) (Spring-2024 homework, Problem Set 2, Problem 4; catalog id hw2025s2-p4), and the number of triangles through \(v\) is \((A^3)_{v,v}/2\).

Sibling problems from the same pool. In 2024 the Moed C problem used a different trick from the same deck as Moed B, so practise at least one of these.

  • Squaring is as hard as multiplying (Zwick PS1 Ex 1.1; DPV Ex 2.27(c)). Suppose \(n \times n\) matrices can be squared in time \(S(n) = O(n^c)\). For any \(X, Y\), \[ {\begin{pmatrix} 0 & X \\ Y & 0 \end{pmatrix}}^{2} = \begin{pmatrix} XY & 0 \\ 0 & YX \end{pmatrix}, \] so \(XY\) is the top-left block of one \(2n \times 2n\) square. This takes time \(S(2n) + O(n^2) = O(n^c)\). The other direction is trivial, since \(A^2 = A \cdot A\). DPV reaches the same result through \(AB + BA\), in time \(3S(2n) + O(n^2)\).
  • Diameter at most 2 (Seidel's graph). Let \(B_{i,j} = 1\) if \(A_{i,j} = 1\) or \((A^2)_{i,j} > 0\), and \(B_{i,j} = 0\) otherwise. The diameter of \(G\) is at most 2 if and only if \(B_{i,j} = 1\) for all \(i \neq j\). Checking this takes \(O(n^{\omega})\) time. As seen in class, the graph \(G'\) whose adjacency matrix is \(B\) satisfies \(d_{G'}(u,v) = \lceil d_G(u,v)/2 \rceil\).
  • Witnesses for the Boolean product, unique case (Zwick slides, 'Exercise n+1 (a)'). Let \(B'_{k,j} = k \cdot B_{k,j}\). Then \((AB')_{i,j} = \sum_{k} k\, A_{i,k} B_{k,j}\), and this equals the witness \(k\) whenever position \((i,j)\) has exactly one witness. That is one product, in \(O(n^{\omega})\) time.

Promotion variant (about 0.03). Traces and the characteristic polynomial were T/F items in both 2026A and 2026B. Statement: Let \(G\) be a simple undirected graph with adjacency matrix \(A\), \(m\) edges and \(t\) triangles, and write \(\det(xI - A) = x^n + c_1 x^{n-1} + c_2 x^{n-2} + c_3 x^{n-3} + \cdots + c_n\). Prove that \(c_1 = 0\), \(c_2 = -m\) and \(c_3 = -2t\).

Solution. Let \(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(A\), and let \(p_k = \sum_i \lambda_i^k\). As we have seen in class, the eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are \(\lambda_i^k\), so \(p_k = \mathrm{tr}(A^k)\). Therefore \(p_1 = \mathrm{tr}(A) = 0\) (there are no self-loops), \(p_2 = \mathrm{tr}(A^2) = \sum_v d_v = 2m\), and \(p_3 = \mathrm{tr}(A^3) = 6t\). The coefficient of \(x^{n-k}\) is \((-1)^k e_k(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)\). By Newton's identities (from class): \[ e_1 = p_1 = 0, \qquad 2e_2 = e_1 p_1 - p_2 = -2m, \qquad 3e_3 = e_2 p_1 - e_1 p_2 + p_3 = 6t. \] So \(e_2 = -m\) and \(e_3 = 2t\), which gives \(c_1 = -e_1 = 0\), \(c_2 = e_2 = -m\) and \(c_3 = -e_3 = -2t\). This was checked numerically on random graphs. A related variant: \(A\) is nilpotent if and only if \(A^n = 0\) (by Cayley-Hamilton, since the characteristic polynomial is then \(x^n\)), and \(A^n\) can be computed by repeated squaring in \(O(n^{\omega} \log n)\) time.

items.src: Randomized construction (Chernoff + union bound), 16 pts; Volk's 2026B-P3 with 2 colors changed to 3, the step that turned 2024B-P6 into 2025C-P5; ancestors 2023B-P6 and Mitzenmacher-Upfal 4.4
items.stem: Exam rules as in 2026A/B: you may use any claim that was presented in class or proved in the homework. Unless stated otherwise, prove the correctness of your claims and analyze the running times of your algorithms.

parts.summary: Prove that for large enough n, a graph on n vertices whose minimum degree is at least log squared n has a 3-coloring in which every vertex has at least 0.3 of its neighbors in each color class.
parts.q:
Problem 3 (16 points). Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph with \(n\) vertices in which the degree of every vertex is at least \(\log^2 n\). Prove that for large enough \(n\), there's a coloring of the vertices in three colors, red, green and blue, such that every vertex \(v\in V\) has at least \(0.3\deg(v)\) neighbors in each of the three color classes.

Moed C wording to expect (the form of 2024B-P6 and 2025C-P5): Prove that for large enough \(n\), there is a randomized algorithm that, given \(G\), runs in time polynomial in \(n\) and with probability at least \(0.9\) outputs a coloring with this property.
parts.basis:
Why this problem. It is 2026B-P3 with two colors changed to three. That is the step Volk used to turn 2024B-P6 into 2025C-P5. 2025C is the paper after 2025B, whose own Chernoff problem was an estimator.

  • Both Moed C papers re-skinned a Moed B Chernoff construction. 2024C-P3 (a vector at Hamming distance at least \(n/3\) from up to \(n^{2024}\) given vectors) applied the 2024B-P6 template to a new object in the same year. 2025C-P5 (the \(k\)-tertiary matrix) is the previous year's 2024B-P6 with 2 symbols changed to 3: entries \(\{0,1\}\) became \(\{0,1,2\}\) and \(\frac{1}{2}\) became \(\frac{1}{3}\). The two official solutions share whole sentences: Set \(C\) large enough such that for \(m=C\log n\), the above is at most \(\frac{1}{10n}\), and now do a union bound for all \(k\le m\le n\). In that step the tolerance did not change: \(\big||E(S,T)|-\frac{1}{2}m^2\big|\le\frac{1}{100}m^2\) became "the number of entries of \(S\times T\) equal to \(b\) is within \(0.01|S||T|\) of \(\frac{1}{3}|S||T|\)" (2024B paper, 2025C paper). The literal analogue for 2026B-P3, where \(0.4=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{10}\), keeps \(\varepsilon=\frac{1}{10}\) and gives \(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{10}=\frac{7}{30}\approx 0.233\), which a paper would state as "at least \(0.2\deg(v)\)" (\(\varepsilon=\frac{2}{15}\), same proof). The \(0.3\) used here is one natural round threshold, not the literal analogue: \(0.3=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{30}\) changes \(\varepsilon\) from \(\frac{1}{10}\) to \(\frac{1}{30}\) and the allowed deviation from 20% to 10% of the mean. Only the constant in the exponent changes, so both versions are drilled below.
  • The slot. In both 2026 papers, P3 was a single-part, 16-point randomized construction: 2026A-P3 (shattering, union bound) and 2026B-P3 (the 2-coloring, Chernoff plus a union bound). P3 was worth 16 points in 7 of Volk's 10 exams (2023A, 2023B, 2025A, 2025B, 2025C, 2026A, 2026B), including all five from 2025 and 2026; in 2024A/B/C it was worth 14, 12 and 18.
  • The topic. A Chernoff or union-bound written problem appeared in 9 of the 10 exams from 2023A to 2026B. The only exception is 2023A, and both Moed C papers had one. Constructions outnumber estimators 7 to 2. The constructions are 2023B-P6, 2024B-P6, 2024C-P3, 2025A-P4, 2025C-P5, 2026A-P3 and 2026B-P3. The estimators are 2024A-P2 (the fraction of satisfying assignments of a CNF formula) and 2025B-P5.
  • Taught material. The 2026 recitation 3 works the 2024B-P6 exam question as a slide titled "Exam Question (2024B)". 2026A-P1(d) is the same template as a True/False item; 2023B-P6 (18 points, Small Discrepancy: a coloring with \(\mathrm{Disc}_h(F)\le C\sqrt{n\log m}\)) is the same template as a written problem. The Moed C analysis and the lecture-flow analysis both predict a re-skin of 2026A-P3 or 2026B-P3.
  • Against. 2026A/B reused no older written problem near-verbatim, so this exact skin is one of several. Other skins: \(k\) colors, a two-sided band, a set family, a re-skin of the 2026A-P3 shattering problem, or the Jukna tournament theorem. The coverage analysis prefers a sampling estimator (last used in 2025B-P5) as the variation that avoids repeating 2026; that is the alternate alt-p3-a.

Calibrated probabilities. This exact re-skin (3 or \(k\) colors, any constant thresholds): 0.06. A Chernoff or union-bound construction as P3: 0.48. A Chernoff or union-bound written problem anywhere in 2026C: 0.85.
parts.sol:
The random coloring. Color every vertex independently and uniformly at random with one of the colors \(1,2,3\) (red, green, blue), each with probability \(1/3\). We show that for large enough \(n\), with probability at least \(0.9\) every vertex \(v\) has at least \(0.3\deg(v)\) neighbors of each color. In particular, such a coloring exists.

One vertex, one color. Fix \(v\in V\) and a color \(c\in\{1,2,3\}\). For every neighbor \(u\) of \(v\), let \(X_{u,c}\) be an indicator random variable for the event that \(u\) is colored \(c\), and let\[ R_{v,c}=\sum_{u:\,(u,v)\in E} X_{u,c} \]be the number of neighbors of \(v\) colored \(c\). \(G\) has no self-loops, so \(v\) is not one of its own neighbors, and the color of \(v\) plays no role. Since \(\mathbb{E}[X_{u,c}]=\frac{1}{3}\), linearity of expectation gives \(\mathbb{E}[R_{v,c}]=\frac{\deg(v)}{3}\).

Different vertices are colored independently. So \(R_{v,c}\) is a sum of \(m=\deg(v)\) independent indicator random variables, each equal to 1 with probability \(p=\frac{1}{3}\). As we have seen in class (the Chernoff bound), such a sum \(X\) satisfies, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),\[ \Pr\left[\left|X-pm\right|\ge \varepsilon m\right]\le 2e^{-2\varepsilon^2 m}. \]We apply it with \(\varepsilon=\frac{1}{30}\). Note that \(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{30}=\frac{9}{30}=0.3\). Hence\[ \Pr\left[R_{v,c}<0.3\deg(v)\right]\le \Pr\left[\left|R_{v,c}-\frac{\deg(v)}{3}\right|\ge \frac{\deg(v)}{30}\right]\le 2e^{-2\deg(v)/900}=2e^{-\deg(v)/450}\le 2e^{-(\ln n)^2/450}. \]The last step uses \(\deg(v)\ge\log^2 n\ge(\ln n)^2\), which holds when \(\log\) is to base 2 or base \(e\). Any other fixed base only changes the constant 450.

Union bound. There are \(3n\) pairs \((v,c)\). The events for different pairs are not independent, because neighborhoods overlap. The union bound does not need independence:\[ \Pr\left[\exists v\in V,\ \exists c\in\{1,2,3\}:\ R_{v,c}<0.3\deg(v)\right]\le 3n\cdot 2e^{-(\ln n)^2/450}=6e^{\ln n-(\ln n)^2/450}. \]The exponent tends to \(-\infty\), so for large enough \(n\) this is at most \(0.1\). Concretely, if \(\ln n\ge 455\) then \(\frac{(\ln n)^2}{450}\ge\frac{455}{450}\ln n\ge\ln n+5\), so the bound is at most \(6e^{-5}<0.05\).

Therefore, with probability at least \(0.9\), the random coloring gives every vertex \(v\) at least \(0.3\deg(v)\) neighbors of each of the three colors. This probability is positive, so such a coloring exists.

The algorithmic (Moed C) wording. The algorithm colors the vertices at random as above and outputs the coloring. It runs in \(O(n)\) time and, by the analysis above, is correct with probability at least \(0.9\). A coloring can also be checked in \(O(n+|E|)\) time by counting, for every vertex, its neighbors of each color. So, for \(n\) beyond the threshold of the proof (\(\ln n\ge 455\)), one can re-sample until the check passes. Each round succeeds with probability at least \(0.9\), so the expected number of rounds is at most \(\frac{1}{0.9}<2\). For small \(n\) a valid coloring may not exist at all (see the next paragraph), and then this loop never stops.

Where marks are lost.

  • "For large enough \(n\)" is needed. Without it the claim is false. In the complete graph \(K_{20}\) every degree is \(19\ge(\log_2 20)^2\approx 18.68\), but every vertex needs at least \(\lceil 0.3\cdot 19\rceil=6\) neighbors of each color. So every color class has at least 6 vertices, and then a vertex \(v\) in a class needs 6 more vertices of its own color besides itself, so every class has at least 7 vertices, \(3\cdot 7=21>20\). The complete graphs \(K_n\) with \(n\in\{22,23,25,26,28,29,32,35,38\}\) fail in the same way. Keep the hypothesis in your answer, and say where the proof uses it (the last step of the union bound).
  • Why \(\log^2 n\). With a constant \(\varepsilon\), one pair \((v,c)\) fails with probability \(e^{-\Omega(\deg(v))}\), and this has to beat the factor \(3n\) of the union bound. When \(\deg(v)\ge\log^2 n\), it is \(e^{-\Omega(\log^2 n)}=n^{-\omega(1)}\). If only \(\deg(v)\ge\ln n\) is given, the bound is \(2n^{-1/450}\), and \(6n\cdot n^{-1/450}\) is useless. You would need \(\deg(v)\ge C\ln n\) with \(C>450\); for \(C=900\) the union bound gives \(6n\cdot n^{-2}=\frac{6}{n}\).
  • The constant-free form. The official 2026B solution writes "at most \(2^{-c\deg(v)}\le 2^{-c\log^2 n}\) for some constant \(c>0\)". The 2024B-P6 and 2025C-P5 solutions write \(e^{-cm^2}\) in the same way. This is fine if you say which Chernoff bound you use and what \(\varepsilon\) is. Here \(2e^{-\deg(v)/450}=2\cdot 2^{-\deg(v)/(450\ln 2)}\).
  • Use the class form of Chernoff. The 2026 lecture deck and recitation 3 present only the additive form \(\Pr[|X-pm|\ge\varepsilon m]\le 2e^{-2\varepsilon^2 m}\); neither they nor the 2026 homework state a multiplicative bound. The lower-tail bound \(\Pr[X\le(1-\delta)\mu]\le e^{-\delta^2\mu/2}\) (Mitzenmacher-Upfal Theorem 4.5) would give \(e^{-\deg(v)/600}\) here (\(\mu=\frac{\deg(v)}{3}\), \(\delta=\frac{1}{10}\), since \(0.9\cdot\frac{1}{3}=0.3\)), but it is not a claim presented in class or proved in the homework, so under the exam rules you would have to prove it. The class form above is the safe choice.
  • Two-sided for free. The same event \(\left|R_{v,c}-\frac{\deg(v)}{3}\right|<\frac{\deg(v)}{30}\) also gives \(R_{v,c}<\frac{11}{30}\deg(v)<0.37\deg(v)\). So the band variant, "between \(0.3\deg(v)\) and \(0.37\deg(v)\) neighbors of each color", has the same proof.

Same template, other skins (worth drilling).

  • Three colors with the 2026B tolerance, at least \(0.2\deg(v)\) neighbors of each color (the literal analogue of the 2024B-P6 to 2025C-P5 step keeps \(\varepsilon=\frac{1}{10}\), giving \(\frac{7}{30}\approx 0.233\), rounded down to \(0.2\)). Take \(p=\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\varepsilon=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}=\frac{2}{15}\). One pair fails with probability at most \(2e^{-2(2/15)^2\deg(v)}=2e^{-8\deg(v)/225}\le 2e^{-8(\ln n)^2/225}\), and the union bound over \(3n\) pairs gives \(6e^{\ln n-8(\ln n)^2/225}\), which is below \(0.1\) once \(\ln n\ge 32\).
  • \(k\) colors, at least \(\frac{\deg(v)}{2k}\) neighbors of each, when \(\deg(v)\ge Ck^2\ln n\). Take \(p=\frac{1}{k}\) and \(\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2k}\). One pair fails with probability at most \(2e^{-\deg(v)/(2k^2)}\le 2n^{-C/2}\). The union bound over \(kn\le n^2\) pairs gives \(2n^{2-C/2}=\frac{2}{n}\) for \(C=6\).
  • Set family (a variant inspired by 2023B-P6 and 2026A-P1(d), not a past exam problem as stated). Let \(T_1,\dots,T_m\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\) with \(m=n^{c}\) and \(|T_i|\ge\log^2 n\). Show there is a red/blue coloring in which every \(T_i\) is between 40% and 60% red. Take \(p=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\varepsilon=\frac{1}{10}\). One set fails with probability at most \(2e^{-|T_i|/50}\le 2e^{-(\ln n)^2/50}\), and the union bound over \(n^c\) sets tends to 0.
  • Far vector (2024C-P3). A uniform \(u\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfies \(\Pr[d(u,v)
  • Balanced bipartite graph and \(k\)-tertiary matrix (2024B-P6, 2025C-P5). Apply Chernoff to one pair \(S,T\) with \(|S|=|T|=m\). Take a union bound over the \(\binom{n}{m}^2\le n^{2m}\) pairs, and then over all \(m\ge C\log n\).
  • Tournaments (Jukna, Extremal Combinatorics, Thm 3.1, Erdős). If \(n\ge k^2 2^{k+1}\), there is a tournament on \(n\) players in which, for every \(k\) players, some other player beats all of them. For a set \(S\) of \(k\) players, \(\Pr[A_S]=(1-2^{-k})^{n-k}\le e^{-(n-k)/2^k}\). Then take a union bound over the \(\binom{n}{k}\) sets. This is the theorem right before Thm 3.2, the source of 2026A-P3; about 0.03.
parts.srcline: A re-skin of Volk's own problem. Parent: Advanced Algorithms 2026 Moed B, Problem 3 (16 pts, Aug 17, 2026; 2026B official solution). Two colors became three and \(0.4\) became \(0.3\) (one natural threshold; the tolerance-preserving analogue is \(0.2\)). Same step: 2024B-P6 (2024B paper) became 2025C-P5 (2025C paper). Ancestors: 2023B-P6 (Small Discrepancy); Mitzenmacher-Upfal §4.4 "Application: Set Balancing", Theorem 4.11, p. 71; 2026A-P1(d). Chernoff form used: the Randomized lecture deck (Randomized lecture deck, slide "Chernoff Bound", formula on) and the recitation 3 worked exam question "Exam Question (2024B)" (recitation 3; the Chernoff form it uses is on).

items.src: LP duality, 20 pts (6+6+8); LP deck 'Min-cut Max-flow' slides + DPV Exercise 7.25(c)-(e); same-year sibling of 2026A-P4 (DPV 7.28)
items.stem:
Problem 4 (6+6+8=20 points)

Recall the max-flow LP from class. Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a directed graph with a source \(s\) and a sink \(t \neq s\), such that no edge enters \(s\) and no edge leaves \(t\). Every edge \((u,v) \in E\) has a capacity \(c_{uv} \ge 0\). The maximum flow problem is described by the following linear program:

\[\begin{array}{lll} (P) & \text{maximize} & \sum_{v:(s,v)\in E} f_{sv} \\ & \text{subject to} & 0 \le f_{uv} \le c_{uv} \quad \text{for every } (u,v)\in E \\ & & \sum_{u:(u,v)\in E} f_{uv} = \sum_{w:(v,w)\in E} f_{vw} \quad \text{for every } v \in V \setminus \{s,t\} \end{array}\]

An \(s\)-\(t\) cut is a set \(S \subseteq V\) with \(s \in S\) and \(t \notin S\). Its capacity is \(c(S) = \sum_{(u,v)\in E:\, u \in S,\, v \notin S} c_{uv}\), the total capacity of the edges leaving \(S\).

parts.summary: Derive the dual of the max-flow LP through standard form and bring it to the min-cut LP with x_s = 1, x_t = 0 and y_uv >= x_u - x_v.
parts.q:
[6 points] Compute the dual linear program of \((P)\), and show that it can be written as

\[\begin{array}{lll} (D) & \text{minimize} & \sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv} y_{uv} \\ & \text{subject to} & y_{uv} \ge x_u - x_v \quad \text{for every } (u,v)\in E \\ & & x_s = 1, \quad x_t = 0 \\ & & y_{uv} \ge 0 \quad \text{for every } (u,v)\in E \end{array}\]

where there is a variable \(y_{uv}\) for every edge \((u,v) \in E\) and a variable \(x_v\) for every vertex \(v \in V\), and the variables \(x_v\) are unrestricted in sign.
parts.basis:
Probability. This problem or a near variant (a 2-3 part max-flow/min-cut dual problem): about 0.04. The family 'derive a dual and interpret it' in the P4 slot: 0.15 (0.30 anywhere on the exam). An LP-duality part anywhere on the exam: 0.60.

For.

  • It is a sibling of 2026A-P4 (min-cost unit flow, dual = shortest path, also 6+6+8). It comes from the same slides: LP deck 'Another example: Max flow' (txt) and 'Min-cut Max-flow'. It also comes from the same exercise block of Dasgupta-Papadimitriou-Vazirani. Exercise 7.25, 'The dual of maximum flow', is three exercises before 7.28, the plausible source of 2026A-P4. Moed C re-skins problems from the same year: 2024C-P2 (Boolean matrix product) followed 2024B-P4 (diameter via matrix powers).
  • The deck prints (D) without a derivation ('After taking the dual and cleaning it up a little bit, we get'). Every Moed C so far has a problem that fills in or re-runs a lecture proof: 2024C-P5 (LLL bound), 2024C-P6 (Farkas case of strong duality), 2025C-P3 (lazy random walk; its official solution works out the new eigenvalue bounds and then says that the rest of the proof is identical to the proof from class).
  • 2026B had only 7 LP points (T/F 1a). After the LP-light 2024B (12 points), 2024C gave LP 36 points. The lecture-flow analysis ranks this card 4.5/5.

Against. the coverage analysis and the mined digest rate it lower because it repeats 2026A's flow LP in the same year. So the exact instance stays at 0.04, only marginally above the Farkas twin (0.035).

This part. The task is 2026A-P4(b), 'Compute the dual LP to (P)', also worth 6 points there, and it is DPV 7.25(c). Here the target (D) is printed, because it is on the slide, so the part is graded on the derivation.
parts.sol:
As we have seen in class, the dual of the standard-form LP \(\min c^T x\) subject to \(Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\) is \(\max b^T y\) subject to \(A^T y \le c\). We first bring \((P)\) to this form:

  • Maximizing \(\sum_{v:(s,v)\in E} f_{sv}\) is the same as minimizing \(-\sum_{v:(s,v)\in E} f_{sv}\).
  • For every edge add a slack variable \(g_{uv} \ge 0\) and replace \(f_{uv} \le c_{uv}\) by \(f_{uv} + g_{uv} = c_{uv}\).
  • Write the conservation constraint of \(v \neq s,t\) as (flow in) minus (flow out) equals 0.

We get the standard-form LP

\[\begin{array}{lll} (P') & \text{minimize} & -\sum_{v:(s,v)\in E} f_{sv} \\ & \text{subject to} & f_{uv} + g_{uv} = c_{uv} \quad \text{for every } (u,v)\in E \\ & & \sum_{u:(u,v)\in E} f_{uv} - \sum_{w:(v,w)\in E} f_{vw} = 0 \quad \text{for every } v \neq s,t \\ & & f \ge 0, \quad g \ge 0 \end{array}\]

Its dual has a variable \(\alpha_{uv}\) for the capacity row of every edge and a variable \(\beta_v\) for the conservation row of every \(v \neq s,t\). They are unrestricted because they come from equality rows. The objective is to maximize \(\sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv}\alpha_{uv}\), since the conservation rows have right-hand side 0. There is one dual constraint per column of \((P')\):

  • The column of \(g_{uv}\) has a single 1, in the capacity row of \((u,v)\), and cost 0. It gives \(\alpha_{uv} \le 0\).
  • The column of \(f_{uv}\) has a 1 in the capacity row of \((u,v)\), a \(+1\) in the conservation row of \(v\) (if \(v \neq t\)) and a \(-1\) in the conservation row of \(u\) (if \(u \neq s\)). Its cost is \(-1\) if \(u = s\) and 0 otherwise. No edge enters \(s\) and no edge leaves \(t\), so \(v \neq s\) and \(u \neq t\) always hold. This is where the assumption is used, and it leaves exactly four cases:
\[\begin{array}{ll} u=s,\ v=t: & \alpha_{st} \le -1 \\ u=s,\ v\neq t: & \alpha_{sv} + \beta_v \le -1 \\ u\neq s,\ v=t: & \alpha_{ut} - \beta_u \le 0 \\ u\neq s,\ v\neq t: & \alpha_{uv} + \beta_v - \beta_u \le 0 \end{array}\]

Now substitute \(y_{uv} = -\alpha_{uv}\) and \(x_v = -\beta_v\). Negating a free variable leaves it free. The constraint \(\alpha_{uv}\le 0\) becomes \(y_{uv} \ge 0\). The objective becomes maximizing \(-\sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv}y_{uv}\), that is, minimizing \(\sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv} y_{uv}\). After multiplying by \(-1\), the four cases become

\[y_{st} \ge 1, \qquad y_{sv} \ge 1 - x_v, \qquad y_{ut} \ge x_u, \qquad y_{uv} \ge x_u - x_v.\]

Finally, add the two variables \(x_s, x_t\) with the constraints \(x_s = 1\) and \(x_t = 0\). Then \(1 = x_s - x_t\), \(1 - x_v = x_s - x_v\) and \(x_u = x_u - x_t\), so all four cases read \(y_{uv} \ge x_u - x_v\). This is exactly \((D)\).

About the values: \(\mathrm{OPT}(P') = -\mathrm{OPT}(P)\), and the dual of \((P')\) has optimum \(-\mathrm{OPT}(D)\). The two minus signs cancel. So the duality theorems from class, applied to \((P')\) and its dual, say for \((P),(D)\) that the value of every feasible solution of \((P)\) is at most the value of every feasible solution of \((D)\), and that the two optima are equal when both LPs are feasible.

(A shortcut, with the same result: by the general rules, a \(\le\) constraint of a maximization LP gets a nonnegative dual variable, an equality gets a free one, and a nonnegative primal variable gives a \(\ge\) constraint. With \(y_{uv}\) on the capacity constraints and \(x_v\) on the conservation constraints written as in minus out, this gives the four constraints above directly.)

Grading notes. The deck already prints \((D)\), so the points are for the derivation. Typical errors:

  • The wrong sign on the free variables. Taking \(x_v = \beta_v\) gives \(y_{uv} \ge x_v - x_u\) with \(x_s = -1\). This is the same LP after renaming \(x \to -x\), but the renaming has to be written out.
  • Mishandling the edges at \(s\) and \(t\). The objective coefficient of \(f_{sv}\) becomes \(x_s = 1\). There are no conservation rows for \(s\) and \(t\); the constants \(x_s\) and \(x_t\) stand in for them.
  • Putting a sign constraint on the \(x_v\). They come from equality constraints and are free.

parts.summary: Turn every s-t cut into a feasible dual solution of the same value and conclude by weak duality that every flow is at most every cut.
parts.q: [6 points] Show that for every \(s\)-\(t\) cut \(S\) there is a feasible solution of \((D)\) whose value is exactly \(c(S)\). Conclude that the value of every flow is at most the capacity of every \(s\)-\(t\) cut.
parts.basis: This is DPV 7.25(e) almost word for word: 'Show that any s-t cut in the network can be translated into a dual feasible solution whose cost is exactly the capacity of that cut.' It is also the lecture's own interpretation of (D): 'Suppose we have a solution where \(x_u \in \{0,1\}\)... Let \(S = \{u : x_u = 1\}\)... The objective is to minimize the sum of \(c_{ij}\)'s crossing the cut'. The 'conclude' clause is weak duality. Volk asked students to prove weak duality in 2023B-P2 and to prove it for SDPs in 2026B-P5(c). If this problem appears, this part is near certain (DPV has it as a separate item), and it is the easy 6 points of the problem.
parts.sol:
Let \(S\) be an \(s\)-\(t\) cut. Set \(x_u = 1\) for \(u \in S\) and \(x_u = 0\) for \(u \notin S\). For every edge set \(y_{uv} = 1\) if \(u \in S\) and \(v \notin S\) (the edge leaves \(S\)), and \(y_{uv} = 0\) otherwise.

Feasibility. \(x_s = 1\) since \(s \in S\), \(x_t = 0\) since \(t \notin S\), and \(y \ge 0\). For \(y_{uv} \ge x_u - x_v\) we check the cases:

  • \(u \in S,\ v \notin S\): \(x_u - x_v = 1 = y_{uv}\).
  • \(u, v \in S\) or \(u, v \notin S\): \(x_u - x_v = 0 = y_{uv}\).
  • \(u \notin S,\ v \in S\): \(x_u - x_v = -1 < 0 = y_{uv}\).

Value. \(\sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv}y_{uv} = \sum_{(u,v)\in E:\, u\in S,\, v\notin S} c_{uv} = c(S)\).

Conclusion. By (a), \((D)\) is the dual of \((P)\). By weak duality, as we have seen in class, the value of every feasible solution of \((P)\), that is, of every flow \(f\), is at most the value of every feasible solution of \((D)\). Applied to the solution above, \(\mathrm{val}(f) \le c(S)\) for every flow \(f\) and every \(s\)-\(t\) cut \(S\).

Weak duality for this pair can also be checked directly. Let \(f\) be a flow and \((x,y)\) feasible for \((D)\). We use \(x_s = 1\), \(x_t = 0\), the fact that no edge enters \(s\), and conservation at every \(v \neq s,t\):

\[\mathrm{val}(f) = \sum_{v\in V} x_v \left(\sum_{w:(v,w)\in E} f_{vw} - \sum_{u:(u,v)\in E} f_{uv}\right) = \sum_{(u,v)\in E} f_{uv}(x_u - x_v) \le \sum_{(u,v)\in E} f_{uv}y_{uv} \le \sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv}y_{uv}.\]

The first inequality uses \(f \ge 0\) and \(y_{uv} \ge x_u - x_v\). The second uses \(y \ge 0\) and \(f_{uv} \le c_{uv}\).

Grading notes. All three sign cases must be checked, including the edges that enter \(S\), where \(y_{uv} = 0\) is only feasible because the constraint is an inequality. For 'conclude', citing weak duality is enough.
parts.srcline: DPV, Algorithms, Exercise 7.25(e), p.244. LP deck slide 'Min-cut Max-flow', the cut reading of 0/1 dual solutions. DPV §7.4 'Duality', p.222 (dpv-chap7.txt): 'it is possible to assign interpretations to the dual variables that show the dual to be none other than the minimum-cut problem (Exercise 7.25)'.

parts.summary: Prove the class claim that the dual has an optimal 0/1 solution by rounding any dual solution with a random threshold r, conclude that the dual optimum is the minimum cut, and get max-flow min-cut from strong duality.
parts.q:
[8 points] Prove the following claim, which was stated in class without proof: \((D)\) has an optimal solution in which \(x_u \in \{0,1\}\) for every \(u \in V\). Conclude that the optimal value of \((D)\) equals the minimum capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut in \(G\), and that the maximum value of a flow equals the minimum capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut. You may not use the max-flow min-cut theorem in this part.

Hint: given a feasible solution \((x,y)\) of \((D)\), choose \(r\) uniformly at random in \((0,1]\) and consider \(S_r = \{u \in V : x_u \ge r\}\).
parts.basis:
This is the step the lecture skips: 'One can also prove that the optimum of the dual is such that \(x_u \in \{0,1\}\) for every \(u\)... This proves (using LP duality) the min cut max flow theorem' (LP deck). The deck repeats the claim on the matching-relaxation slide: 'A similar thing happened earlier when we considered the dual of the max flow LP, which was the min cut LP'. Filling in a skipped lecture step is the Moed C re-prove habit (2024C-P5, 2024C-P6, 2025C-P3), and the wording follows 2024C-P6, 'Prove the following case of the strong duality theorem'. The threshold rounding \(S_r = \{u : x_u \ge r\}\) with \(r\) uniform is the \(r\)-trick of hw2026 sheet 3 Q3 (densest subgraph: \(S(r) = \{v : y_v \ge r\}\), with \(\Pr[r \le y_v] = y_v\) for \(r\) uniform in \([0,1]\)). So the tool counts as proved in the homework. The exam rules allow any claim presented in class, so a statement that only asked for 'optimum of \((D)\) = minimum cut' would let a student cite the slide's integrality claim and finish in three lines. Asking to prove that claim rules this out. The clause forbidding the max-flow min-cut theorem closes the other shortcut: with (b) and strong duality, the theorem gives the claim at once. The hint keeps this a fair 8 points. If Volk wants a lighter (c), expect DPV 7.25(d) (every \(s\)-\(t\) path has \(y\)-length at least 1), the same telescoping sum as 2026A-P4(c).

LP-slot variants to practise.

  • The Farkas twin, hw2026 sheet 3 Q5(b): if \((D)\) is infeasible and \((P)\) is feasible, then \((P)\) is unbounded. Its twin, 2024C-P6, was taken from the homework verbatim. About 0.035. The official solution is at 2026 homework 3 solution.
  • The dual of the vertex-cover LP is fractional matching, and weak duality gives that every matching is at most every vertex cover. This is 2023A-P4 in reverse.
  • Pre-Volk 2015B-P7: the independent-set LP has value at least \(n/2\) (all halves), a clique shows the gap, and the dual ILP is minimum edge cover. Volk has reused pre-Volk items 3 times (2014A to 2023A, 2014B to 2024C, 2021B to 2023A), once in a Moed C.
  • The densest-subgraph LP (hw2026 sheet 3 Q3).
parts.sol:
Step 1: a 0/1 solution of value equal to the minimum cut. There is at least one \(s\)-\(t\) cut (\(S = \{s\}\)) and there are finitely many. Let \(S^*\) be a cut of minimum capacity. By (b), the solution \((x^*,y^*)\) with \(x^*_u = 1\) for \(u \in S^*\), \(x^*_u = 0\) for \(u \notin S^*\), and \(y^*_{uv} = 1\) exactly on the edges leaving \(S^*\), is feasible for \((D)\) and has value \(c(S^*)\). All its \(x^*_u\) are in \(\{0,1\}\).

Step 2: every feasible solution of \((D)\) has value at least \(c(S^*)\). Let \((x,y)\) be feasible for \((D)\). Choose \(r\) uniformly at random in \((0,1]\) and let \(S_r = \{u \in V : x_u \ge r\}\).

  • \(S_r\) is always an \(s\)-\(t\) cut: \(x_s = 1 \ge r\), so \(s \in S_r\), and \(x_t = 0 < r\), so \(t \notin S_r\).
  • For an edge \((u,v)\in E\), let \(X_{uv}\) be an indicator random variable for the event that \((u,v)\) leaves \(S_r\), that is, \(u \in S_r\) and \(v \notin S_r\). This happens exactly when \(x_v < r \le x_u\), that is, when \(r\) lies in the interval \((x_v, x_u]\).
    • If \(x_u \le x_v\), the interval is empty and \(\Pr[X_{uv}=1] = 0 \le y_{uv}\).
    • Otherwise, since \(r\) is uniform in \((0,1]\), \(\Pr[X_{uv}=1]\) is the length of \((x_v,x_u] \cap (0,1]\). This is at most \(x_u - x_v \le y_{uv}\). The \(x_v\) need not lie in \([0,1]\), but intersecting with \((0,1]\) only shortens the interval.
    In both cases \(\mathbb{E}[X_{uv}] = \Pr[X_{uv}=1] \le y_{uv}\).
  • Since \(c(S_r) = \sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv} X_{uv}\), linearity of expectation and \(c_{uv}\ge 0\) give
\[\mathbb{E}[c(S_r)] = \sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv}\,\mathbb{E}[X_{uv}] \le \sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv} y_{uv}.\]

A random variable is at most its expectation with positive probability. So there is an \(r \in (0,1]\) with \(c(S^*) \le c(S_r) \le \sum_{(u,v)\in E} c_{uv}y_{uv}\).

Proof of the claim. By Step 2, every feasible solution of \((D)\) has value at least \(c(S^*)\). By Step 1, \((x^*,y^*)\) is feasible and has value exactly \(c(S^*)\). So \((x^*,y^*)\) is an optimal solution of \((D)\), and \(x^*_u \in \{0,1\}\) for every \(u \in V\).

The optimum of \((D)\). The same two steps give \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) = c(S^*) = \min_{S} c(S)\), the minimum capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut. (Starting instead from any optimal solution with \(x \in \{0,1\}\): for \(S = \{u : x_u = 1\}\) every edge leaving \(S\) has \(y_{uv} \ge 1\), so \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) \ge c(S) \ge c(S^*)\), and (b) gives the other inequality.)

Max-flow min-cut. \((P)\) is feasible (take \(f = 0\)), and \((D)\) is feasible by (b). By strong duality, as we have seen in class, \(\mathrm{OPT}(P) = \mathrm{OPT}(D)\). So the maximum value of a flow equals the minimum capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut.

Remark (no randomness needed). \(S_r\) changes only when \(r\) passes one of the values \(x_u\). For every \(r \in (0,1]\), \(S_r = S_{r'}\) where \(r' = \min\{x_u : x_u \ge r\}\). This minimum exists and lies in \((0,1]\) because \(x_s = 1 \ge r\). So trying the at most \(n\) values \(r \in \{x_u : 0 < x_u \le 1\}\) finds a cut of capacity at most the value of \((x,y)\). Applied to an optimal solution of \((D)\), this computes a minimum cut in polynomial time.

Grading notes. Common gaps:

  • not checking that \(S_r\) contains \(s\) and not \(t\);
  • writing \(\Pr = x_u - x_v\) without handling \(x_u \le x_v\) or values of \(x\) outside \([0,1]\);
  • proving only one of the two inequalities;
  • citing the claim itself (it is what the part asks to prove), or the max-flow min-cut theorem: with (b) and strong duality, the theorem gives the claim at once, so it earns nothing here.

A route through total unimodularity is also acceptable, but only if it proves that the constraint matrix of \((D)\), brought to the form of the class claim, is TUM, and that an optimal vertex exists. It still needs a rounding step, since TUM gives integral \(x\), not \(x \in \{0,1\}\): for \(S = \{u : x_u \ge 1\}\), integrality gives \(x_u - x_v \ge 1\) on every edge leaving \(S\), so the cut solution of \(S\) from (b) has value at most the optimum and is itself optimal.

Lighter variant (DPV 7.25(d)). 'Show that every feasible solution of \((D)\) satisfies \(\sum_{(u,v)\in p} y_{uv} \ge 1\) for every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path \(p\).' Solution: for \(p = (s=v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = t)\),

\[\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_{v_{i-1}v_i} \ge \sum_{i=1}^{k} \left(x_{v_{i-1}} - x_{v_i}\right) = x_s - x_t = 1,\]

a telescoping sum, exactly as in 2026A-P4(c).

This proves (using LP duality) the min cut max flow theorem. Rule of life: if you have a linear program, try to take its dual and interpret it!' Threshold rounding as in hw2026 sheet 3 Q3(d) (2026 homework 3 solution: \(S(r)\) defined in Q3(c), \(\mathbb{E}_r|S(r)| = \sum_v y_v\) in Q3(d)). items.stem:
Problem 5 (6+6+8 = 20 points)

Let (P) be the following SDP problem:

\[\begin{array}{lll} (P) & \text{minimize} & \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} c_{i,j} x_{i,j} \\ & \text{subject to} & \exists u_1,\ldots,u_n \in \mathbb{R}^n \text{ such that} \\ & & x_{i,j} = \langle u_i,u_j \rangle \quad \text{for every } i,j \in \{1,\ldots,n\} \\ & & \|u_i\|^2 = 1 \quad \text{for every } i \in \{1,\ldots,n\} \end{array}\]

Let \(C \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) be the matrix whose \((i,j)\)-th entry is \(c_{i,j}\), and suppose \(C\) is symmetric. For \(n\) variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), let \(\mathrm{diag}(y)\) denote a diagonal matrix whose \((i,i)\)-th entry is \(y_i\). The dual problem (D) is the following problem:

\[\begin{array}{lll} (D) & \text{maximize} & \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i \\ & \text{subject to} & C - \mathrm{diag}(y) \text{ is PSD} \end{array}\]

You may use without proof the weak duality theorem: if \(x\) is a feasible solution for (P) and \(y\) is a feasible solution for (D), then \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i \le \sum_{i,j} c_{i,j} x_{i,j}\). Denote by \(\mathrm{OPT}(P)\) the optimal (minimum) value of (P).

Let \(G = (V,E)\) be an undirected graph with \(V = \{1,\ldots,n\}\). Recall the SDP relaxation of Max Cut that we saw in class:

\[\mathrm{SDP}(G) = \max \left\{ \sum_{\{i,j\} \in E} \frac{1 - \langle u_i,u_j \rangle}{2} \;:\; u_1,\ldots,u_n \in \mathbb{R}^n, \ \|u_i\|^2 = 1 \text{ for every } i \right\}\]

(every edge appears once in the sum), and let \(\mathrm{MaxCut}(G)\) denote the maximum number of edges crossing a cut \((U, V \setminus U)\) of \(G\).

parts.summary: Show that the Max-Cut SDP value equals |E|/2 minus the optimum of the 2026B primal (P) with C = A/4, and that it is at least the max cut.
parts.q: (6 points) Let \(A\) be the adjacency matrix of \(G\), and consider (P) with \(C = \frac{1}{4}A\), that is, \(c_{i,j} = \frac{1}{4}\) if \(\{i,j\} \in E\) and \(c_{i,j} = 0\) otherwise. Prove that \(\mathrm{SDP}(G) = \frac{|E|}{2} - \mathrm{OPT}(P)\), and that \(\mathrm{SDP}(G) \ge \mathrm{MaxCut}(G)\).
parts.basis:
Why this problem. Moed C continues same-year problems: 2025C-P2 continued 2025B-P2 with the set-cover preamble word for word (the B part did primal threshold rounding and the C part did dual rounding, W&S section 1.4). 2024C and 2025C each re-used 36-38 points of same-year templates. This problem copies the (P) and (D) preamble of 2026B-P5 word for word and turns 2026B-P5(c), the weak duality theorem that students had to prove, into a given fact. So a student who solved 2026B-P5 already has every tool. Part (a) is the glue any such continuation needs. It identifies 2026B's abstract (P) with the Max-Cut SDP of the Approximation deck (slides 'Max Cut SDP' and 'Bounding the ratio'). That identification is exactly what W&S Exercise 6.1 takes for granted. W&S 6.1 is the plausible source of 2026B-P5 (graded PLAUSIBLE/NEAR in the findings, not confirmed): 2026B-P5 proves weak duality for a general symmetric \(C\) through the vectors \(z_k\), while W&S 6.1 is the Max-Cut special case.

Slot. P5 was a 6+6+8 = 20 problem from the Approximation deck in both 2026A (Max DiCut) and 2026B (SDP duality).

Estimated probability (this item's own rough estimates; no research report gives these numbers). This continuation, whether the triangle or the general bound \(\mathrm{SDP}(G) \le \frac{|E|}{2} - \frac{n}{4}\lambda_{\min}(A)\) with the same (P) and (D): about 0.045. Any SDP or Goemans-Williamson problem anywhere on the paper: about 0.22. Some Approximation-deck problem at P5: about 0.55. For comparison, the Moed C analysis rates, as families anywhere on the paper, a multi-part LP/SDP duality problem at about 80% and an LP-based approximation problem at about 65%.
parts.sol:
Fix unit vectors \(u_1,\ldots,u_n \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(x_{i,j} = \langle u_i,u_j \rangle\). The only nonzero entries of \(C\) are \(c_{i,j} = c_{j,i} = \frac{1}{4}\) for \(\{i,j\} \in E\) (there are no self-loops, so \(c_{i,i} = 0\)). Every edge \(\{i,j\}\) therefore appears twice in the objective of (P), once as \((i,j)\) and once as \((j,i)\), and \(x_{i,j} = x_{j,i}\). Hence

\[\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} c_{i,j} x_{i,j} = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{4} \sum_{\{i,j\} \in E} \langle u_i,u_j \rangle = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\{i,j\} \in E} \langle u_i,u_j \rangle.\]

The Max-Cut SDP objective of the same vectors is therefore

\[\sum_{\{i,j\} \in E} \frac{1 - \langle u_i,u_j \rangle}{2} = \frac{|E|}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\{i,j\} \in E} \langle u_i,u_j \rangle = \frac{|E|}{2} - \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} c_{i,j} x_{i,j}.\]

Both problems range over exactly the same feasible solutions (\(n\) unit vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)), and on every feasible solution the Max-Cut objective equals \(\frac{|E|}{2}\) minus the objective of (P). So a solution maximizes the first objective if and only if it minimizes the second, and \(\mathrm{SDP}(G) = \frac{|E|}{2} - \mathrm{OPT}(P)\). (Both optima are attained, because the set of \(n\)-tuples of unit vectors is compact and both objectives are continuous.)

For the second claim, let \((U, V \setminus U)\) be any cut and let \(e_1 = (1,0,\ldots,0)\). Set \(u_i = e_1\) if \(i \in U\) and \(u_i = -e_1\) if \(i \notin U\). These are unit vectors, and \(\langle u_i,u_j \rangle = 1\) if \(i,j\) are on the same side of the cut and \(-1\) otherwise. So \(\frac{1 - \langle u_i,u_j \rangle}{2}\) is \(1\) if the edge \(\{i,j\}\) crosses the cut and \(0\) otherwise, and the SDP objective of this solution is exactly the number of edges crossing the cut. Since \(\mathrm{SDP}(G)\) is a maximum over all feasible solutions, it is at least the size of every cut, and in particular \(\mathrm{SDP}(G) \ge \mathrm{MaxCut}(G)\). (This is the fact \(\mathrm{SDPOPT} \ge \mathrm{OPT}\) used in class: the SDP is a relaxation of the \(\pm 1\) integer program.)
