That is safe for set cover, whose natural IP is unique up to notation, but it is not safe here. Stating \((P)\) shows a correct answer to (a) to anyone who reads ahead. Most of the (a) points are for the explanation (the meaning of the variables and both directions of the correspondence), which \((P)\) does not supply.

Structure. Volk usually splits such a statement into a warm-up step and a main proof, as he split W&S 5.6 in 2026A-P5 and as hw2026 set 3 Q3 is split into parts (a) to (f). The warm-up here is exactly hw2026 set 3 Q3(b) (densest subgraph: replace \(x_{uv}\) by \(\min\{y_u, y_v\}\); it stays feasible and the objective does not drop). Part (c) then uses it the way Q3(c) does: in the min form, a threshold on the actor variables decides the investor variables. The inequality \(\mathrm{LPOPT} \ge \mathrm{OPT}\) is the recitation slide "OPT(BIP) \(\le\) OPT(reduced-LP)". It is also the relaxation-bounds-OPT step at the end of the official solution of 2026A-P5(c), a maximization problem like this one (\(\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{LPOPT} \ge \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{OPT}\)). The minimization versions, with \(\mathrm{LPOPT} \le \mathrm{OPT}\), end 2025B-P2(b) (\(f \cdot \mathrm{LPOPT} \le f \cdot \mathrm{OPT}\)) and 2026B-P4(b) (\(3\,\mathrm{LPOPT} \le 3\,\mathrm{OPT}\)). Given that an IP appears, a "relax it and compare with \(\mathrm{OPT}\)" part is very likely. This exact part goes with the problem (about 0.03).
parts.sol:
The relaxation of \((P)\) is

\[ \begin{array}{lll} \text{maximize} & \sum_{j=1}^{m} p_j y_j - \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i x_i & \\ \text{subject to} & y_j \le x_i & \text{for every } 1 \le j \le m \text{ and every } i \in L_j \\ & 0 \le x_i \le 1,\ 0 \le y_j \le 1 & \text{for every } 1 \le i \le n,\ 1 \le j \le m \end{array} \]

It is feasible (all variables equal to \(0\)) and bounded (every variable is in \([0,1]\), so the objective is at most \(\sum_{j} p_j\)), so, as we have seen in class, it has an optimal solution.

\(\mathrm{LPOPT} \ge \mathrm{OPT}\). Every feasible solution of \((P)\) satisfies \(0 \le x_i, y_j \le 1\), so it is a feasible solution of the relaxation with the same objective value. In particular an optimal solution of \((P)\), whose value is \(\mathrm{OPT}\) (as given, and as shown in the solution of (a)), is feasible for the relaxation, and therefore \(\mathrm{LPOPT} \ge \mathrm{OPT}\).

The minimum form. Let \((x, y)\) be any optimal solution of the relaxation and define \(y'_j = \min_{i \in L_j} x_i\) for every \(j\). This is well defined since \(L_j \neq \emptyset\). The pair \((x, y')\) is feasible:

  • \(y'_j \le x_i\) for every \(i \in L_j\), by the definition of the minimum;
  • \(0 \le y'_j \le 1\), since \(y'_j\) is the minimum of numbers in \([0,1]\);
  • the constraints \(0 \le x_i \le 1\) are unchanged.

Its value is at least the value of \((x,y)\). Feasibility of \((x,y)\) gives \(y_j \le x_i\) for every \(i \in L_j\), hence \(y_j \le \min_{i \in L_j} x_i = y'_j\), and since \(p_j \ge 0\), \[ \sum_{j=1}^{m} p_j y'_j - \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i x_i \ge \sum_{j=1}^{m} p_j y_j - \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i x_i = \mathrm{LPOPT}. \] Because \(\mathrm{LPOPT}\) is the maximum, equality holds. So \((x^*, y^*) = (x, y')\) is an optimal solution with \(y^*_j = \min_{i \in L_j} x^*_i\) for every \(j\).
parts.srcline: DPV Algorithms, Exercise 7.29(b), first half ("Now relax this to a linear program"), p.245. Stating the IP before relaxing it follows 2026A-P5(b) and (c). The minimum step is Volk's hw2026 set 3 Q3(b) (densest-subgraph LP, \(x_{uv} = \min\{y_u, y_v\}\)).

parts.summary: Prove the relaxation has an integral optimal solution by hiring the actors above a uniformly random threshold, and conclude a polynomial time algorithm.
parts.q:
(c) [8 points] Prove that the relaxation from (b) has an optimal solution which is integral, that is, all of its coordinates are in \(\{0,1\}\). Conclude that \(\mathrm{LPOPT} = \mathrm{OPT}\) and that there is a polynomial time algorithm for the problem.

Hint: let \((x^*, y^*)\) be an optimal solution as in (b), pick \(r \in (0,1]\) uniformly at random, and consider the set of actors \(A_r = \{i : x^*_i \ge r\}\).
parts.basis: The hint is the threshold trick from hw2026 set 3 Q3(c) to (f). There, with \(x_{uv} = \min\{y_u, y_v\}\) from Q3(b), the set \(S(r) = \{v : y_v \ge r\}\) satisfies \(u, v \in S(r) \iff x_{uv} \ge r\), then \(\mathbb{E}_r[|S(r)|] = \sum_v y_v\), and finally "there exists \(r\)". Here the min form of (b) gives \(L_j \subseteq A_r \iff y^*_j \ge r\) in the same way. Every 2026 student has written this argument once. Deterministic threshold rounding was the core of 2025B-P2(b) (set cover, \(1/f\)) and 2026B-P4 (prize-collecting vertex cover, \(1/3\)); a random threshold is the natural next step. LP integrality (the LP deck's "Totally Unimodular Matrices" slides and the Kőnig proof in recitations 7 to 9) has never been examined as a primary topic in 10 Volk exams; it appears only as a remark in the 2023A-P4(c) solution. Every Moed C so far has added one or two class topics that its year's Moed A and B skipped. DPV itself frames the question as integrality "as is the case, for example, with maximum flow and bipartite matching", which is exactly the LP deck's slide before the TUM definition. My estimate for an integrality or TUM proof part on 2026C is about 0.08, and for this exact part 0.03.
parts.sol:
Let \((x^*, y^*)\) be an optimal solution of the relaxation with \(y^*_j = \min_{i \in L_j} x^*_i\) for every \(j\), which exists by (b). For \(r \in (0,1]\) let \(A_r = \{i : x^*_i \ge r\}\).

The investors that pay for \(A_r\). For every investor \(j\) and every \(r\), \[ L_j \subseteq A_r \iff x^*_i \ge r \text{ for every } i \in L_j \iff \min_{i \in L_j} x^*_i \ge r \iff y^*_j \ge r. \] Hence \[ \mathrm{profit}(A_r) = \sum_{j \,:\, y^*_j \ge r} p_j - \sum_{i \,:\, x^*_i \ge r} s_i. \]

Expectation. Pick \(r \in (0,1]\) uniformly at random. For every actor \(i\), let \(X_i\) be an indicator random variable for the event that \(x^*_i \ge r\), that is, \(i \in A_r\). For every investor \(j\), let \(Y_j\) be an indicator random variable for the event that \(y^*_j \ge r\), which by the above is the event that \(L_j \subseteq A_r\). Then \(\mathrm{profit}(A_r) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} p_j Y_j - \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i X_i\). Since \(0 \le x^*_i \le 1\) and \(r\) is uniform in \((0,1]\), \[ \mathbb{E}[X_i] = \Pr[r \le x^*_i] = x^*_i, \] and in the same way \(\mathbb{E}[Y_j] = \Pr[r \le y^*_j] = y^*_j\). By linearity of expectation, \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{profit}(A_r)] = \sum_{j=1}^{m} p_j y^*_j - \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i x^*_i = \mathrm{LPOPT}. \]

Some \(r\) is optimal. For every \(r\), \(A_r\) is a set of actors, so \(\mathrm{profit}(A_r) \le \mathrm{OPT}\) by the definition of \(\mathrm{OPT}\), and \(\mathrm{OPT} \le \mathrm{LPOPT}\) by (b). Hence \(\mathrm{profit}(A_r) \le \mathrm{LPOPT}\) for every \(r \in (0,1]\). The set \(A_r\) changes only when \(r\) passes one of the \(n\) numbers \(x^*_i\), and the sets \(A_r\) are nested, so \(A_r\) takes at most \(n + 1\) distinct values, and so does \(\mathrm{profit}(A_r)\). If all of these values were smaller than \(\mathrm{LPOPT}\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{profit}(A_r)]\) would be at most the largest of them, which is smaller than \(\mathrm{LPOPT}\), a contradiction. So there is some \(r_0\) with \(\mathrm{profit}(A_{r_0}) \ge \mathrm{LPOPT}\), and together with the upper bound, \(\mathrm{profit}(A_{r_0}) = \mathrm{OPT} = \mathrm{LPOPT}\).

An integral optimal solution. Set \(\hat{x}_i = 1\) if \(i \in A_{r_0}\) and \(\hat{x}_i = 0\) otherwise, and \(\hat{y}_j = 1\) if \(L_j \subseteq A_{r_0}\) and \(\hat{y}_j = 0\) otherwise. This is a feasible solution of \((P)\): if \(\hat{y}_j = 1\) then every \(i \in L_j\) is in \(A_{r_0}\), so \(\hat{y}_j = 1 = \hat{x}_i\). Its value is exactly \(\mathrm{profit}(A_{r_0}) = \mathrm{LPOPT}\). It is also feasible for the relaxation, so it is an optimal solution of the relaxation, and all of its coordinates are in \(\{0,1\}\).

(In fact every \(r\) works. \(\mathrm{profit}(A_r)\) is constant on each interval between consecutive values of \(\{x^*_i\} \cup \{0, 1\}\), and each such interval has positive length. The function \(\mathrm{LPOPT} - \mathrm{profit}(A_r)\) is non-negative with expectation \(0\), so it is \(0\) on every interval.)

(Remark. The min form is what makes \(Y_j\) exactly the indicator that investor \(j\) pays for \(A_r\). Without it, one can still round both families at threshold \(r\): if \(y^*_j \ge r\) then \(x^*_i \ge y^*_j \ge r\) for every \(i \in L_j\), so the rounded point is feasible for \((P)\), and the same expectation argument goes through.)

Conclusion. We showed \(\mathrm{LPOPT} = \mathrm{OPT}\) and that \(A_{r_0}\) is an optimal set of actors. The algorithm follows:

  • Solve the relaxation in polynomial time (as we have seen in class, e.g. with the ellipsoid method) and obtain an optimal solution \((x^*, y^*)\). By (b), replacing \(y^*_j\) by \(\min_{i \in L_j} x^*_i\) keeps it optimal and does not change \(x^*\), so the analysis above applies to this \(x^*\).
  • Compute \(\mathrm{profit}(A)\), in time \(O(n + \sum_j |L_j|)\) each, for the at most \(n + 1\) candidate sets \(A = \emptyset\) and \(A = \{i : x^*_i \ge x^*_k\}\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, n\). Every \(A_r\) with \(r \in (0,1]\) is one of them: if \(A_r \neq \emptyset\), let \(x^*_k\) be the smallest value \(x^*_i\) with \(x^*_i \ge r\); then \(A_r = \{i : x^*_i \ge x^*_k\}\).
  • Output the best candidate.

Since \(A_{r_0}\) is a candidate, the output has profit \(\mathrm{OPT}\), and the total running time is polynomial.

Alternative proof (total unimodularity). Let \(M\) be the constraint matrix of the relaxation of \((P)\). It has one row \(y_j - x_i \le 0\) for every \(j\) and \(i \in L_j\), with exactly one \(+1\) and one \(-1\), and the rows \(x_i \le 1\) and \(y_j \le 1\), each with a single \(1\). We show that \(M\) is TUM by induction on the size of a square submatrix \(B\), as in the recitation proof for bipartite incidence matrices:

  • If \(B\) has a zero row, \(\det B = 0\).
  • If some row of \(B\) has exactly one nonzero entry \(\pm 1\), expanding along it gives \(\det B = \pm \det B'\) for a smaller square submatrix \(B'\), which is in \(\{0, \pm 1\}\) by induction.
  • Otherwise every row of \(B\) contains a \(+1\) and a \(-1\), so the columns of \(B\) sum to \(0\) and \(\det B = 0\).

Adding slack variables brings the LP to standard form with matrix \((M \mid I)\), which is still TUM (expand along the identity columns), and the right-hand side (zeros and ones) is integral. As we have seen in class, all vertices are then integral. The LP is feasible and bounded, so it has an optimal vertex, and that vertex is integral.
parts.srcline: DPV Algorithms, Exercise 7.29(b), second half ("show that there must in fact be an integral optimal solution (as is the case, for example, with maximum flow and bipartite matching)"), p.245. The hint and the proof re-use hw2026 set 3 Q3(c) to (f) (the threshold set \(S(r)\) on top of the min form of Q3(b)). The TUM route uses the LP deck's "Totally Unimodular Matrices" slides (corpus LP deck) and the recitation 7 to 9 TUM proof for bipartite incidence matrices.

items.src: LP duality + approximation, 20 pts (6+6+8); continuation of 2026B-P4 (prize-collecting vertex cover) by the 2025B-P2 to 2025C-P2 step; Williamson-Shmoys section 1.4 (Lemma 1.7, Theorem 1.8)
items.stem:
Problem 4 (6+6+8=20 points)

In the prize-collecting vertex cover problem, the input is an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\). Every vertex \(v \in V\) has a non-negative weight \(w_v\), and every edge \(e\) has a non-negative "penalty" \(p_e\). We can either pay \(w_v\) to include \(v\) in our cover, or pay a penalty \(p_e\) if the edge \(e\) is uncovered. The goal is to find a subset of the vertices such that the total weight of the vertices in the set, plus the sum of penalties of uncovered edges, is minimal.

Consider the following LP relaxation:

\[ \begin{array}{lll} \text{(P)} & \text{minimize} & \sum_{v \in V} w_v x_v + \sum_{e \in E} p_e z_e \\ & \text{subject to} & x_u + x_v + z_e \ge 1 \quad \text{for every edge } e=(u,v) \in E \\ & & x_v, z_e \ge 0 \quad \forall v \in V, e \in E \end{array} \]

You may use any claim presented in class or proved in the homework.

parts.summary: Derive the dual of the prize-collecting vertex cover relaxation by adding slack variables and reading off the transposed constraints.
parts.q:
(a) [6 points] Show that the following LP is the dual of (P):

\[ \begin{array}{lll} \text{(D)} & \text{maximize} & \sum_{e \in E} y_e \\ & \text{subject to} & \sum_{e \in E : v \in e} y_e \le w_v \quad \text{for every } v \in V \qquad \text{(1)} \\ & & 0 \le y_e \le p_e \quad \text{for every } e \in E \end{array} \]
parts.basis:
Whole problem: 0.03. Any continuation of 2026B-P4 (dual rounding, randomized rounding, or the set-cover generalisation): 0.07.

The mechanism. 2025C-P2 continued 2025B-P2 in the same slot, P2. It copied the set-cover preamble nearly word for word (the element index \(i\) became \(j\), and 2025B's part (a), 'Write an integer linear program that corresponds to this problem', was replaced by the given 'Recall the integer LP that corresponds to this problem') and moved from Williamson-Shmoys section 1.3 (threshold rounding, which is what 2025B-P2(b) asked) to section 1.4, 'Rounding a dual solution'. The official 2025C solution file still has 2025B's point header, '(10+10=20 points)', although the question paper says 6+8+8=22. So the C paper was made by editing the B file. 2026B-P4 is a section 1.3-type threshold rounding (threshold 1/3, 3-approximation, 6+12=18 points). Taking the same step gives exactly this problem in slot P4.

This part. It is 2025C-P2(a), 'Show that the following LP is the dual of the relaxation' (6 points), with the vertex-cover LP. 2026A-P4(b), 'Compute the dual LP to (P)', has the same 6-point size. The class states the primal-dual pair for the standard form min \(c^{T}x\), \(Ax=b\), \(x \ge 0\) (LP deck, 'Duality' slides), and it also takes duals of LPs in other forms. The LP deck works a max/\(\le\) factory example with the rule 'Variable for every primal constraint / Constraint for every primal variable' (LP lecture deck), and then the dual of the max-flow LP. Recitation 7-9 derives, with a slack variable, that the primal \(Ax \ge b\), \(x \ge 0\) has the dual \(A^{T}y \le c\), \(y \ge 0\) ('Some Duality Exercise (2025A)', recitations7_8_9). hw2026 ex3 Q2 derives a dual with surplus variables (Homework_2026-solutions_ex3). The official 2025C solution adds slack variables and reads off \(A^{T}y \le c\), and the model solution above does the same. Quoting the recitation rule for the \(\ge\) form with the matrix \((M \mid I)\) is an equally valid shortcut; the solution notes it.

This LP pair was shown in class. Recitation 7-9, 'Bipartite Matching-VC Duality' (recitations7_8_9), takes the dual of the relaxed matching LP: maximize \(\sum_{e} x_e\) subject to \(\sum_{e \ni v} x_e \le 1\) for every \(v\) and \(0 \le x_e \le 1\). That LP is exactly (D) with \(w_v = p_e = 1\) (rename \(x_e\) to \(y_e\)). Its correct dual is exactly (P) with unit weights, since the upper bounds \(x_e \le 1\) produce the variables \(z_e\). The recitation's own dual, '\(y_u+y_v \ge 1\), \(0 \le y_i \le 1\)', drops the \(z_e\) and adds a bound \(y_i \le 1\) that the primal does not produce. So students have seen this pair, in the unit-weight case and with a sloppy dual. That makes part (a) a natural exam item. It also names the error to expect when grading: a derivation that ignores the \(z\) columns loses the constraints \(y_e \le p_e\) and cannot reach (D) (see the grading notes in the solution). This evidence does not answer the discounts below, so the estimate stays at 0.03.

Discounted because: dual rounding, primal-dual and complementary slackness appear in no 2026 deck or recitation. The only 'dual' in the Approximation deck is 'dual of max flow'. 2024C did not continue 2024B-P5. If 2026C also has a separate LP-duality problem, this would put two dual derivations on one paper, which no Volk exam has done.
parts.sol:
Solution. Let \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and let \(M\) be the \(m \times n\) incidence matrix of \(G\): \(M_{e,v}=1\) if \(v\) is an endpoint of \(e\), and \(M_{e,v}=0\) otherwise. Let \(\mathbf{1}\) be the all-ones vector of length \(m\). The row of \(M\) that belongs to \(e=(u,v)\) has exactly two ones, at \(u\) and \(v\), so the constraints of (P) are \(Mx + z \ge \mathbf{1}\).

We bring (P) to standard form by adding a slack variable \(s_e \ge 0\) for every edge:

\[ \text{minimize } w^{T} x + p^{T} z \quad \text{subject to } Mx + Iz - Is = \mathbf{1}, \quad x, z, s \ge 0. \]

This is an LP of the form: minimize \(c^{T} X\) subject to \(AX=b\), \(X \ge 0\), with variable vector \(X=(x,z,s) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+2m}\), constraint matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} M & I & -I \end{pmatrix}\) (one row per edge), \(b=\mathbf{1}\) and \(c=(w,p,0)\). As we have seen in class, its dual is: maximize \(b^{T} y\) subject to \(A^{T} y \le c\), with one variable \(y_e\) per row of \(A\), that is, per edge constraint of (P). Here the dual is

\[ \text{maximize } \sum_{e \in E} y_e \quad \text{subject to } \begin{pmatrix} M^{T} \\ I \\ -I \end{pmatrix} y \le \begin{pmatrix} w \\ p \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Reading the constraints row by row (there is one dual constraint per primal variable):

  • the row of \(M^{T}\) that belongs to \(x_v\) gives \((M^{T} y)_v = \sum_{e} M_{e,v} y_e = \sum_{e \in E : v \in e} y_e \le w_v\), which is constraint (1);
  • the row of \(I\) that belongs to \(z_e\) gives \(y_e \le p_e\);
  • the row of \(-I\) that belongs to \(s_e\) gives \(-y_e \le 0\), that is, \(y_e \ge 0\).

This is exactly (D).

Shortcut. (P) has the form: minimize \(c^{T}X\) subject to \(BX \ge \mathbf{1}\), \(X \ge 0\), with \(X=(x,z)\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix} M & I \end{pmatrix}\) and \(c=(w,p)\). As we have seen in the recitation, the dual of an LP of this form is: maximize \(\mathbf{1}^{T}y\) subject to \(B^{T}y \le c\), \(y \ge 0\). The rows of \(B^{T}\) are the rows of \(M^{T}\) and of \(I\) above, so this gives (D) directly. An answer that quotes this rule correctly earns full marks.

Grading notes. Typical errors:

  • Ignoring the columns of \(z\). This loses the constraints \(y_e \le p_e\), so the derivation cannot end at (D). Recitation 7-9 makes the mirror-image slip on the unit-weight case of this LP pair: its dual of the relaxed matching LP has no \(z_e\).
  • Showing only that the value of every feasible \(y\) of (D) is at most the value of every feasible solution of (P) (weak duality). This does not show that (D) is the dual of (P).
parts.srcline: 2025C-P2(a) (2025C paper) with the 2026B-P4 preamble and LP (2026B official solution). The dual is Williamson & Shmoys, section 1.4, LP (1.3), p.20-21 (ws-book.txt), adapted to the penalty variables. Recitation 7-9 'Bipartite Matching-VC Duality' (recitation 7-8-9) dualizes the unit-weight case of (D), and its 'Some Duality Exercise (2025A)' gives the rule for the \(\ge\) form.

parts.summary: Show that in an optimal dual solution every edge with no tight endpoint has its dual variable equal to its penalty.
parts.q:
(b) [6 points] Let \(y^*\) be an optimal solution for (D), and let \(C\) be the set of vertices \(v\) for which the constraint (1) holds with equality, that is,

\[ C = \left\{ v \in V : \sum_{e \in E : v \in e} y^*_e = w_v \right\}. \]

Prove that every edge \(e \in E\) that has no endpoint in \(C\) satisfies \(y^*_e = p_e\).
parts.basis: This is 2025C-P2(b) ('the sets whose constraint (2) holds with equality form a set cover') with one change: an edge may now stay uncovered, and then it must pay its penalty. The official 2025C solution replaces \(y^*_j\) by \(y^*_j+\epsilon\) and uses optimality, which is Williamson-Shmoys Lemma 1.7. The same argument works here once the upper bound \(y_e \le p_e\) is added to the minimum that defines \(\epsilon\). That is the only new idea in the part, and it is the kind of small twist Volk adds when he reuses a problem (as 2025C-P5 did with 2024B-P6, changing 2 symbols to 3). Probability as for part (a): about 0.03 for this exact problem.
parts.sol:
Solution. Suppose, towards a contradiction, that some edge \(e=(u,v)\) has \(u \notin C\), \(v \notin C\) and \(y^*_e \ne p_e\). Since \(y^*\) is feasible, \(y^*_e < p_e\). Since \(u, v \notin C\), constraint (1) is strict for both endpoints:

\[ \sum_{f \in E : u \in f} y^*_f < w_u, \qquad \sum_{f \in E : v \in f} y^*_f < w_v. \]

Let \(\epsilon\) be the smallest of the three slacks:

\[ \epsilon = \min \left\{ w_u - \sum_{f \in E : u \in f} y^*_f,\; w_v - \sum_{f \in E : v \in f} y^*_f,\; p_e - y^*_e \right\} > 0. \]

Define \(y'\) by \(y'_e = y^*_e + \epsilon\) and \(y'_f = y^*_f\) for every \(f \ne e\). Then \(y'\) is feasible for (D). The variable \(y_e\) appears only in constraint (1) for \(u\), in constraint (1) for \(v\), and in \(0 \le y_e \le p_e\).

  • For \(u\): \(\sum_{f : u \in f} y'_f = \sum_{f : u \in f} y^*_f + \epsilon \le w_u\) by the choice of \(\epsilon\). The same holds for \(v\).
  • For every other vertex, the left-hand side of (1) does not change.
  • \(0 \le y^*_e < y'_e = y^*_e + \epsilon \le p_e\) by the choice of \(\epsilon\).

But \(\sum_{f \in E} y'_f = \sum_{f \in E} y^*_f + \epsilon > \sum_{f \in E} y^*_f\), which contradicts the optimality of \(y^*\). Hence \(y^*_e = p_e\) for every edge with no endpoint in \(C\).
parts.srcline: Williamson & Shmoys, Lemma 1.7, p.22 (ws-book.txt): 'The collection of subsets \(S_j\), \(j \in I'\), is a set cover', proved by setting \(y'_k = y^*_k + \epsilon\). Also the official solution of 2025C-P2(b) (2025C official solution).

parts.summary: Prove that taking the tight vertices and paying penalties of uncovered edges is a 2-approximation via charging and weak duality.
parts.q: (c) [8 points] Consider the algorithm that solves (D), outputs the set \(C\) from item (b), and pays the penalty \(p_e\) of every edge \(e\) that has no endpoint in \(C\). Prove that this is a 2-approximation algorithm for the prize-collecting vertex cover problem.
parts.basis:
This is 2025C-P2(c), 'Show an efficient \(f\)-approximation algorithm... based on solving (D) and picking a set cover as described in item (b)' (8 points), for the prize-collecting vertex cover. The official 2025C solution uses exactly the charging chain of Williamson-Shmoys Theorem 1.8: cost \(= \sum_{i \in C} \sum_{j \in S_i} y^*_j \le f \sum_j y^*_j \le f \cdot \mathrm{LPOPT}\). The only new step is that uncovered edges enter the sum once, through part (b).

Checked. A brute-force test on about 1,500 random graphs with 2 to 6 vertices solved (P) and (D) with an LP solver and compared the result with the exact OPT. It confirmed that the optima of (P) and (D) are equal, so (D) really is the dual. It confirmed the claim of (b) (\(y^*_e = p_e\) on every uncovered edge) and the bound of (c), \(\mathrm{ALG} \le 2\sum_e y^*_e \le 2\,\mathrm{OPT}\) (worst ratio exactly 2). It also found a worst ratio of 3 for the tight-edge variant and 2 for the primal-dual variant. A separate test on 800 random instances, with the expectation computed exactly, confirmed \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}] \le 2\,\mathrm{LPOPT}\) for the randomized variant (worst ratio 2).

Other forms of the same slot (together about 0.07 with this one): randomized rounding of (P); prize-collecting set cover with frequency \(f\); local ratio (W&S Exercise 7.3); VC half-integrality (W&S Exercise 1.5(a)). The randomized rounding taught in the course is the Approximation deck's rule 'set \(x_i = 1\) with probability \(x_i\)' ('Will see an example in HW'). Its homework example, hw2026 s4-p3 (Homework_2026-solutions_ex4), takes each set with probability \(x^*_S\), repeats \(\ln(n/\epsilon)\) rounds and takes a union bound, so here it would give only an \(O(\log n)\) guarantee. The factor-2 randomized variant in the solution (probability \(\min(1, 2x^*_v)\), then the AM-GM step) scales the LP values first; no deck, recitation or 2026 homework does that. Feige's handout 1 Q1 only partly overlaps W&S Exercise 1.5; the handout itself says 'Partly overlaps Problem 1.5 in [WS11]'. Its (b) is close to W&S 1.5(a), but its bipartite-doubling part (a) and its part (c) (an optimal integral cover that keeps the 1s and drops the 0s) are not in W&S, and W&S 1.5(b) (planar graphs, 3/2) is not in Feige.
parts.sol:
Solution. Running time. (D) is feasible (\(y=0\)) and bounded (its value is at most \(\sum_e p_e\)), so it has an optimal solution \(y^*\). As we have seen in class, an LP can be solved in polynomial time (for example with the ellipsoid method). (D) has \(|E|\) variables and \(|V|+2|E|\) constraints, so \(y^*\) is found in polynomial time, and \(C\) is then computed in time \(O(|V|+|E|)\). Every subset of \(V\) is a feasible solution of the problem, so the output is feasible.

Cost. Let \(U\) be the set of edges with no endpoint in \(C\). The cost of the output is

\[ \mathrm{ALG} = \sum_{v \in C} w_v + \sum_{e \in U} p_e. \]

For every \(v \in C\), \(w_v = \sum_{e : v \in e} y^*_e\) by the definition of \(C\). For every \(e \in U\), \(p_e = y^*_e\) by item (b). Hence

\[ \mathrm{ALG} = \sum_{v \in C} \sum_{e \in E : v \in e} y^*_e + \sum_{e \in U} y^*_e = \sum_{e \in E} |e \cap C| \cdot y^*_e + \sum_{e \in U} y^*_e, \]

where the second equality changes the order of summation: \(y^*_e\) appears once for every endpoint of \(e\) that lies in \(C\). (This is the charging argument: every vertex of \(C\) is paid for by its incident edges, and every uncovered edge pays its own penalty.) An edge \(e \in U\) has \(|e \cap C| = 0\), and an edge \(e \notin U\) has \(|e \cap C| \le 2\). Since \(y^* \ge 0\),

\[ \mathrm{ALG} = \sum_{e \notin U} |e \cap C| \cdot y^*_e + \sum_{e \in U} y^*_e \le 2 \sum_{e \notin U} y^*_e + \sum_{e \in U} y^*_e \le 2 \sum_{e \in E} y^*_e. \]

Comparison with OPT. By weak duality, \(\sum_{e} y^*_e \le \mathrm{LPOPT}\), the optimum of (P). Directly: for every feasible \((x,z)\) of (P),

\[ \sum_{e \in E} y^*_e \le \sum_{e=(u,v) \in E} y^*_e (x_u + x_v + z_e) = \sum_{v \in V} x_v \sum_{e : v \in e} y^*_e + \sum_{e \in E} y^*_e z_e \le \sum_{v \in V} w_v x_v + \sum_{e \in E} p_e z_e, \]

using \(y^* \ge 0\) and the constraints of (P) for the first inequality, and \(x, z \ge 0\) with the constraints of (D) for the last one. Also \(\mathrm{LPOPT} \le \mathrm{OPT}\): if \(S^*\) is an optimal solution, then setting \(x_v=1\) exactly for \(v \in S^*\) and \(z_e=1\) exactly for the edges not covered by \(S^*\) gives a feasible solution of (P) whose value is the cost of \(S^*\). Therefore

\[ \mathrm{ALG} \le 2 \sum_{e \in E} y^*_e \le 2 \cdot \mathrm{LPOPT} \le 2 \cdot \mathrm{OPT}. \]

Remarks.

  • The factor 2 is tight for this algorithm. Take a single edge \(e=(u,v)\) with \(w_u=w_v=1\) and \(p_e=2\). Then (D) is: maximize \(y_e\) subject to \(y_e \le 1\) and \(y_e \le 2\), so \(y^*_e=1\), both \(u\) and \(v\) are tight, and \(\mathrm{ALG}=2\) while \(\mathrm{OPT}=1\).
  • It matters that the algorithm pays only for edges not covered by \(C\). If it paid \(p_e\) for every edge with \(y^*_e=p_e\) (the 'take all tight sets' rule of the set-cover view, where every edge lies in 3 sets: \(u\), \(v\) and its own penalty), the same computation gives only \(\mathrm{ALG} \le 3 \sum_e y^*_e\). On a single edge with \(w_u=w_v=p_e=1\), that rule pays 3 while \(\mathrm{OPT}=1\).
  • Compare with 2026B-P4: threshold rounding of (P) at \(1/3\) gives only 3. Dual rounding gives 2.

Variants of this part.

  • Primal-dual (no LP solver). Start with \(y=0\) and \(C=\emptyset\). While some edge \(e\) has no endpoint in \(C\) and \(y_e < p_e\), raise \(y_e\) until constraint (1) of an endpoint or \(y_e \le p_e\) becomes tight, and add the tight endpoints to \(C\). No edge at a vertex of \(C\) is raised again, so the vertices of \(C\) stay tight. At the end \(y\) is feasible for (D) and every uncovered edge has \(y_e=p_e\). The same charging gives \(\mathrm{ALG} \le 2 \sum_e y_e \le 2\,\mathrm{OPT}\).
  • Prize-collecting set cover with frequency \(f\). The same proof gives an \(f\)-approximation: an uncovered element is charged once and a covered one at most \(f\) times. Threshold rounding of the primal at \(1/(f+1)\) gives \(f+1\). For \(f=2\) this is 2026B-P4.
  • Randomized rounding of (P). Put each \(v\) in the cover independently with probability \(\min(1, 2x^*_v)\). The expected vertex cost is at most \(2 \sum_v w_v x^*_v\). An edge is uncovered only if \(x^*_u, x^*_v < 1/2\). Then, with \(a=1-2x^*_u\) and \(b=1-2x^*_v\), it is uncovered with probability \(ab \le \left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2 = (1-x^*_u-x^*_v)^2 \le \min(1, z^*_e)^2 \le z^*_e\). So the expected cost is at most \(2\,\mathrm{LPOPT}\).
parts.srcline: Williamson & Shmoys, Theorem 1.8, p.22-23 (ws-book.txt): 'The dual rounding algorithm described above is an \(f\)-approximation algorithm for the set cover problem' (charging argument plus weak duality). The primal-dual variant is W&S section 1.5. The official solution of 2025C-P2(c) (2025C official solution) uses the same chain.

items.src: LP-rounding approximation, 20 pts (6+6+8); Feige, Weizmann Approximation algorithms final exam (20 Feb 2019) Q1 'K3 removal' items 2-3 (item 1, the strongly polynomial factor-3 algorithm, is a variant under (b)); re-skins Volk 2023B-P3 / 2026B-P4 (1/3-threshold rounding) and the random partition of 2023A-P3 / 2026A-P5(a), derandomized as on the approximation deck's conditional-expectations slides
items.stem: Problem (6+6+8 = 20 points). In the triangle removal problem, the input is an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n\) vertices, where every edge \(e \in E\) has a non-negative weight \(w_e\). A triangle in \(G\) is a set of three vertices \(\{u,v,w\}\) such that \((u,v),(v,w),(u,w) \in E\). The goal is to find a set of edges \(F \subseteq E\) of minimum total weight \(w(F)=\sum_{e \in F} w_e\) such that the graph \((V, E \setminus F)\) contains no triangle.

parts.summary: Write an integer linear program with a 0/1 variable per edge and one covering constraint per triangle for minimum-weight triangle removal.
parts.q: (a) [6 points] Write an integer linear program that corresponds to this problem, with a variable \(x_e\) for every edge \(e \in E\). Explain your answer briefly.
parts.basis:
Template: write an IP from scratch. A part of the form 'write an integer linear program for X' appeared in 5 of the 8 Volk exams from 2023A to 2025C (2023A-P2 dominating set, 2024A-P4 weighted Max-SAT, 2024C-P4 bin packing, 2025A-P3 makespan, 2025B-P2(a) set cover) and in neither 2026 exam. The research analyses treat its return as possible, not likely. The flow research says only that 'A write-an-ILP item may return' and lists it as one of three candidate slots missing from 2026A/B. The coverage research rates 'an LP-theory proof and/or an ILP formulation' Medium-high, as one candidate among several, on the 2024B-to-2024C precedent (an LP-light Moed B followed by a Moed C with a bin-packing ILP). The format research dissents: 'A from-scratch "write the ILP" part is less likely (0.30)'. The wording here is 2025B-P2(a) ('Write an integer linear program that corresponds to this problem. Explain your answer briefly.'). The constraint has the same shape as the hyperedge constraint \(x_u + x_v + x_w \ge 1\) in the LP-based solution of Volk's 2023B-P3, because the triangles of \(G\) form a 3-uniform hypergraph whose vertices are the edges of \(G\).

Source adjacency. Feige's Weizmann final exam (20 Feb 2019) asks exactly this in Question 1, item 2 ('Write an integer program (IP) representing the K3R problem, in which the variables are \(x_{i,j}\) for every edge'). The homework handouts of the same Feige course contain the three Williamson-Shmoys exercises that this research matched to Volk problems: 5.1 (extended in handout 5 Q2; the NEAR source of 2023A-P3), 5.3 + 5.6 (handout 5 Q3, in the exact (a)/(b)/(c) layout of 2026A-P5; confirmed verbatim) and 6.1 (handout 6 Q1; graded only PLAUSIBLE/NEAR as the source of 2026B-P5). The handouts are derivatives of W&S, and no Volk problem has yet been traced to Feige's exam itself, so the exam is a plausible co-source, not a confirmed one. It is a take-home exam. Its items 1-3 are the short ones (10, 10 and 5 points); items 4 and 5 are open-ended ('Up to 15 points, depending on what you find', 'Up to 10 points'). This problem uses items 2 and 3. Item 1, a strongly polynomial factor-3 algorithm, is listed as a variant under (b).

Probability. About 0.03 for this exact problem (this item's own estimate). The wider families, with the source of each figure: an LP-rounding approximation problem at P5, about 0.28 (the mock-p5 item's estimate); the format research's P4 'LP-based' slot, 0.55, which also covers pure duality problems ('given LP/IP (explain or compute the dual) or relaxation + rounding'), and its P5 Approximation-deck slot (approximation algorithm, SDP/PSD or lattice), 0.50; a from-scratch write-an-IP part, 0.30 from the format research and about 0.35 in the sibling item alt-p4-a. Of the three parts, this one transfers best: any write-an-IP part tests the same skill, one 0/1 variable per decision and one covering constraint per forbidden structure.
parts.sol:
Solution. Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the set of triangles of \(G\). For every edge \(e \in E\) we use a variable \(x_e \in \{0,1\}\) which indicates whether \(e\) is removed, that is, \(x_e = 1\) if and only if \(e \in F\).

\[\begin{array}{lll} \text{minimize} & \sum_{e \in E} w_e x_e & \\ \text{subject to} & x_{uv} + x_{vw} + x_{uw} \ge 1 & \text{for every triangle } \{u,v,w\} \in \mathcal{T} \\ & x_e \in \{0,1\} & \text{for every } e \in E \end{array}\]

Correctness. Sets \(F \subseteq E\) and vectors \(x \in \{0,1\}^E\) are in bijection via \(x_e = 1\) if and only if \(e \in F\), and the objective is exactly \(\sum_{e \in E} w_e x_e = w(F)\). Removing edges cannot create a new triangle, so the triangles of \((V, E \setminus F)\) are exactly the triangles \(\{u,v,w\} \in \mathcal{T}\) none of whose three edges is in \(F\), i.e. with \(x_{uv} = x_{vw} = x_{uw} = 0\). This is exactly the case in which the constraint of \(\{u,v,w\}\) is violated. Hence \(x\) is feasible if and only if \((V, E \setminus F)\) has no triangle, and the optimum of the program equals the optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}\) of the problem.

Size. There are \(|E| \le \binom{n}{2}\) variables and \(|\mathcal{T}| \le \binom{n}{3} = O(n^3)\) triangle constraints, and \(\mathcal{T}\) can be listed in time \(O(n^3)\) by checking every triple of vertices, so the program has polynomial size. (If \(G\) has no triangle there are no covering constraints and the optimum is \(F = \emptyset\).)
parts.srcline: Feige, Approximation algorithms (Weizmann Institute, 2018/19; course page wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~feige/Apx2018/), final exam of 20 February 2019, Question 1 'K3 removal (K3R)', item 2 (IP with a variable \(x_{i,j}\) per edge). The constraint shape comes from Volk 2023B-P3 (the LP-based 'different solution' in the official solution: \(x_u + x_v + x_w \ge 1\) for every hyperedge), and the wording from Volk 2025B-P2(a).

parts.summary: Prove that solving the LP relaxation and removing every edge whose fractional value is at least one third is a 3-approximation.
parts.q: (b) [6 points] We relax the integer program from (a) by replacing the constraints \(x_e \in \{0,1\}\) by \(0 \le x_e \le 1\). Consider the algorithm that solves the relaxation and, given an optimal solution \(x^*\), returns the set \(F = \{e \in E : x^*_e \ge 1/3\}\). Prove that this algorithm is a 3-approximation algorithm for the triangle removal problem.
parts.basis:
Template: threshold \(1/f\) rounding. This is Volk's most repeated approximation problem. It appeared in 2023B-P3 (vertex cover in a 3-uniform hypergraph, 3-approximation, 16 pts; the official solution first gives the greedy algorithm that takes all three vertices of an arbitrary remaining hyperedge, so the chosen hyperedges are disjoint, and then gives this 1/3 rounding as 'A different solution'), 2024B-P5 (the recitation 10 weighted hitting set, threshold \(1/d\), 16 pts), 2025B-P2(b) (set cover with frequency \(f\), 10 pts) and 2026B-P4 (prize-collecting vertex cover, threshold 1/3, 6+12 = 18 pts): 16+16+10+18 = 60 points over 4 exams, the total the coverage research gives for 'LP threshold rounding'. Triangle removal is weighted vertex cover in the 3-uniform hypergraph of triangles, so \(f = 3\) and the proof is 2026B-P4(b) line by line.

Moed C pattern. Moed C problems are siblings of that year's A/B problems applied to a new object (2024C-P2 of 2024B-P4, 2024C-P3 of 2024B-P6, 2025C-P2 of 2025B-P2), so a 1/3-threshold rounding on a new covering problem is a natural sibling of 2026B-P4. Against: 2025C followed 2025B's primal threshold rounding with dual rounding rather than repeating it. The P5 slot may therefore ask for the dual (variant below) or for randomized rounding instead.

Variant (Feige item 2, second half). Write the dual of the relaxation. With \(x_e \le 1\) dropped, which does not change the optimum since weights are non-negative, the dual is \(\max \sum_{T \in \mathcal{T}} y_T\) subject to \(\sum_{T \ni e} y_T \le w_e\) for every \(e \in E\) and \(y \ge 0\): a fractional packing of triangles. A 2025C-P2-style follow-up would ask to show that the edges whose dual constraint is tight in an optimal dual solution remove every triangle and weigh at most \(3\,\mathrm{OPT}\) (W&S §1.4 with \(f = 3\)). This is likely only if no other dual appears on the paper.

Variant (Feige item 1, 10 points there). 'Design a strongly polynomial time algorithm that provides a factor 3 approximation for K3R.' The algorithm of (b), with the LP solved as in class, does not qualify: the ellipsoid method takes a number of steps that grows with the bit length of the weights. (Tardos' algorithm for LPs with a 0/1 constraint matrix would make it strongly polynomial, but it is not part of the course.) With unit weights, the greedy solution of 2023B-P3 carries over: while a triangle is left, remove all three of its edges. The chosen triangles are edge-disjoint, so if there are \(k\) of them then \(\mathrm{OPT} \ge k\) and \(\mathrm{ALG} = 3k\). With weights, use local ratio. Keep residual weights \(r_e\), initially \(r_e = w_e\). While some triangle \(T\) has \(r_e > 0\) on all three of its edges, let \(\varepsilon_T = \min_{e \in T} r_e\) and subtract \(\varepsilon_T\) from the residual weight of each edge of \(T\). Return \(F = \{e : r_e = 0\}\). Every step makes at least one more residual weight 0, so there are at most \(|E|\) steps, each using \(O(n^3)\) comparisons and subtractions. When the loop stops, every triangle has an edge in \(F\). Setting \(y_T = \varepsilon_T\) (and \(y_T = 0\) for triangles never chosen) gives a feasible solution of the dual above, since residual weights stay non-negative, so \(\sum_T y_T \le \mathrm{LPOPT} \le \mathrm{OPT}\). Every \(e \in F\) has \(w_e = \sum_{T \ni e} y_T\), hence \(w(F) = \sum_T y_T\,|T \cap F| \le 3\sum_T y_T \le 3\,\mathrm{OPT}\). (Checked against the exact optimum on 1500 random weighted graphs in scratchpad/k3_localratio_check.py; the worst ratio was exactly 3.) Local ratio and primal-dual proofs are not on the 2026 approximation deck, which has only the unweighted greedy vertex cover, so on Volk's paper this variant is less likely than (b).

Probability. About 0.28 for an LP-rounding approximation at P5 (the mock-p5 item's estimate) and about 0.03 for this problem (this item's own estimate).
parts.sol:
Solution. By (a) the relaxation has polynomially many variables and constraints, so as we have seen in class it can be solved in polynomial time (e.g. by the ellipsoid algorithm). It is feasible (\(x_e = 1\) for all \(e\)) and its objective is non-negative, so an optimal solution \(x^*\) exists. Denote its value by \(\mathrm{LPOPT}\). For every edge let \(x_e = 1\) if \(x^*_e \ge 1/3\) and \(x_e = 0\) otherwise, so that \(F = \{e : x_e = 1\}\).

Feasibility. Let \(\{u,v,w\}\) be a triangle of \(G\). Since \(x^*\) is feasible, \(x^*_{uv} + x^*_{vw} + x^*_{uw} \ge 1\), so at least one of the three values is at least \(1/3\) (otherwise the sum would be smaller than 1). That edge is in \(F\), so \(\{u,v,w\}\) is not a triangle of \((V, E \setminus F)\). Every triangle of \((V, E \setminus F)\) is a triangle of \(G\), hence \((V, E \setminus F)\) contains no triangle.

Cost. For every edge \(e\) it holds that \(x_e \le 3x^*_e\): if \(x_e = 0\) this is true since \(x^*_e \ge 0\), and if \(x_e = 1\) then \(x^*_e \ge 1/3\) by the rounding rule. Since all weights are non-negative,

\[\mathrm{ALG} = \sum_{e \in E} w_e x_e \le 3\sum_{e \in E} w_e x^*_e = 3\,\mathrm{LPOPT} \le 3\,\mathrm{OPT}.\]

The last inequality holds because the program is a relaxation: the 0/1 vector of an optimal set \(F^*\) is a feasible solution of the LP of value \(\mathrm{OPT}\), so \(\mathrm{LPOPT} \le \mathrm{OPT}\).

Running time. Listing the triangles takes \(O(n^3)\), solving the LP takes polynomial time, and rounding takes \(O(|E|)\). This is the vertex cover rounding we saw in class, with the threshold \(1/3\) in place of \(1/2\), because every constraint has three variables.

Remark (not required). The factor 3 cannot be improved for this rounding rule. Take \(G = K_4\) with unit weights. Every edge lies in exactly 2 of the 4 triangles, so summing the 4 constraints gives \(2\sum_e x_e \ge 4\), i.e. \(\mathrm{LPOPT} \ge 2\). Removing two disjoint edges destroys all 4 triangles, so \(\mathrm{OPT} = \mathrm{LPOPT} = 2\). The vector \(x^*_e = 1/3\) for all 6 edges is an optimal LP solution, and rounding it returns all 6 edges, which is \(3\,\mathrm{OPT}\).
parts.srcline: Feige, Weizmann Approximation algorithms final exam (20 Feb 2019), Question 1 item 2 ('Show how to round the linear programming relaxation of this IP so as to get a factor 3 approximation for K3R'). The proof re-skins Volk 2026B-P4(b), 2025B-P2(b) and 2023B-P3 with \(f = 3\), and the approximation deck slides 'Rounding Scheme for VC' / 'Bounding the Approximation Ratio'. Item 1 of the same question (a strongly polynomial factor-3 algorithm, 10 points) is the variant in the basis.

parts.summary: Show with a random bipartition that some triangle-removing edge set has at most half the total weight, and derandomize it by conditional expectations.
parts.q:
(c) [8 points] Prove that for every graph \(G\) there is a set \(F \subseteq E\) such that \((V, E \setminus F)\) contains no triangle and \(w(F) \le \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in E} w_e\). Give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that finds such a set.
(Hint: a bipartite graph contains no triangle.)
parts.basis:
Template: random cut plus derandomization by conditional expectations. The approximation deck proves 'Claim: in every graph \(G\) with \(m\) edges, there’s a cut whose size is at least \(m/2\)' with a random cut, and derandomizes it on the 'Method of Conditional Expectations' slides. Only the random half has been graded so far: 2023A-P3 (Max Triple Cut; the question asks only for 'an efficient algorithm that obtains a 2/3-approximation', and the official solution gives the random 3-partition) and 2026A-P5(a) (a random cut gives 1/4 for Max DiCut). Derandomization is mentioned in one sentence of the 2023A-P3 solution ('This algorithm can be converted to a deterministic algorithm using the conditional expectations method, as seen in class.') and has never been required in a graded part, so the 8 points here would be its first appearance. Here the removed set is the complement of a random cut, and the hint makes feasibility immediate. The coverage research lists conditional expectations among the approximation techniques 2026 has not used, and each Moed C adds 1-2 class topics that its year's A/B skipped.

Source. Feige's final exam, Question 1 item 3, almost word for word: 'Show that every graph contains a solution \(E'\) of cost \(\sum_{e \in E'} w(e) \le \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in E} w(e)\). Give a deterministic algorithm that finds such a solution. (... the hint that bipartite graphs contain no \(K_3\).)'

Variants. W&S Exercise 5.2: the greedy Max-Cut algorithm (put vertex \(k\) on the side that cuts more of its edges to \(1, \dots, k-1\)) is a 1/2-approximation and is the conditional-expectations derandomization. Feige handout 5 Q2(c)(d): a uniformly random balanced \(k\)-partition cuts each edge with probability \(1 - \frac{n/k - 1}{n - 1} \ge \frac{k-1}{k}\), plus a deterministic version (about 0.03, a Moed C re-skin of 2023A-P3).

Probability. About 0.03 for this problem (this item's own estimate). The coverage research rates 'An approximation problem with a technique 2026 did not use (Goemans-Williamson rounding, conditional expectations, greedy, or LLL)' as Medium.
parts.sol:
Existence. Put every vertex in a set \(U\) with probability \(1/2\), independently of all other vertices, and let \(W = V \setminus U\). Let \(F\) be the set of edges whose two endpoints are on the same side (both in \(U\) or both in \(W\)).

\(F\) is always a solution. Every edge of \(E \setminus F\) goes between \(U\) and \(W\), so \((V, E \setminus F)\) is bipartite with sides \(U, W\). It contains no triangle: among any three vertices \(u,v,w\), two lie on the same side (pigeonhole), and the edge between them, if it exists in \(G\), is in \(F\). This holds for every outcome, including \(U = \emptyset\) or \(W = \emptyset\).

Expected weight. For every edge \(e = (u,v) \in E\), let \(X_e\) be an indicator random variable for the event that \(u\) and \(v\) are on the same side. Then

\[\mathbb{E}[X_e] = \Pr[u,v \in U] + \Pr[u,v \in W] = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}.\]

Since \(w(F) = \sum_{e \in E} w_e X_e\), by linearity of expectation

\[\mathbb{E}[w(F)] = \sum_{e \in E} w_e \, \mathbb{E}[X_e] = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in E} w_e.\]

A random variable cannot always be larger than its expectation, so some choice of \(U\) gives a solution \(F\) with \(w(F) \le \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in E} w_e\) (the probabilistic method).

Deterministic algorithm (method of conditional expectations, as seen in class for Max-Cut). Let \(v_1, \dots, v_n\) be the vertices, and suppose \(v_1, \dots, v_i\) have already been assigned to \(U\) or \(W\). Let \(S_i\) be the set of edges whose two endpoints are both among \(v_1, \dots, v_i\) and on the same side, and let \(R_i\) be the set of edges with at least one endpoint not yet assigned. The conditional expectation of \(w(F)\) given these choices is

\[\Phi_i = \sum_{e \in S_i} w_e + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in R_i} w_e,\]

because an edge with both endpoints assigned is in \(F\) with probability 1 or 0, and an edge with an unassigned endpoint is in \(F\) with probability exactly \(1/2\), as before. So \(\Phi_i\) can be computed in polynomial time. We have \(\Phi_0 = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in E} w_e\), and \(\Phi_n = w(F)\) for the final partition. Since \(v_{i+1}\) goes to each side with probability \(1/2\), \(\Phi_i = \frac{1}{2}\Phi^{(U)}_{i+1} + \frac{1}{2}\Phi^{(W)}_{i+1}\), where \(\Phi^{(U)}_{i+1}\) and \(\Phi^{(W)}_{i+1}\) are the conditional expectations after also placing \(v_{i+1}\) in \(U\) or in \(W\). Hence one of the two is at most \(\Phi_i\), and we place \(v_{i+1}\) on that side. The invariant \(\Phi_i \le \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in E} w_e\) holds for every \(i\), so at the end \(w(F) = \Phi_n \le \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in E} w_e\), and by the argument above \((V, E \setminus F)\) is bipartite and hence triangle-free.

Explicit form and running time. Let \(a_U\) (resp. \(a_W\)) be the total weight of the edges from \(v_{i+1}\) to the already assigned vertices in \(U\) (resp. \(W\)). Only these edges change their contribution, from \(w_e/2\) to \(w_e\) or 0, so

\[\Phi^{(U)}_{i+1} - \Phi_i = a_U - \frac{a_U + a_W}{2} = \frac{a_U - a_W}{2}, \qquad \Phi^{(W)}_{i+1} - \Phi_i = \frac{a_W - a_U}{2}.\]

So the algorithm places \(v_{i+1}\) in \(U\) if \(a_U \le a_W\) and in \(W\) otherwise: each vertex goes to the side to which its already assigned neighbours are connected with smaller total weight. One can also check this directly. When \(v_{i+1}\) is placed, \(F\) gains \(\min\{a_U, a_W\} \le \frac{a_U + a_W}{2}\), and every edge is counted in exactly one step (when its later endpoint is placed), so \(w(F) \le \frac{1}{2}\sum_{e \in E} w_e\). With adjacency lists each edge is inspected twice, so the running time is \(O(|V| + |E|)\).
parts.srcline: Feige, Weizmann Approximation algorithms final exam (20 Feb 2019), Question 1 item 3 (5 points there, with the bipartite hint). The technique comes from the Volk approximation deck ('Approximating Max Cut', 'Method of Conditional Expectations'), Volk 2023A-P3 and 2026A-P5(a), and Williamson & Shmoys, Exercise 5.2, pp. 135-136 (greedy Max-Cut equals derandomization by conditional expectations).

items.src: Lattices / LLL (Approximation deck), 20 pts (6+8+6): LLL'82 Prop. 1.6 (the induction in its proof, then (1.7), then (1.8)) = Galbraith Lemma 17.2.8(1),(3) + Thm 17.2.12(4) = Regev TAU HW2 4(b) (the j=i case of (1.7)), 4(d) ((1.7)) and 4(c) ((1.8)); siblings of 2024C-P5 = (1.9), which appears in all three sources, and which one Volk used is not established
items.stem:
Problem 5 (6+8+6=20 points)

Let \(L\) be a lattice and let \(b_1,\dots,b_n\) be a reduced basis for \(L\), as computed by the LLL algorithm. As in class, \(\tilde{b}_1,\dots,\tilde{b}_n\) denote the Gram-Schmidt vectors of the basis: \(\tilde{b}_1=b_1\) and \(\tilde{b}_i=b_i-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\mu_{i,j}\tilde{b}_j\), where \(\mu_{i,j}=\frac{\langle b_i,\tilde{b}_j\rangle}{\langle\tilde{b}_j,\tilde{b}_j\rangle}\). Recall that the basis is reduced if

  • \(|\mu_{i,j}|\le\frac{1}{2}\) for every \(1\le j\lt i\le n\), and
  • \(\|\tilde{b}_{i+1}+\mu_{i+1,i}\tilde{b}_i\|^2\ge\frac{3}{4}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\) for every \(1\le i\le n-1\).

Reminder (the columns of the matrix are \(b_1,\dots,b_n\)):

\[\det L=\left|\det\begin{pmatrix} b_1 & b_2 & \cdots & b_n\end{pmatrix}\right|=\|\tilde{b}_1\|\cdot\|\tilde{b}_2\|\cdots\|\tilde{b}_n\|.\]

You may use any claim presented in class.

parts.summary: Prove that in an LLL-reduced basis the squared Gram-Schmidt lengths shrink by at most a factor 2 per step: ||b~_j||^2 is at most 2^(i-j) ||b~_i||^2 whenever j is at most i.
parts.q:
(a) (6 points) Prove that for every \(1\le j\le i\le n\),

\[\|\tilde{b}_j\|^2\le 2^{i-j}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2.\]
parts.basis:
• Source adjacency (the exact origin is not established). Parts (a), (b) and (c) are the three steps of the proof of Proposition 1.6 in Lenstra, Lenstra and Lovász (1982): first the induction \(|b_j^*|^2\le 2^{i-j}|b_i^*|^2\) (this part), then (1.7) (part (b)), then (1.8) (part (c)). Galbraith, Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography, has the same three statements as Lemma 17.2.8(1), Lemma 17.2.8(3) and Theorem 17.2.12(4). Regev's TAU homework has (1.7) and (1.8) as HW2 Problem 4(b)/(d) and 4(c). All three sources also contain Volk's 2024C-P5, with the same inequality (VERBATIM in content, not in wording). 2024C-P5 reads "Let \(L\) be a lattice and let \(b_1,\dots,b_n\) a reduced basis for \(L\) as computed by the LLL algorithm. Prove that \(\|b_1\|\le 2^{\frac{n-1}{4}}(\det L)^{1/n}\)". LLL'82 reads "Let \(b_1,\dots,b_n\) be a reduced basis for a lattice \(L\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)... (1.9) \(|b_1|\le 2^{(n-1)/4}d(L)^{1/n}\)". Galbraith's Theorem 17.2.12(5) is \(\|b_1\|\le 2^{(n-1)/4}\det(L)^{1/n}\). Regev's Problem 4(a) reads "Show that a δ-LLL reduced basis \(b_1,\dots,b_n\) of a lattice Λ with δ = 3/4 satisfies... (a) \(\|b_1\|\le 2^{(n-1)/4}(\det\Lambda)^{1/n}\)". Which of the three Volk used is not established. Evidence for LLL'82: the wording ("a reduced basis for \(L\)", the letter \(L\)), and the deck's lattice section follows LLL'82 §1, with the same definition of "reduced" and the same constant \(\frac{3}{4}\). The printed "Reminder" \(\det L=\prod_i\|\tilde{b}_i\|\) is a step in both the LLL'82 proof and Galbraith's. The Regev link is PLAUSIBLE: it is a TAU course, and Volk's exams (the 2024C-P5 reminder, the 2026B-1d solution) write \(\tilde{b}_i\) as Regev does, where LLL'82 and Galbraith write \(b_i^*\). Nothing shows that Volk took 2024C-P5 from it. None of these statements except (1.9) has appeared on his exams.
  • Moed C pattern. Every Moed C so far has a problem that re-proves a lecture theorem: 2024C-P5 (the LLL bound), 2024C-P6 (a strong-duality case via Farkas) and 2025C-P3 (the random-walk proof redone for a lazy walk). This part is the chain from the lecture proof of "Short Vector in Reduced Basis" (Approximation deck: \(\|\tilde{b}_n\|^2\ge\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{b}_{n-1}\|^2\ge\cdots\ge\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\|\tilde{b}_1\|^2\)), started at \(\tilde{b}_j\) instead of \(\tilde{b}_1\). The official 2024C-P5 solution opens the same way: "We proved that for a reduced basis, \(\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\ge\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{b}_{i-1}\|^2\). By induction on \(i\)...".
  • Tools. Every step uses a claim from the deck: \(\|\tilde{b}_{i+1}\|^2\ge\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\), the orthogonal expansion from "Lower bound on shortest vector", \(\det L=\prod_i\|\tilde{b}_i\|\) and \(\|\tilde{b}_i\|\le\|b_i\|\). No outside material is needed.
  • Probability. This problem (parts (a)-(c)) or a near variant (the general-\(\delta\) lemma at the end of the solution to (c), or a re-proof of \(\|b_1\|\le 2^{(n-1)/2}\lambda_1(L)\)): 0.025. Any written LLL or lattice problem on 2026C: 0.10.
parts.sol:
As we have seen in class, in a reduced basis \(\|\tilde{b}_{i+1}\|^2\ge\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\) for every \(1\le i\le n-1\). For completeness, here is the argument. The vectors \(\tilde{b}_{i+1}\) and \(\tilde{b}_i\) are orthogonal, so the second property of a reduced basis says

\[\|\tilde{b}_{i+1}\|^2+\mu_{i+1,i}^2\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2=\|\tilde{b}_{i+1}+\mu_{i+1,i}\tilde{b}_i\|^2\ge\frac{3}{4}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2.\]

By the first property \(\mu_{i+1,i}^2\le\frac{1}{4}\), so \(\|\tilde{b}_{i+1}\|^2\ge\left(\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{4}\right)\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2=\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\). Equivalently, \(\|\tilde{b}_k\|^2\le 2\|\tilde{b}_{k+1}\|^2\) for every \(1\le k\le n-1\).

We prove the claim by induction on \(i-j\). If \(i=j\), both sides equal \(\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\). If \(j\lt i\), then \(j\le i-1\) and \((i-1)-j\lt i-j\). So by the induction hypothesis for the pair \(j,i-1\), and by the inequality above with \(k=i-1\),

\[\|\tilde{b}_j\|^2\le 2^{i-1-j}\|\tilde{b}_{i-1}\|^2\le 2^{i-1-j}\cdot 2\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2=2^{i-j}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2.\]

This is the class chain started at \(\tilde{b}_j\) instead of \(\tilde{b}_1\): \(\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\ge\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{b}_{i-1}\|^2\ge\frac{1}{4}\|\tilde{b}_{i-2}\|^2\ge\cdots\ge\frac{1}{2^{i-j}}\|\tilde{b}_j\|^2\).
parts.srcline: Lenstra, Lenstra and Lovász, Factoring polynomials with rational coefficients, Math. Ann. 261 (1982), proof of Proposition 1.6 (https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01457454). From (1.5) and (1.4), \(|b_i^*|^2\ge\frac{1}{2}|b_{i-1}^*|^2\) for \(1\lt i\le n\), "so by induction" \(|b_j^*|^2\le 2^{i-j}|b_i^*|^2\) for \(1\le j\le i\le n\). Local OCR copy:, where the \(\le\) signs are garbled. The same statement is Galbraith, Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography v2.0, Lemma 17.2.8(1), p.370: "\(B_j\le 2^{i-j}B_i\) for \(1\le j\le i\le n\)", with \(B_i=\|b_i^*\|^2\) (http://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~sgal018/crypto-book/crypto-book.html). Regev's homework has no separate item for it. In the course it is the chain in the proof of "Short Vector in Reduced Basis" (Approximation deck).

parts.summary: Prove that ||b_i||^2 is at most 2^(i-1) ||b~_i||^2 for every i, and conclude the same bound for ||b_j||^2 whenever j is at most i (LLL'82 (1.7)).
parts.q:
(b) (8 points) Prove that for every \(1\le i\le n\),

\[\|b_i\|^2\le 2^{i-1}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2,\]

and conclude that \(\|b_j\|^2\le 2^{i-1}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\) for every \(1\le j\le i\le n\).
parts.basis:
• Lineage. This is LLL'82 (1.7), "\(|b_j|^2\le 2^{i-1}|b_i^*|^2\) for \(1\le j\le i\le n\)". Its proof in the paper first does the case \(j=i\), through the intermediate line \(|b_i|^2\le\left(1+\frac{1}{4}(2^i-2)\right)|b_i^*|^2\le 2^{i-1}|b_i^*|^2\), and this part asks for the same two steps. The case \(j=i\) is Regev's HW2 Problem 4(b), "For any \(1\le i\le n\), \(\|b_i\|\le 2^{(i-1)/2}\|\tilde{b}_i\|\)". The general case is 4(d), "For any \(1\le i\le j\le n\), \(\|b_i\|\le 2^{(j-1)/2}\|\tilde{b}_j\|\)", with the names \(i\) and \(j\) swapped. In Galbraith the two steps are Lemma 17.2.8(2), \(\|b_i\|^2\le\left(\frac{1}{2}+2^{i-2}\right)B_i\), and Lemma 17.2.8(3). Volk has not used any of them.
  • Moed C pattern, continued. The lecture lemma gives \(\|b_1\|^2\le 2^{i-1}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\) (deck). This part proves the same bound for every \(b_j\) with \(j\le i\). It is the same kind of one-parameter re-proof as 2025C-P3, which redid the lecture random-walk proof for a lazy walk.
  • Promotion signal (weaker this year). In 2024 Moed A had a Gram-Schmidt T/F, 2024A-1c: "There exists a polynomial time algorithm that given \(v_1,\dots,v_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) finds an orthonormal basis for the subspace spanned by \(v_1,\dots,v_k\)". It sits in the lattice section of the deck but does not mention lattices. Moed B had a lattice T/F (2024B-1c), and Moed C had the 14-point LLL problem 2024C-P5. So the 2024 "promotion" of lattices holds only if 2024A-1c is counted loosely, as a Gram-Schmidt/lattice item. In 2026 lattices appear only in 2026B-1d (the lattice spanned by \((1,1)\) and \((3,1)\)), not in 2026A. The topic asked as T/F in both 2026 sittings is traces and the characteristic polynomial, so the promotion argument favours that topic.
  • Coverage. The mock P5 already covers the SDP and Goemans-Williamson family. Without this alternate the lattice family would be uncovered. Gram-Schmidt/lattice items were worth 26 points in 2024: 6 for 2024A-1c, 6 for 2024B-1c and 14 for 2024C-P5. Counting only the items that mention lattices, the total is 20.
parts.sol:
The case \(j=i\). By the definition of the Gram-Schmidt vectors, \(b_i=\tilde{b}_i+\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\mu_{i,k}\tilde{b}_k\). The vectors \(\tilde{b}_1,\dots,\tilde{b}_i\) are pairwise orthogonal, so when we expand \(\langle b_i,b_i\rangle\), every mixed term \(\langle\tilde{b}_k,\tilde{b}_l\rangle\) with \(k\ne l\) vanishes. This is the same computation as in the class proofs that \(\|v\|\ge\min_i\|\tilde{b}_i\|\) and that \(\|\tilde{b}_i\|\le\|b_i\|\). Hence

\[\|b_i\|^2=\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2+\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\mu_{i,k}^2\|\tilde{b}_k\|^2.\]

By the first property of a reduced basis \(\mu_{i,k}^2\le\frac{1}{4}\), and by part (a) \(\|\tilde{b}_k\|^2\le 2^{i-k}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\) for every \(k\le i\). Therefore

\[\|b_i\|^2\le\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2+\frac{1}{4}\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}2^{i-k}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2=\left(1+\frac{2^i-2}{4}\right)\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2=\frac{2^i+2}{4}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2,\]

because \(\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}2^{i-k}=\sum_{m=1}^{i-1}2^m=2^i-2\). Finally, \(\frac{2^i+2}{4}\le 2^{i-1}\) is equivalent to \(2^i+2\le 2^{i+1}\), that is, to \(2\le 2^i\), which holds for every \(i\ge 1\). So \(\|b_i\|^2\le 2^{i-1}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\). For \(i=1\) both sides are equal, since \(b_1=\tilde{b}_1\).

The general case. Let \(1\le j\le i\le n\). By the case just proved (for the index \(j\)) and by part (a),

\[\|b_j\|^2\le 2^{j-1}\|\tilde{b}_j\|^2\le 2^{j-1}\cdot 2^{i-j}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2=2^{i-1}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2.\]

Note. The expansion needs orthogonality, and the triangle inequality is not enough. For \(i=2\), the triangle inequality and part (a) only give \(\|b_2\|\le\|\tilde{b}_2\|+\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{b}_1\|\le\left(1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\|\tilde{b}_2\|\approx 1.71\|\tilde{b}_2\|\), which is weaker than the required \(\sqrt{2}\|\tilde{b}_2\|\approx 1.41\|\tilde{b}_2\|\).
parts.srcline: Lenstra, Lenstra and Lovász (1982), Proposition 1.6, (1.7): "\(|b_j|^2\le 2^{i-1}|b_i^*|^2\) for \(1\le j\le i\le n\)". Its proof: \(|b_i|^2=|b_i^*|^2+\sum_{j\lt i}\mu_{ij}^2|b_j^*|^2\le\left(1+\frac{1}{4}(2^i-2)\right)|b_i^*|^2\le 2^{i-1}|b_i^*|^2\), and then \(|b_j|^2\le 2^{j-1}|b_j^*|^2\le 2^{i-1}|b_i^*|^2\). Regev, Lattices in Computer Science, Tel Aviv University, Fall 2009, Homework 2, Problem 4(b) (the case \(j=i\)) and Problem 4(d) (the general case) (https://cims.nyu.edu/~regev/teaching/lattices_fall_2009/homework2.pdf). Parts 4(a)-(f) are identical in the Fall 2004 Homework 2; only 4(g) differs. Galbraith v2.0, Lemma 17.2.8(2),(3), pp.370-371.

parts.summary: Prove that the orthogonality defect of an LLL-reduced basis, the product of the basis lengths divided by det L, is at most 2^(n(n-1)/4).
parts.q:
(c) (6 points) Prove that

\[\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|b_i\|\le 2^{n(n-1)/4}\det L.\]

(The ratio \(\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|b_i\|}{\det L}\) is called the orthogonality defect of the basis. It equals 1 when the basis is orthogonal, so this shows that an LLL-reduced basis is not far from orthogonal.)
parts.basis:
• Lineage. This is the right-hand inequality of LLL'82 (1.8), \(d(L)\le\prod_{i=1}^{n}|b_i|\le 2^{n(n-1)/4}d(L)\). The same two-sided statement is Galbraith's Theorem 17.2.12(4), printed next to 17.2.12(5), which is 2024C-P5. It is also Regev's HW2 Problem 4(c), "\(\Pi\|b_i\|\le 2^{n(n-1)/4}\det\Lambda\)", with his remark that this ratio is the orthogonality defect and that Hadamard's inequality makes it at least 1. The footprint research named (1.8) as the natural unused Moed C re-proof. Volk has not used it.
  • Why it is chained to (a) and (b). Given (b) and the class claim \(\det L=\prod_i\|\tilde{b}_i\|\), part (c) takes three lines. Volk builds his parts so that one feeds the next: in 2026B-P5 part (c) says "Use part (b) in order to prove the weak duality theorem", and in the 2026B-P4(b) solution "The first equality is exactly part (a)". The proof of 2024C-P5 was also a product of per-index inequalities.
  • Changed-parameter variant. The remark after (1.9) in LLL'82 says that if \(\frac{3}{4}\) is replaced by \(\delta\in(\frac{1}{4},1)\), then the powers of 2 are replaced by the same powers of \(\frac{4}{4\delta-1}\). This is the kind of change Volk made in 2025C-P3, where he redid the lecture random-walk proof for a lazy walk. The variant is solved at the end of the model solution.
  • Probability. The same as part (a): 0.025 for this problem or a near variant, and 0.10 for any written lattice problem. If lattices come back only as a T/F item, the one-line facts used here are natural candidates: \(\|\tilde{b}_i\|\le\|b_i\|\), an orthogonality defect of at least 1, and \(\det L\) not depending on the basis.
parts.sol:
As we have seen in class (this is also the reminder), \(\det L=\|\tilde{b}_1\|\cdot\|\tilde{b}_2\|\cdots\|\tilde{b}_n\|\). The reason is that the matrix with columns \(b_1,\dots,b_n\) equals the matrix with columns \(\tilde{b}_1,\dots,\tilde{b}_n\) times an upper triangular matrix with 1 on the diagonal, and the \(\tilde{b}_i\) are orthogonal.

By part (b) with \(j=i\), after taking square roots (both sides are non-negative), \(\|b_i\|\le 2^{(i-1)/2}\|\tilde{b}_i\|\) for every \(1\le i\le n\). We multiply these \(n\) inequalities between non-negative numbers:

\[\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|b_i\|\le\prod_{i=1}^{n}2^{\frac{i-1}{2}}\|\tilde{b}_i\|=2^{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(i-1)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|\tilde{b}_i\|=2^{\frac{n(n-1)}{4}}\det L,\]

since \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(i-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\).

Remark (the other direction, in case it is asked). As we have seen in class, \(\|\tilde{b}_i\|\le\|b_i\|\) for every \(i\). This also follows from the identity at the start of the solution to (b). Hence \(\det L=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|\tilde{b}_i\|\le\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|b_i\|\) for every basis of \(L\), reduced or not; this is Hadamard's inequality. So for an LLL-reduced basis,

\[1\le\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|b_i\|}{\det L}\le 2^{\frac{n(n-1)}{4}}.\]

Variant to practise (the lecture lemma with a changed parameter). Let \(\frac{1}{4}\lt\delta\lt 1\), and call the basis \(\delta\)-reduced if \(|\mu_{i,j}|\le\frac{1}{2}\) for all \(j\lt i\) and \(\|\tilde{b}_{i+1}+\mu_{i+1,i}\tilde{b}_i\|^2\ge\delta\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\) for all \(i\). Prove that \(\|b_1\|\le\left(\frac{4}{4\delta-1}\right)^{(n-1)/2}\|v\|\) for every non-zero \(v\in L\).

Solution. Exactly as in part (a), \(\|\tilde{b}_{i+1}\|^2\ge(\delta-\mu_{i+1,i}^2)\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\ge\left(\delta-\frac{1}{4}\right)\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2=\frac{1}{\alpha}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\), where \(\alpha=\frac{4}{4\delta-1}\). Since \(\delta\lt 1\), we have \(\alpha\gt\frac{4}{3}\gt 1\). By induction, \(\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\ge\alpha^{-(i-1)}\|\tilde{b}_1\|^2\ge\alpha^{-(n-1)}\|b_1\|^2\) for every \(i\), so \(\|b_1\|^2\le\alpha^{n-1}\min_i\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\). As we have seen in class, every non-zero \(v\in L\) satisfies \(\|v\|\ge\min_i\|\tilde{b}_i\|\) (the proof in class never used that \(v\) is a shortest vector). Hence \(\|b_1\|^2\le\alpha^{n-1}\|v\|^2\), that is, \(\|b_1\|\le\left(\frac{4}{4\delta-1}\right)^{(n-1)/2}\|v\|\). For \(\delta=\frac{3}{4}\) we get \(\alpha=2\), which is the bound \(2^{(n-1)/2}\) from class.

The same substitution works in (a), (b) and (c); this is the remark after (1.9) in LLL'82. Part (a) becomes \(\|\tilde{b}_j\|^2\le\alpha^{i-j}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\), with the same induction. In part (b), since \(\sum_{m=1}^{i-1}\alpha^m=\frac{\alpha(\alpha^{i-1}-1)}{\alpha-1}\), the sum becomes \(\|b_i\|^2\le\left(1+\frac{\alpha(\alpha^{i-1}-1)}{4(\alpha-1)}\right)\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\), and

\[\alpha^{i-1}-1-\frac{\alpha(\alpha^{i-1}-1)}{4(\alpha-1)}=(\alpha^{i-1}-1)\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{4(\alpha-1)}\right)\ge 0\]

because \(\alpha^{i-1}\ge 1\) and \(\alpha\ge\frac{4}{3}\), that is, \(4(\alpha-1)\ge\alpha\). So \(\|b_i\|^2\le\alpha^{i-1}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\), hence \(\|b_j\|^2\le\alpha^{j-1}\alpha^{i-j}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2=\alpha^{i-1}\|\tilde{b}_i\|^2\) for \(j\le i\). Part (c) becomes \(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|b_i\|\le\alpha^{n(n-1)/4}\det L\).
parts.srcline: Regev, Lattices in Computer Science (TAU, Fall 2009; parts 4(a)-(f) are identical in Fall 2004), Homework 2, Problem 4(c): "\(\Pi\|b_i\|\le 2^{n(n-1)/4}\det\Lambda\)", with the orthogonality-defect remark. It is also LLL'82 (1.8), the right-hand inequality; the left-hand inequality is Hadamard's inequality (1.10). Galbraith v2.0, Theorem 17.2.12(4), p.372: "\(\det(L)\le\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|b_i\|\le 2^{n(n-1)/4}\det(L)\)" (proof). The general-\(\delta\) variant is the remark after (1.9): "the powers of 2... must be replaced by the same powers of \(\frac{4}{4y-1}\)".

sections.title: True/false pool — 12 more statements in his style
sections.blurb: Each statement is a one-line twist on a specific slide or textbook exercise, which is how 39 of his 40 past T/F items were built. Aim for a one-line justification under two minutes each.

items.src: T/F pool for slot P1(a), 4 items x 7 pts: LP deck duality cases, simplex reduced costs, vertices, and the Approx deck Max-Cut IP; lineage hw2025 Set 4 P3(a)/2024C-P6/hw2026 s3-Q5, B&T Thm 3.1(b)/2024A-1d/2025B-P3, 2024B-1b to 2026A-1a, 2026A-P5(b)
items.stem:
Problem 1 (4×7=28 points), candidate items for slot (a). For each of the following statements, write whether they are true or false, and briefly explain your answer.

(Pool: each statement below is a stand-alone 7-point item. Throughout, for \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(b \in \mathbb{R}^m\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}^n\), a linear program in standard form is minimize \(c^T x\) subject to \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\), as in class.)

parts.summary: If the standard-form primal is infeasible then its dual is unbounded: false, since both can be infeasible.
parts.q:
Let (P) and (D) be the following pair of linear programs, where \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(b \in \mathbb{R}^m\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[ \begin{array}{ll} \text{minimize} & c^T x \\ \text{subject to} & Ax = b,\ x \ge 0 \\ (P) & \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{ll} \text{maximize} & b^T y \\ \text{subject to} & A^T y \le c \\ (D) & \end{array} \]

If (P) is infeasible, then (D) is unbounded.
parts.basis:
Lineage. Volk's duality family: 2023B-1a (bounded non-empty primal implies equal optima, True), 2024A-1a (both feasible but the primal optimum strictly larger, False), then the free-response proof 2024C-P6 ‘if (P) is infeasible and (D) is feasible, then (D) is unbounded’. That problem was already Problem 3(a) of the homework Problem Set 4 filed in the corpus as hw2025 (its solution file is headed ‘Spring Semester, 2024&rsquo), and the official 2024C solution repeats the homework solution almost word for word. It was then recycled as hw2026 Set 3 Q5(a) with the same (P)/(D) display. So the chain is homework → 2024C-P6 → hw2026. The T/F form of this family has not appeared since 2024A. This item is that proof statement with the hypothesis ‘(D) is feasible’ dropped. Dropping a hypothesis is one of his standard T/F traps: 2024A-1b (PSD from \(\det A \ge 0\) alone, without the other principal minors), 2024C-1c (BPP without \(\alpha < \beta\)), 2026A-1b (Schwartz-Zippel without the product set).

Slide. The LP deck's ‘Strong Duality’ slide lists ‘Easier cases: 1. (P) and (D) infeasible 2. (P) infeasible, (D) unbounded 3. (D) infeasible, (P) unbounded’. The item merges cases 1 and 2: it claims that an infeasible (P) always falls into case 2. The T/F research's list of lecture claims that were never examined includes ‘both primal and dual infeasible’.

Slot. Slot (a) was an LP item in 7 of Volk's 10 exams (exceptions 2025A and 2025B; 2025C put it in (d)), including both 2026 exams. The T/F answer key is about 3T/1F, and 4 of the 11 LP items were False.

Probability. About 0.05 for this exact item. It is the strongest of the four because it has the longest lineage (slide, two homework sets, 2024C-P6). The four pool items together have about 0.165 (0.05 + 0.045 + 0.04 + 0.03). Adding the mock exam's ellipsoid item (about 0.06) gives about 0.225. These are probabilities that the item appears in the 2026C T/F block in any slot. Item (d) is at least as likely to sit in slot (d) as in slot (a), so the share of slot (a) itself is closer to 0.15 for the pool and 0.21 with the mock's item.

Variants for the same slot. ‘It is possible that both (P) and (D) are infeasible’: True, with the same example. ‘The dual of the dual is the primal’: True, stated on the deck's ‘Duality’ slide. Write (D) in standard form with \(y = y^+ - y^-\) and a slack \(s\). Its dual forces \(Aw = -b\), \(w \le 0\), and the substitution \(x = -w\) gives back (P).
parts.sol:
False. It is possible that both (P) and (D) are infeasible (this is one of the ‘easier cases’ of the strong duality theorem listed in class). For example, take \(m = n = 1\), \(A = (0)\), \(b = 1\), \(c = -1\). Then (P) requires \(0 \cdot x = 1\), so it is infeasible, and (D) requires \(0 \cdot y \le -1\), so it is infeasible as well. In particular (D) is not unbounded: an unbounded program must have feasible solutions of arbitrarily large value.

(If one insists that \(A\) have full row rank, take \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), \(b = -1\), \(c = (0, -1)^T\): (P) forces \(x_1 = -1 < 0\), and (D) contains the constraint \(0 \cdot y \le -1\).)

The statement becomes true if we add the hypothesis that (D) is feasible, as we proved in the homework: by Farkas' lemma there is \(y'\) with \(A^T y' \ge 0\) and \(b^T y' < 0\), and for a feasible \(y\) of (D) the points \(y - \lambda y'\), \(\lambda > 0\), are feasible with objective value \(b^T y - \lambda b^T y' \to \infty\).
parts.srcline: LP deck, ‘Strong Duality’ slide (LP lecture deck): ‘Easier cases: 1. (P) and (D) infeasible 2. (P) infeasible, (D) unbounded 3. (D) infeasible, (P) unbounded’. Goemans' LP notes (the deck's reading), p.LP-16: ‘We should point out however that both the primal and the dual might be infeasible.’ The item drops the hypothesis ‘(D) is feasible’ from 2024C Problem 6 (2024C official solution). The same proof is Problem 3(a) of hw2025 Problem Set 4 (2025 homework 4 solution: ‘Let y be a feasible solution for (D). Since (P) is infeasible, by the version Farkas Lemma from Problem 1, there’s y′ such that (y&prime)TA ≥ 0 and (y&prime)Tb < 0... hence (D) is unbounded&rsquo), and again hw2026 Set 3 Q5(a) (2026 homework 3 solution).

parts.summary: A negative reduced cost at a basic feasible solution rules out optimality: false, because of degeneracy.
parts.q: Let (P) be a linear program in standard form, minimize \(c^T x\) subject to \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\). Let \(z\) be a basic feasible solution of (P) with a basis \(B\), and let \(\tilde{c}_N\) be the reduced cost vector corresponding to \(z\) and the basis \(B\). If some entry of \(\tilde{c}_N\) is strictly negative, then \(z\) is not an optimal solution of (P).
parts.basis:
Direct source (NEAR). Bertsimas-Tsitsiklis Theorem 3.1(b), Section 3.1: ‘If x is optimal and nondegenerate, then \(\bar{c} \ge 0\)’. Its contrapositive reads: if \(x\) is nondegenerate and some reduced cost is negative, then \(x\) is not optimal. The item is exactly this contrapositive with ‘nondegenerate’ dropped, which is his drop-a-hypothesis trap (2024A-1b, 2024C-1c, 2026A-1b). B&T is already a verified source for this family: 2024A-1d is B&T Ex 3.6(a), and 2023A-1a is close to B&T Ex 3.18(a).

Lineage. The reduced-cost family: 2024A-1d (‘if in the vector \(\tilde{c}_N\) all entries are strictly positive, then \(z\) is the unique optimal solution’, True; this is Bertsimas-Tsitsiklis Ex 3.6(a)) and 2025B-P3 (prove that \(\tilde{c}_N \ge 0\) implies optimality, 16 points). The remaining natural item is the converse direction. The converse is false without non-degeneracy, which is exactly why B&T Ex 3.6(b) carries the hypothesis ‘and is nondegenerate’. Degeneracy was already his trap in 2023A-1a (can the simplex move to a new vertex at equal cost?), an item traced to B&T Ex 3.18(a) and to Goemans p.LP-8. A closer ancestor is the homework: hw2025 Problem Set 4, Problem 2 proves that Bland’s rule cannot cycle. In a cycle a variable \(s\) enters the basis with \(\tilde{c}_s < 0\) while the ‘fickle’ variables ‘remain 0 throughout the process’, so the pivot does not move the vertex or lower the cost. That is the same phenomenon as this item.

Slide. The simplex slide says ‘If there's \(j \in N\) such that \(\tilde{c}_j < 0\), we can reduce the cost by increasing \(x_j\)’. The deck assumes non-degeneracy only afterwards (‘Suppose \(x_i > 0\) for all \(i \in B\). We say \(x\) is non-degenerate&rsquo) and names the failure on the ‘Issues with the Simplex Method’ slide: ‘In this case we can't increase \(x_j\). We call such solutions degenerate’. That is a slide claim with a hidden hypothesis, the kind of claim Volk turns into a False item (see 2026B-1a, feasible centre assumed optimal).

Probability. About 0.045. The wording copies 2024A-1d (‘a basic feasible solution with a basis \(B\)’, ‘the reduced cost vector corresponding to&rsquo), so it is cheap for him to write. Here ‘and the basis \(B\)’ is added, because a degenerate \(z\) has several bases with different vectors \(\tilde{c}_N\), and the item must say which one is meant. It is slightly below item (a) because 2025B-P3 already covered this slide in 2025.
parts.sol:
False. As we saw in class, every feasible \(x\) satisfies \(c^T x = c_B^T A_B^{-1} b + \tilde{c}_N^T x_N\), so \(\tilde{c}_j < 0\) means the cost goes down if we increase \(x_j\). But if \(z\) is degenerate (some basic variable is \(0\)), it may be impossible to increase \(x_j\) at all while staying feasible.

Counterexample: minimize \(-x_1\) subject to \(x_1 + x_2 = 0\), \(x_1, x_2 \ge 0\). The only feasible point is \(z = (0, 0)\), so \(z\) is optimal. With the basis \(B = \{2\}\) we have \(A_B = (1)\), \(z_B = A_B^{-1} b = 0\), \(z_N = z_1 = 0\), so \(z\) is a basic feasible solution for \(B\), and

\[ \tilde{c}_1 = c_1 - c_B^T A_B^{-1} A_1 = -1 - 0 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = -1 < 0. \]

Note that \(\tilde{c}_N\) depends on the basis \(B\) and not only on the vertex \(z\). For the other basis \(\{1\}\) of the same vertex, \(\tilde{c}_2 = 0 - (-1) \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1 \ge 0\), which certifies optimality. What we saw in class is only that \(\tilde{c}_N \ge 0\) implies optimality, not the converse.

The statement is true when \(z\) is non-degenerate. If no entry \(\bar{A}_{i,j}\) is positive, then \(x_j\) can grow without bound and (P) is unbounded, as we saw in class. Otherwise the step size \(\varepsilon = \min_{i : \bar{A}_{i,j} > 0} \hat{b}_i / \bar{A}_{i,j}\) is strictly positive, because \(\hat{b} = z_B > 0\). Increasing \(x_j\) by \(\varepsilon\) gives a feasible point of cost \(c^T z + \varepsilon \tilde{c}_j < c^T z\).
parts.srcline: LP deck, simplex-method slide (LP lecture deck): ‘If \(\tilde{c}_N \ge 0\): \(z\) is an optimal solution!... If there's \(j \in N\) such that \(\tilde{c}_j < 0\), we can reduce the cost by increasing \(x_j\)’. Non-degeneracy assumption: ‘Suppose \(x_i > 0\) for all \(i \in B\). We say \(x\) is non-degenerate’. ‘Issues with the Simplex Method’ slide: ‘What if there's \(x_i\) with \(i \in B\) that equals 0? In this case we can't increase \(x_j\). We call such solutions degenerate’. Bertsimas & Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Linear Optimization, Section 3.9, Exercise 3.6 : ‘If x is the unique optimal solution and is nondegenerate, then the reduced cost of every nonbasic variable is positive’. Its part (a) was 2024A-1d. B&T Section 3.1 ‘Optimality conditions’, Theorem 3.1 (grep ‘Theorem 3.1 Consider’; the OCR drops the bar and the ≥ sign): ‘Theorem 3.1 Consider a basic feasible solution x associated with a basis matrix B, and let \(\bar{c}\) be the corresponding vector of reduced costs. (a) If \(\bar{c} \ge 0\), then x is optimal. (b) If x is optimal and nondegenerate, then \(\bar{c} \ge 0\).’ The item is the contrapositive of (b) without ‘nondegenerate’. Homework ancestor: hw2025 Problem Set 4, Problem 2, Bland’s rule (2025 homework 4 solution: ‘since s enters the basis, by the description of the simplex algorithm, c̃s < 0’;: ‘the fickle variables remain 0 throughout the process&rsquo).

parts.summary: Every non-empty polyhedron given by inequalities has a vertex: false, a strip in the plane has none.
parts.q: Every non-empty polyhedron \(P = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : Cx \le d\}\) has at least one vertex.
parts.basis:
Lineage. The vertex/BFS chain is Volk's most regular T/F lineage: 2024B-1b (decide whether \(y\) is a vertex, True), 2024C-1a (at most \(2^n\) vertices, True), 2025C-1d (‘x is optimal iff x is a vertex’, False), 2026A-1a (a BFS stays a BFS under a new objective, True). That is 4 of the 7 exams from 2024B to 2026B. Also, every later sitting within a year reused at least one T/F sub-topic of the previous sitting (6 of 6), and BFS (2026A-1a) is one of the 2026 sub-topics available for reuse. 2025C-1d was an over-generalization of ‘some optimum is a vertex’. This item over-generalizes the standard-form corollary in the same way (the same trap as 2026B-1a).

Slide. The deck's ‘Vertices’ slide states the counterexample outright: ‘Not every polyhedron has a vertex. E.g., \(\{x : 0 \le x_1 \le 1\}\)’. Goemans' notes, the course reading that already fed 2023A-1a, 2023B-1b and 2024C-1a, have the same remark on p.LP-5. ‘Polyhedra without vertices’ is on the research's list of lecture claims that were never examined.

Probability. About 0.04. The lineage is strong, but 2026A-1a has just used this chain, and the answer can be read straight off one slide.

Variant for the same slot (ellipsoid, from the same deck). ‘In the ellipsoid algorithm, the volume of the ellipsoid at least halves in every iteration’: False.
