Class shows that the ratio of volumes in one step is \(\frac{n}{n+1}\left(\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\right)^{(n-1)/2} \le e^{-1/(2(n+1))}\), so class only guarantees a drop by a factor \(\frac{1}{e}\) every \(2(n+1)\) steps (LP deck: ‘After 2(n + 1) steps: volume decreased by \(\le \frac{1}{e}\)&rsquo). For \(n = 2\) the ratio is exactly \(\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}} \approx 0.77 > \frac{1}{2}\), and it increases towards \(1\) as \(n\) grows. Keep this only if the mock's ellipsoid item is replaced, since one ellipsoid item is enough.
parts.sol:
False. Take \(P = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : 0 \le x_1 \le 1\}\), that is, \(C = egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(d = (1, 0)^T\). \(P\) is non-empty. For every \(x \in P\), the vector \(y = (0, 1) e 0\) satisfies \(x + y \in P\) and \(x - y \in P\), so by the definition from class \(x\) is not a vertex. Equivalently, every row of \(C\) is a multiple of \((1, 0)\), so no point has \(2\) linearly independent tight constraints.

What we saw in class holds for standard form: if \(P = \{x : Ax = b, x \ge 0\} e \emptyset\), then \(P\) has a vertex. To see this, apply the theorem ‘if \(\min\{c^T x : x \in P\}\) is finite, then for every \(x \in P\) there is a vertex \(x'\) with \(c^T x' \le c^T x\)’ with \(c = 0\). The minimum is then \(0\), which is finite because \(P e \emptyset\). A standard-form polyhedron cannot contain a line because of the constraints \(x \ge 0\).
parts.srcline: LP deck, ‘Vertices’ slide (LP lecture deck): ‘Not every polyhedron has a vertex. E.g., \(\{x : 0 \le x_1 \le 1\}\). However, we will prove that if an LP in standard form has an optimal solution, then it is obtained by a vertex’. Goemans, LP lecture notes, p.LP-5 : ‘such a set P might not have any vertex. For example, consider \(P = \{(x_1, x_2) : 0 \le x_2 \le 1\}\)’ and ‘Corollary 3: If \(P = \{x : Ax = b, x \ge 0\} \ne \emptyset\), then P has a vertex.’

parts.summary: An efficient algorithm can output, from G, an integer linear program whose optimum is the max-cut size: true.
parts.q: There exists an efficient algorithm that, given an undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\), outputs an integer linear program (that is, a linear objective function, linear equality and inequality constraints, and the constraint that all variables are integers) whose optimal value equals the size of a maximum cut in \(G\).
parts.basis:
Slide. The Approximation deck introduces Max-Cut with an IP whose key constraint is ‘Not a linear constraint! Recall that for min-cut this was possible (dual of max flow). Weird.’ A student who remembers only that line answers False. The item tests whether you can linearize it (the item asks for an efficient algorithm that outputs the program; without that, ‘maximize \(t\) subject to \(t \le k\), \(t\) integer’ with \(k\) the max-cut size would make it trivially true), which is the move used in 2026A-P5(b) (\(z_{u,v} \le x_u\), \(z_{u,v} \le 1 - x_v\) for directed cut). The undirected constraints are exactly those in Williamson-Shmoys Ex 4.7(b), and Volk lifted 2026A-P5 from Williamson-Shmoys Ex 5.3 and 5.6.

Lineage. 2024B-1a (a polynomial-time ILP solver implies P=NP, True) is the other ILP-expressiveness item. Writing an ILP from scratch appeared in 5 of the 8 exams from 2023A to 2025C and was skipped in 2026A/B apart from the given DiCut program. A T/F item is a cheap way to bring it back.

Probability. About 0.03, the lowest of the four. The Max-Cut material belongs to the approximation unit, so it is at least as likely to sit in slot (d). 2026A-P5 has also just spent the linearization trick. It is the pool's only True item. 29 of the 40 past T/F items were True, but slot (a) was True in only 6 of 10 exams, so the slot leans only mildly towards True.

Variant for the same slot (integrality). ‘If \(\{x : Ax = b, x \ge 0\}\) has only integral vertices for every integral \(b\), then \(A\) is totally unimodular’: False. Take \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\): \(\det A = 1\) and \(A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) is integral, so the polyhedron is empty or the single integral point \(A^{-1} b\), but the \(1 \times 1\) submatrix \((2)\) has determinant \(2\). This is the converse of the deck's TUM claim.
parts.sol:
True. The constraint \(x_{u,v} = y_u \oplus y_v\) we wrote in class is not linear. We rename the variables: \(x_v\) for every vertex (instead of \(y_v\)) and \(z_{u,v}\) for every edge (instead of \(x_{u,v}\)). Since we maximize, it suffices to bound \(z_{u,v}\) from above by linear constraints. The algorithm outputs the following program:

\[ \begin{array}{lll} \text{maximize} & \sum_{(u,v) \in E} z_{u,v} & \\ \text{subject to} & z_{u,v} \le x_u + x_v & \text{for every } (u,v) \in E \\ & z_{u,v} \le 2 - x_u - x_v & \text{for every } (u,v) \in E \\ & x_v \in \{0, 1\} & \text{for every } v \in V \\ & z_{u,v} \in \{0, 1\} & \text{for every } (u,v) \in E \end{array} \]

If \(x_u = x_v = 0\), the first constraint forces \(z_{u,v} \le 0\). If \(x_u = x_v = 1\), the second forces \(z_{u,v} \le 0\). If \(x_u \ne x_v\), both constraints only say \(z_{u,v} \le 1\). Given a cut \((U, V \setminus U)\), set \(x_v = 1\) iff \(v \in U\) and \(z_{u,v} = 1\) iff \((u,v)\) crosses the cut. This is feasible with value equal to the size of the cut. Conversely, for a feasible \((x, z)\), let \(U = \{v : x_v = 1\}\). Then \(z_{u,v} = 1\) only for edges crossing \((U, V \setminus U)\), so the value is at most the size of that cut. Hence the optimum is exactly the size of a maximum cut. This is the same argument as for the directed-cut program in 2026A Problem 5(b).

Each constraint \(x_v \in \{0, 1\}\) stands for \(0 \le x_v \le 1\) together with \(x_v\) integer, and the same for \(z_{u,v}\). The program has \(|V| + |E|\) variables and \(2|E|\) constraints besides the bounds, and all its numbers are small constants (coefficients \(0\) and \(\pm 1\), right-hand sides \(0\), \(1\) or \(2\)). So the algorithm writes it down in polynomial time (in time \(O(|V| + |E|)\) with a sparse encoding of the constraints), without knowing the value of the maximum cut. (The word ‘efficient’ matters: the program ‘maximize \(t\) subject to \(t \le k\), \(t\) integer’ also has optimum \(k\), but writing it requires computing \(k\), i.e. solving Max-Cut, which is NP-hard.)
parts.srcline: Approximation deck, ‘Max Cut’ IP slide (Approximation lecture deck): ‘Variables: \(x_{uv}\) for every edge, \(y_v\) for every vertex... \(x_{u,v} = y_u \oplus y_v\)... Not a linear constraint! Recall that for min-cut this was possible (dual of max flow). Weird.’ The linear form is Williamson & Shmoys, Exercise 4.7(b), p.103 : ‘\(z_{ij} \le x_i + x_j\), \(z_{ij} \le 2 - x_i - x_j\), \(\forall (i,j) \in E\)’. Directed sibling: 2026A Problem 5(b) = W&S Ex 5.6(a) (\(z_{ij} \le x_i\), \(z_{ij} \le 1 - x_j\)).

items.src: T/F pool for P1(b)/(d), 7 pts each: BPP with a 1/poly gap (2023A-1c, 2024C-1c; Motwani-Raghavan Problem 4.8), isolation for the maximum (2025C-1c, 2026B-1b; Jukna Ex 11.4), the matching determinant (deck slide; 2024C-1d), random walks on bipartite graphs (2025B-1d; deck lazy walk)
items.stem:
Problem 1 (\(4\times 7=28\) points). For each of the following statements, write whether they are true or false, and briefly explain your answer.

This is a pool: each statement is a candidate for one slot of Problem 1, most likely (b) or (d). A real paper would carry at most one or two of them.

parts.summary: True: a BPP algorithm whose two acceptance thresholds differ by only 1/(n+1) can be amplified to error 1/3 by a majority vote over polynomially many runs.
parts.q: \(\mathrm{BPP}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2(n+1)},\ \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2(n+1)}\right)=\mathrm{BPP}\left(\frac{1}{3},\ \frac{2}{3}\right)\) (\(n\) is the input length).
parts.sol:
True. Write \(\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2(n+1)}\), so the class on the left is \(\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon)\). Its thresholds satisfy \(0\le\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon<\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon\le 1\) for every \(n\ge 0\).

The inclusion \(\supseteq\). For \(n\ge 2\) we have \(\varepsilon\le\frac{1}{6}\), so \(\frac{1}{3}\le\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon\) and \(\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon\le\frac{2}{3}\). So an algorithm that shows \(A\in\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})\) also meets the new thresholds on every input of length at least 2. The finitely many inputs of length at most 1 are answered from a fixed table, with no error. Hence \(\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon)\).

The inclusion \(\subseteq\). Let \(A\in\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon)\) via a polynomial time algorithm \(M\). The algorithm \(M'\) runs \(M\) on \(x\) for \(t=4(n+1)^2\) times, each time with fresh independent random coins. It accepts iff more than \(t/2\) of the runs accept (a majority vote, as in class). Fix an input \(x\) and let \(p=\Pr[M \text{ accepts } x]\). Let \(X_i\) be an indicator random variable for the event that the \(i\)-th run accepts, and let \(X=\sum_{i=1}^{t}X_i\). The \(X_i\) are i.i.d. with \(\Pr[X_i=1]=p\), so by the Chernoff bound we saw in class\[\Pr\left[|X-pt|\ge\varepsilon t\right]\le 2e^{-2\varepsilon^2 t}=2e^{-2\cdot\frac{1}{4(n+1)^2}\cdot 4(n+1)^2}=2e^{-2}.\]

  • If \(x\notin A\) then \(p\le\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon\), and \(M'\) errs only if \(X>\frac{t}{2}\ge pt+\varepsilon t\).
  • If \(x\in A\) then \(p\ge\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon\), and \(M'\) errs only if \(X\le\frac{t}{2}\le pt-\varepsilon t\).

In both cases the error event implies \(|X-pt|\ge\varepsilon t\), so the error probability is at most \(2e^{-2}<0.28<\frac{1}{3}\). \(M'\) makes \(4(n+1)^2\) calls to a polynomial time algorithm, so it runs in polynomial time, and \(A\in\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})\).

(Taking \(t=2(n+1)^3\) instead gives error at most \(2e^{-(n+1)}<2^{-n}\), which is Motwani-Raghavan Problem 4.8. What matters is that the gap \(\beta-\alpha=\frac{1}{n+1}\) is at least an inverse polynomial. With gap 0, as in 2024C-1c, the claim is false.)
parts.basis:
BPP amplification is a two-item Randomized T/F chain, and its answer flipped once: 2023A-1c (\(\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{4})=\mathrm{BPP}(2^{-n},1-2^{-n})\), True), then 2024C-1c (\(\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})=\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})\), False, the gap is dropped). It has not been asked in the five sittings since (2025A, 2025B, 2025C, 2026A and 2026B; a grep for BPP over the exam corpus finds only 2023A and 2024C), and its last use was a Moed C. The obvious next link lies between the two: a gap that shrinks with \(n\) but stays inverse-polynomial. This is exactly Motwani-Raghavan Problem 4.8, and Motwani-Raghavan is the course textbook for the Randomized unit. The T/F analysis names 'BPP amplification (unused since 2024C)' as a slot (b) candidate and lists \(\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{n},\frac{2}{n})=\mathrm{BPP}(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})\), another inverse-polynomial-gap equality, among its most likely reused twists. The statement copies the form of 2023A-1c, including '(\(n\) is the input length)'. It rests on the deck's 'Error reduction' slides (\(\mathrm{BPP}(\alpha,\beta)\), majority vote) and on the class Chernoff bound \(\Pr[|X-pm|\ge\varepsilon m]\le 2e^{-2\varepsilon^2 m}\), so checking the constant is a one-line computation. The offset from \(\frac{1}{2}\) is written as \(\frac{1}{2(n+1)}\) rather than \(\frac{1}{n}\) or \(\frac{1}{2n}\). With \(\frac{1}{n}\) the lower threshold is negative at \(n=1\), and \(\frac{1}{2n}\) is undefined for the empty input (\(n=0\)). With \(\frac{1}{2(n+1)}\) the thresholds meet the class condition \(0\le\alpha<\beta\le 1\) for every \(n\ge 0\) (they are 0 and 1 at \(n=0\)).

Probability: about 0.07 for this item or a variant with the same idea (an inverse-polynomial gap that shrinks with \(n\)), the highest in this pool. The figure is a product of two estimates. (1) A BPP item in the 2026C T/F block: about 0.2. The Moed C analysis puts 'BPP amplification' at about 0.35 as a C-flavoured candidate, but that figure rests on 2024C alone. Against it: BPP was a T/F item in 2 of the 10 Volk papers and in 1 of the 2 Moed C's (2025C took isolation instead); the July 2026 prediction that BPP was 'due back' missed in both 2026A and 2026B (format scorecard); the 2026 homework dropped the RP/ZPP/BPP exercise that hw2025 set 1 had; and the same-year reuse rule pulls the Randomized T/F slot toward isolation (2026B-1b) and Schwartz-Zippel (2026A-1b). (2) Given a BPP item, the twist is an inverse-polynomial gap: about 0.35. The two earlier items covered a constant gap and a zero gap, so this is the one untested case; the alternatives are another constant pair or a one-sided RP/ZPP claim. So \(0.2\cdot 0.35\approx 0.07\). About 0.18 that at least one of the four pool items appears in 2026C: they compete for the same one or two Randomized slots, so the four estimates roughly add.

Variants for the same slot (Randomized-deck claims never yet asked as T/F):

  • 'Let \(X=\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_i\) where the \(X_i\in\{0,1\}\) are only pairwise independent with \(\Pr[X_i=1]=p\). Then \(\Pr\left[|X-pm|\ge t\right]\le\frac{pm}{t^2}\).' True: the variance computation from class uses only \(\mathbb{E}[(X_i-p)(X_j-p)]=0\) for \(i\neq j\), which needs only pairwise independence (the deck says 'So far we only used pairwise independence').
  • 'The cycle \(C_n\) (\(n\ge 3\)) has exactly \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) minimum cuts.' True: the minimum cut has 2 edges, and every pair of edges splits the cycle into two arcs, giving \(\binom{n}{2}\) distinct minimum cuts. So Karger's bound is tight (Zwick PS2 Ex 2.3, hw2026 set 1 problem 3).
parts.srcline: Randomized lecture deck, 'Error reduction' and 'Error Reduction, Two-sided Case' slides (corpus) and the 'Chernoff Bound' slide. Motwani & Raghavan, Randomized Algorithms, Problem 4.8 (Chapter 4 problems, p.98): 'Consider a BPP algorithm that has an error probability of \(1/2-1/p(n)\)... Using the Chernoff bound... show that a polynomial number of independent repetitions of this algorithm suffice to reduce the error probability to \(1/2^n\).' Re-parameterizes 2023A-1c and 2024C-1c.

parts.summary: True: the isolation lemma also isolates a unique maximum-weight set with probability at least one half when the weights come from 1 to 2n.
parts.q: Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a nonempty family of subsets of \(\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(w:\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,2,\ldots,2n\}\) be a weight function chosen at random, uniformly and independently for each element. The weight of a set \(S\) is \(w(S)=\sum_{i\in S}w(i)\). Then with probability at least \(1/2\), there is a unique set in \(\mathcal{F}\) of maximum weight.
parts.sol:
True. This is the isolation lemma for the maximum. As remarked in class, the lemma also holds for the maximum weight. With \(N=2n\), the probability that the maximum-weight set is not unique is at most \(\frac{n}{N}=\frac{1}{2}\).

The proof from class carries over. For \(x\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) define\[\alpha'(x)=\max_{S\in\mathcal{F},\,x\notin S}w(S)-\max_{S\in\mathcal{F},\,x\in S}w(S\setminus\{x\}),\]and \(\alpha'(x)=0\) if one of the two maxima is over an empty family. \(\alpha'(x)\) depends only on the weights of elements other than \(x\), so \(\Pr[w(x)=\alpha'(x)]\le\frac{1}{2n}\). Now suppose \(A\neq B\) both have the maximum weight \(M\). Weights are positive, so neither set contains the other, and there is some \(x\in A\setminus B\). The first maximum is then \(w(B)=M\) and the second is \(w(A)-w(x)=M-w(x)\), so \(\alpha'(x)=w(x)\). By a union bound over the \(n\) elements, the maximum is not unique with probability at most \(n\cdot\frac{1}{2n}=\frac{1}{2}\).

(Applying the lemma to \(w'=2n+1-w\) does not work directly: \(w'(S)=(2n+1)|S|-w(S)\), and the sets in \(\mathcal{F}\) may have different sizes. Compare 2026B-1b, with the same \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(w\): the lemma isolates the extreme set. It does not make all set weights distinct.)
parts.basis:
Same-year reuse: every later sitting has reused at least one T/F sub-topic from the previous sitting of the same year (6 out of 6). Isolation was 2026B-1b (same \(\mathcal{F}\), same random \(w\) into \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\), claim 'all subset sums distinct', False). Its official solution already names the true statement: 'the isolation lemma only guarantees that the minimum weight set is unique with high probability'. The exact ancestor is a Moed C item, 2025C-1c: edge weights from \(\{1,\ldots,4|E|\}\), a unique minimum cut and a unique maximum cut with probability at least \(1/2\), True. Its official solution uses the maximum version of the lemma. There are two sources. One is the deck's remark 'Same holds with maximum weight', right under the lemma. The other is Jukna Exercise 11.4 ('With what probability will there be a unique set with the maximal weight?'), next to Exercise 11.5 (product weights), which matches 2023A-1b. The isolation family so far has three T/F items, 2023A-1b (True), 2025C-1c (True) and 2026B-1b (False), so the chain went T, T, then F. It also has one free-response problem, 2024A-P3 (random edge weights from \(\{1,\ldots,p(n)\}\) give a unique minimum weight path between every pair of vertices with probability at least 0.9). This item keeps the parameters of 2026B-1b word for word and asks for the uniqueness of the extreme set, with the maximum twist of 2025C-1c. The case for it is the same-year reuse rule, not the answer pattern of the chain.

Probability: about 0.04, discounted because it nearly repeats 2025C-1c.
parts.srcline: Randomized deck, Isolation Lemma slide, 'Remarks: 1. Only meaningful when \(N>n\) 2. Same holds with maximum weight' (corpus), proof on. Jukna, Extremal Combinatorics, 2nd ed., Exercise 11.4, p.163. Re-skins 2026B-1b (same \(\mathcal{F}\), \(w\), \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\)) with the answer of 2025C-1c.

parts.summary: True: if a bipartite graph has exactly one perfect matching, its 0/1 biadjacency matrix has determinant plus or minus one.
parts.q: Let \(G=(L\cup R,E)\) be a bipartite graph with \(|L|=|R|=n\) that has exactly one perfect matching. Let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) be its biadjacency matrix: rows are indexed by \(L\), columns by \(R\), and \(A_{i,j}=1\) if \((i,j)\in E\), \(A_{i,j}=0\) otherwise. Then \(\det A\neq 0\).
parts.sol:
True. By definition\[\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}(-1)^{\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}A_{i,\sigma(i)}.\]As we have seen in class, the term of \(\sigma\) is nonzero iff \((i,\sigma(i))\in E\) for every \(i\), that is, iff \(\{(i,\sigma(i)):1\le i\le n\}\) is a perfect matching. In that case the product equals 1. So the permutations with a nonzero term correspond one-to-one to the perfect matchings of \(G\). \(G\) has exactly one perfect matching, so exactly one term of the sum is nonzero, and \(\det A=\pm 1 eq 0\).

(The hypothesis 'exactly one' matters. 'If \(G\) has a perfect matching then \(\det A eq 0\)' is false: the class counterexample \( egin{pmatrix}1&1\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) has two perfect matchings whose terms cancel. More generally, since \(-1\equiv 1 \pmod 2\), \(\det A\) has the same parity as the number of perfect matchings of \(G\) (this is 2024C-1d). So an odd number of perfect matchings already forces \(\det A eq 0\).)
parts.basis:
This comes straight from a slide. The deck's 'Matchings and Determinants' slide asks 'Is the converse also true? Perfect Matching \(\Rightarrow\) non-zero det? No. Counterexample \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\)', and blames the signs: 'the + and - can cancel out'. Volk usually builds a T/F by changing one hypothesis of a slide claim (dropping a hypothesis, swapping a constant, overgeneralizing). Here the True version adds the hypothesis that removes the cancellation (a unique matching), and the False version asks the bare converse. The family has been examined once, and it was a Moed C item: 2024C-1d (\(\det A \bmod 2\) decides the parity of the number of perfect matchings, True). Recitation 2 repeats the claim that \(\det\neq 0\) implies a perfect matching. Neither 2026 exam touched matchings or had a PIT free-response problem (PIT appeared only as the Schwartz-Zippel T/F 2026A-1b), although PIT free-response appeared in every Moed A from 2023 to 2025 and in 2025C. 2026B-P2 did use the same bipartite biadjacency matrix (rows indexed by \(L\), columns by \(R\)), but to count common neighbours, and the statement above copies the definition from its official solution. So the matching unit is due, and a T/F is the cheapest way to cover it.

Probability: about 0.035. The True version (unique matching) and the False version ('has a perfect matching') are about equally likely.
parts.srcline: Randomized deck, 'Matchings and Determinants' slides: 'Claim: if \(A\) doesn't have a perfect matching, \(\det A=0\)... Is the converse also true? Perfect Matching \(\Rightarrow\) non-zero det? No. Counterexample... The problem is with the signs' (corpus). Recitation 2, 'Perfect Matching on Bipartite Graph'. Sibling of 2024C-1d.

parts.summary: False: on a connected regular bipartite graph such as the 4-cycle the non-lazy random walk alternates between the two sides and never converges to the uniform distribution.
parts.q: Let \(G\) be an undirected connected \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices with normalized adjacency matrix \(A\). For a vertex \(s\), let \(p_s\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be the vector which is 1 in the \(s\)-th coordinate and 0 elsewhere. Then for every vertex \(s\), the vectors \(A^k p_s\) converge to the uniform distribution \(\frac{1}{n}(1,1,\ldots,1)\) as \(k\to\infty\).
parts.sol:
False. Let \(G\) be the 4-cycle \(C_4\) with vertices \(1,2,3,4\) and edges \(\{1,2\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\},\{4,1\}\), which is connected and 2-regular. Then \(Ap_1=\frac{1}{2}(p_2+p_4)\), \(A\cdot\frac{1}{2}(p_2+p_4)=\frac{1}{2}(p_1+p_3)\) and \(A\cdot\frac{1}{2}(p_1+p_3)=\frac{1}{2}(p_2+p_4)\), so\[A^kp_1=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}(p_2+p_4) & k \text{ odd},\\ \frac{1}{2}(p_1+p_3) & k\ge 2 \text{ even}.\end{cases}\]In both cases \(\left\|A^kp_1-\frac{1}{4}(1,1,1,1)\right\|_2=\frac{1}{2}\), so the sequence does not converge: the walk alternates between the two sides of the bipartition.

In spectral terms: as we have seen in class, \(G\) is bipartite iff \(\mu_n=-1\). The component of \(p_s\) along the eigenvector \(v_n\) is multiplied by \((-1)^k\) and never decays. For \(C_4\), \(v_4=\frac{1}{2}(1,-1,1,-1)\) and \(\langle p_1,v_4\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\). This is why in class we worked with the lazy walk \(B=\frac{1}{2}I+\frac{1}{2}A\). Its eigenvalues \(\lambda_i=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mu_i\) lie in \([0,1]\), and \(\lambda_2<1\) when \(G\) is connected, so \(B^kp_s\) does converge to uniform. (The statement is true for connected regular graphs that are not bipartite.)
parts.basis:
Spectral and random-walk facts have filled slot (d) three times: 2023B-1d (all nontrivial eigenvalues at most \(1/2\) in absolute value, so a walk reaches \(t\) within \(C\log n\) steps, True), 2025A-1d (the eigenspace of 1 is one-dimensional for connected \(G\), True) and 2025B-1d (\(\det(A+I)=0\Rightarrow G\) bipartite, True). The topic was then promoted to a free-response problem in 2025C-P3 (a lazy walk with stay probability \(1/3\)). Random walks are absent from both 2026 exams, though hw2026 set 2 Question 1 kept the spectral facts about the lazy walk in play. The deck says only 'For technical reasons: we'll work with the lazy random walk matrix'. The reason is the bipartite fact on the next slide ('\(G\) bipartite iff \(\mu_n=-1\)'). A T/F that drops the laziness is Volk's usual 'drop a hypothesis' trap (2024C-1c, 2026A-1b). It would also be the first False item in the spectral family.

Probability: about 0.035.

Variants in the same family:

  • 'Let \(G\) be an undirected connected \(d\)-regular graph of diameter at most 3, and let \(\lambda_2\) be the second largest eigenvalue of its lazy random walk matrix \(B=\frac{1}{2}I+\frac{1}{2}A\). Then \(\lambda_2<0.9\).' False. This is lifted from a recitation slide: recitation 4 states the converse of its Claim 2 ('If \(\lambda_2<0.9\) then the diameter of \(G\) is \(O(\log n)\)') as false, 'diameter of \(G\) is \(O(\log n)\not\Rightarrow\mu_2<1-\epsilon\)', with two cliques of size \(n/2\) joined by 2 edges, 'regularized by deleting an edge from each clique', of diameter 3 and \(\mu_2=1-o(1)\) (corpus; Claim 2 with \(\lambda_2<0.9\) follows on). Concretely, take two copies of \(K_6\), delete the edge \(\{a_1,a_2\}\) from the first and \(\{b_1,b_2\}\) from the second, and add \(\{a_1,b_1\}\) and \(\{a_2,b_2\}\). The graph has \(n=12\), is 5-regular and has diameter 3. The vector \(x\) that is 1 on the first clique and \(-1\) on the second is orthogonal to \((1,\ldots,1)\), and \(\frac{x^TAx}{x^Tx}=\frac{2\cdot 28-2\cdot 2}{5\cdot 12}=\frac{13}{15}\), so \(\mu_2\ge\frac{13}{15}\) and \(\lambda_2=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mu_2\ge\frac{14}{15}>0.9\) (numerically \(\lambda_2\approx 0.946\)).
  • 'In every strongly connected directed graph, a random walk from \(s\) reaches \(t\) within \(n^3\) steps with probability at least \(1/2\).' False (the deck: 'This doesn't work for directed graphs'). Take edges \(i\to i+1\) for \(1\le i\le n-1\), \(i\to 1\) for \(2\le i\le n-1\), and \(n\to 1\), with \(s=1\) and \(t=n\). Each attempt from 1 reaches \(n\) with probability \(2^{-(n-2)}\), and there are at most \(n^3\) attempts, so the probability is at most \(n^3\cdot 2^{-(n-2)}\to 0\).
parts.srcline: Randomized deck, 'Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of A' ('For technical reasons: we'll work with the lazy random walk matrix \(B=\frac{1}{2}I+\frac{1}{2}A\)', corpus) and 'Spectral Graph Theory' ('\(G\) bipartite iff \(\mu_n=-1\)'). Sibling of 2025B-1d. The Moed C precedent for the lazy walk is 2025C-P3.

items.src: T/F pool, 4 items x 7 pts for slots P1(c)/(d): Algebraic deck (Newton identities; Bounding omega) and Approximation deck (Gram-Schmidt lower bound; PSD). Lineage: 2026B-1c, 2023A-1d/2025C-1b, 2026B-1d, 2024A-1b.
items.stem:
Problem 1-style items (7 points each). For each of the following statements, write whether it is true or false, and briefly explain your answer. You may use any claim presented in class or proved in the homework.

Pool for slots (c) (algebraic) and (d) (linear algebra from the Approximation deck); on the real paper at most one or two of these would appear.

parts.summary: True or false: two real matrices whose powers up to n have equal traces are similar.
parts.q: Let \(A, B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\). If \(\mathrm{trace}(A^i) = \mathrm{trace}(B^i)\) for every \(i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}\), then \(A\) and \(B\) are similar (that is, \(B = PAP^{-1}\) for some invertible matrix \(P\)).
parts.basis:
Same-year reuse. Characteristic polynomial / traces / Newton's identities is the only sub-topic asked as a T/F item in both 2026 sittings: 2026A-1c (\(\sum_i \lambda_i^n = \mathrm{trace}(A^n)\) with fewer than \(n^3\) operations, True) and 2026B-1c (equal traces of \(A^i\), \(i \le n\), give the same eigenvalues, True). The chain is 2024B-1d, then 2026A-1c, then 2026B-1c. Every later sitting has reused at least one T/F sub-topic of the sitting before it in the same year, 6 times out of 6 (2023A to B, 2024A to B, 2024B to C, 2025A to B, 2025B to C, 2026A to B), so a 2026B topic is very likely to come back in 2026C.

The twist. Changing one word of 2026B-1c ('same eigenvalues' to 'similar') is the cheapest False version. It is Volk's usual move of overgeneralizing a slide claim (2026B-1a 'feasible' to 'optimal', 2025C-1d 'some optimum is a vertex' to 'iff'). The official 2026B-1c solution is a one-line appeal to Newton's identities, so students who memorised it will answer True.

Source. Algebraic deck, slides 'Power sum polynomials' and 'Newton's identities'. Horn and Johnson 2.4.P10 states the fact exactly: equal traces of \(A^k\) for \(k \le n\) give the same characteristic polynomial, and nothing more.

Probability that this item (or its \(\mathbb{F}_2\) variant) appears: about 0.05. Slot (c) is algebraic in about 80% of papers.

Algebraic-slot variants in the same pool:

  • 'For every invertible \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\), \(A^{-1}\) is a polynomial in \(A\) of degree at most \(n-1\).' True: by Cayley-Hamilton (the deck's 'Matrix Inversion' slide), \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{e_n}\left(e_{n-1} I - e_{n-2} A + \cdots + (-1)^{n-1} A^{n-1}\right)\), and \(e_n = \det(A) \ne 0\).
  • '\(\sum_{i < j} \lambda_i \lambda_j\) can be computed with \(O(n^2)\) arithmetic operations.' True: it equals \(e_2 = \frac{\mathrm{trace}(A)^2 - \mathrm{trace}(A^2)}{2}\), and \(\mathrm{trace}(A^2) = \sum_{i,j} A_{ij} A_{ji}\) needs only \(O(n^2)\) operations.
  • 'A graph \(G\) contains a cycle of length 4 iff \(\mathrm{trace}(A^4) \ne 0\).' False: every edge \(uv\) gives the closed walk \(u, v, u, v, u\) of length 4 (Zwick's slides count closed walks, not cycles).
  • Seidel: 'If \(G'\) has an edge \(uv\) iff \(d_G(u,v) \in \{1,2\}\), then \(d_{G'}(u,v) = \lceil d_G(u,v)/2 \rceil\).' True.
parts.sol:
False. As we have seen in class, Newton's identities let us compute the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial from \(\mathrm{trace}(A^i)\), \(1 \le i \le n\). So the hypothesis does imply that \(A\) and \(B\) have the same characteristic polynomial, and hence the same eigenvalues with the same algebraic multiplicities (this was 2026B-1c). But two matrices with the same eigenvalues need not be similar. Take \(n = 2\) and

\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\]

Then \(A^2 = 0\), so \(\mathrm{trace}(A) = \mathrm{trace}(A^2) = 0 = \mathrm{trace}(B) = \mathrm{trace}(B^2)\). However, for every invertible \(P\) we have \(PBP^{-1} = 0 \ne A\), so \(A\) and \(B\) are not similar.

Remarks. (1) The conclusion does hold when both matrices are known to be diagonalizable (for example, symmetric): then both are similar to the same diagonal matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)\). (2) Over a field of characteristic \(p \le n\) even the eigenvalue claim fails, because Newton's identities divide by \(k\): over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), \(I_2\) and \(0\) have \(\mathrm{trace}(I_2) = \mathrm{trace}(I_2^2) = 2 = 0\), but their characteristic polynomials are \((t-1)^2 \ne t^2\).
parts.srcline: Algebraic deck, 'Power sum polynomials' and 'Newton's identities' slides (Algebraic lecture deck). Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis, Problem 2.4.P10: 'Show that \(A, B \in M_n\) have the same characteristic polynomials, and hence the same eigenvalues, if and only if \(\mathrm{tr}\, A^k = \mathrm{tr}\, B^k\) for all \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, n\).' One-word twist of 2026B-1c.

parts.summary: True or false: applying a 48-multiplication algorithm for 4 by 4 matrices recursively beats Strassen's exponent.
parts.q: Suppose there is an algorithm that multiplies two \(4 \times 4\) matrices over any ring (not necessarily commutative) using \(48\) multiplications (and any number of additions and subtractions). Then applying this algorithm recursively to the decomposition of the input matrices into \(4 \times 4\) blocks gives an algorithm that multiplies two \(n \times n\) real matrices using \(O(n^{\beta})\) arithmetic operations, for some constant \(\beta < \log_2 7\).
parts.basis:
Lineage. The matrix-multiplication count family ran in three sittings in a row: 2025A-1c (\(n\) products \(Av_i\) need time \(n^3\), False), 2025B-1b (an \(n \times n\) by \(n \times n^2\) product in fewer than \(n^4\) operations, True) and 2025C-1b (\(\alpha_{k^2} \le (\alpha_k)^2\), True). It goes back to 2023A-1d ('\(4 \times 4\) with at most 49 multiplications', True) and skipped both 2026 sittings. A family that has rested for one year and matches a slot filled by algebra about 80% of the time is a reasonable return candidate for Moed C.

Source. Algebraic deck, slide 9 'Bounding \(\omega\)': 'If we can multiply \(m \times m\) matrices with \(k\) multiplications, \(\omega \le \log_m k\)'. This claim has never been a T/F item (the T/F analysis lists it among the unexamined lecture claims). Slide 10 'Known bounds on \(\omega\)' is an image that plots the history of the upper bound, from Strassen's 2.81 down below 2.4 with Coppersmith-Winograd (1990) and on to Alman-Williams and later work. Slide 11 mentions the Google search for \(4 \times 4\) and \(5 \times 5\) algorithms ('They did not lower \(\omega\)') without giving a count. That gap invites a concrete number. 48 is the natural number to choose: it is one less than the 49 of 2023A-1d, and the comparison needs no calculator, only \(\log_4 48 < \log_4 49 = \log_2 7\). Volk's Hebrew notes give the same bound (Thm 3.6 \(\omega \le \log_2 7\); Thm 5.8: if \(\mathrm{rank}\langle m,n,t \rangle \le r\) then \(\omega \le 3 \log_{mnt} r\), which for \(m = n = t = 4\), \(r = 48\) is \(\log_4 48\)).

Why the conclusion names the recursive algorithm. Because slide 10 shows \(\omega < 2.38\), a conclusion such as 'then there is an algorithm that multiplies \(n \times n\) matrices in \(O(n^{\beta})\) for some \(\beta < \log_2 7\)', or 'then \(\omega \le X\)' for any \(X > 2.372\), is true without the hypothesis, and 'True, since \(\omega < 2.38\)' would be a complete answer that never uses the 48. Volk's own solutions use the known bounds on \(\omega\) in exactly this way (2025A-1c: 'We've seen in class how to do it using fast matrix multiplication in time \(O(n^{\omega})\), regardless of the assumption'; 2025B-1b: '\(n^{\omega+1}\) which is less than \(n^4\)'). So the statement asks what the algorithm built from the hypothesis achieves. The answer then depends only on comparing \(\log_4 48\) with \(\log_2 7\).

Probability: about 0.045, counting the False twin below.

Variants:

  • False twin: 'Suppose there is an algorithm that multiplies two \(3 \times 3\) matrices over any ring using \(23\) multiplications. Then applying this algorithm recursively to the decomposition of the input matrices into \(3 \times 3\) blocks gives an algorithm that multiplies two \(n \times n\) real matrices using \(O(n^{\beta})\) arithmetic operations, for some constant \(\beta < \log_2 7\).' False: for \(n = 3^t\) the recursive algorithm performs exactly \(23^t = n^{\log_3 23}\) scalar multiplications, so it is not \(O(n^{\beta})\) for any \(\beta < \log_3 23\). And \(\log_3 23 > \frac{17}{6} > \log_2 7\), since \(23^6 = 148035889 > 129140163 = 3^{17}\) and \(7^6 = 117649 < 131072 = 2^{17}\) (numerically \(\log_3 23 \approx 2.854 > 2.807 \approx \log_2 7\)). The hypothesis actually holds (Laderman 1976; Bläser's survey: '\(19 \le R(\langle 3,3,3 \rangle) \le 23\)... (We would need \(\le 21\) to get an improvement.)'), which makes the trap sharper. The conclusion has to name the recursive algorithm: 'then there is an algorithm with exponent below \(\log_2 7\)' would be True by slide 10.
  • DPV Exercise 2.27(b), as a T/F item about the specific algorithm: 'Since \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}^2 = \begin{pmatrix} a^2 + bc & b(a+d) \\ c(a+d) & bc + d^2 \end{pmatrix}\), a \(2 \times 2\) matrix can be squared with 5 multiplications. Consider the following algorithm for squaring an \(n \times n\) matrix: use a divide-and-conquer approach as in Strassen's algorithm, except that instead of getting 7 subproblems of size \(n/2\), we now get 5 subproblems of size \(n/2\) thanks to this formula. This algorithm correctly computes \(A^2\) and runs in time \(O(n^{\log_2 5})\).' False because the algorithm computes the wrong result, not because of the time bound. For blocks the formula relies on \(bc = cb\) and \(ab + bd = b(a+d)\), and both fail for matrices. For example, take \(n = 4\) and the \(2 \times 2\) blocks \(a = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), \(b = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), \(c = d = 0\). Then the top-right block of \(A^2\) is \(ab + bd = ab = b \ne 0\), but the formula gives \(b(a+d) = ba = 0\). Also, three of the five products (\(bc\), \(b(a+d)\), \(c(a+d)\)) are products of two different matrices, not squarings, so they are not subproblems of the same kind. The statement must be about this algorithm (DPV asks 'What is wrong with the following algorithm'), because 'squaring is possible in \(O(n^{\log_2 5})\)' on its own is an open problem: \(\log_2 5 \approx 2.32\) is below the best known bound on \(\omega\), and by DPV 2.27(c) squaring is as hard as multiplication.
parts.sol:
True. As we have seen in class, if we can multiply \(m \times m\) matrices with \(k\) multiplications then \(\omega \le \log_m k\), and the proof is exactly the recursive algorithm in the statement. Let us analyze it. We may assume \(n = 4^t\) (otherwise pad the matrices with zeros up to the next power of \(4\), which multiplies \(n\) by less than \(4\) and does not change the \(O(\cdot)\) bound). Split each matrix into \(4 \times 4\) blocks, each of size \(\frac{n}{4} \times \frac{n}{4}\). The \(4 \times 4\) algorithm works over any ring, in particular over the (non-commutative) ring of \(\frac{n}{4} \times \frac{n}{4}\) real matrices, so it correctly computes the product from \(48\) products of \(\frac{n}{4} \times \frac{n}{4}\) matrices, each computed recursively, plus a constant number (depending only on the fixed \(4 \times 4\) algorithm) of block additions and subtractions, which cost \(O(n^2)\). Hence

\[T(n) = 48\, T\left(\frac{n}{4}\right) + O(n^2), \qquad \text{so} \qquad T(n) = O\left(n^{\log_4 48}\right),\]

since \(\log_4 48 > \log_4 16 = 2\). Finally,

\[\log_4 48 < \log_4 49 = \log_4 7^2 = 2 \log_4 7 = \log_2 7,\]

so \(\beta = \log_4 48 \approx 2.79\) is below Strassen's exponent \(\log_2 7 \approx 2.81\). (Strassen's algorithm applied recursively once multiplies \(4 \times 4\) matrices with \(7^2 = 49\) multiplications (2023A-1d), so any \(4 \times 4\) scheme with fewer than \(49\) products beats it.)

Remarks. (1) The words 'over any ring' are needed, because the recursion applies the algorithm to blocks, and blocks do not commute. Over commutative rings, Winograd's 1968 inner-product trick already multiplies \(4 \times 4\) matrices with \(\frac{4^3}{2} + 4^2 = 48\) multiplications, but it uses \(xy = yx\), so it cannot be applied to blocks and says nothing about \(\omega\). (2) The statement is about the recursive algorithm on purpose. The weaker conclusion 'there is an algorithm that multiplies \(n \times n\) matrices using \(O(n^{\beta})\) operations for some \(\beta < \log_2 7\)' holds regardless of the hypothesis, since we saw in class (slide 'Known bounds on \(\omega\)') that \(\omega < 2.38\). The point here is that the hypothesis on its own already gives the exponent \(\log_4 48 < \log_2 7\).
parts.srcline: Algebraic deck, slide 9 'Bounding \(\omega\)' (Algebraic lecture deck): 'If we can multiply \(m \times m\) matrices with \(k\) multiplications, \(\omega \le \log_m k\)'; slide 10 'Known bounds on \(\omega\)' (image only; the plot drops below 2.4 from Coppersmith-Winograd 1990 on); slide 11 (the Google \(4 \times 4\)/\(5 \times 5\) search). Volk's Hebrew notes, Thm 3.6 (\(\omega \le \log_2 7\), from Strassen) and Thm 5.8. Chain: 2023A-1d (\(49 = 7^2\)), then 2025C-1b (\(\alpha_{k^2} \le (\alpha_k)^2\)). Winograd's commutative trick: Bläser, 'Fast Matrix Multiplication', ToC Graduate Surveys 5 (2013), Example 4.8, stated there only for \(M \times 2\) times \(2 \times N\) matrices with \(MN + M + N\) products. The count 48 for \(4 \times 4\) is derived here, not quoted: a \(4 \times 4\) product is the sum of two \((4 \times 2)(2 \times 4)\) products, each costing \(16 + 4 + 4 = 24\) by Example 4.8, so \(48 = \frac{4^3}{2} + 4^2\) in total. Twin: Laderman's 23 for \(3 \times 3\), Bläser. DPV variant: Dasgupta, Papadimitriou and Vazirani, Algorithms, Exercise 2.27(b).

parts.summary: True or false: in the lattice spanned by (2,0) and (1,2), the vector (2,0) is a shortest non-zero vector.
parts.q: Let \(L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2\) be the lattice spanned by the vectors \((2,0)\) and \((1,2)\). Then the vector \((2,0)\) is a shortest non-zero vector in \(L\).
parts.basis:
Lineage. Lattices were a T/F topic in 2024A-1c (Gram-Schmidt), 2024B-1c (sorted orthogonal basis, so \(b_1\) is shortest, True) and 2026B-1d (lattice spanned by \((1,1), (3,1)\), \((1,1)\) shortest, True). After two T/F appearances in 2024 the topic became the free-response 2024C-P5 (LLL bound). By the same-year reuse rule (6 of 6), the 2026B lattice item is one of four 2026B T/F topics that could get a 2026C sibling.

Source. The basis \((2,0), (1,2)\) is Micciancio's CSE206A Lecture 1, Example 9, the standard example that Gram-Schmidt vectors need not lie in the lattice. The Approximation deck makes the same point ('Note that this operation doesn't preserve the lattice spanned by \(b_1, \ldots, b_n\)!') right before the 'Lower bound on shortest vector' claim that decides the item.

The twist. The answer stays True, but the argument of the official 2026B-1d solution no longer works. That solution used \(\mu_{2,1} = 2 \in \mathbb{Z}\), so \(\tilde{b}_2 \in L\) and \(\tilde{b}_1, \tilde{b}_2\) is an orthogonal basis. A student who copies that argument either gets stuck on \((0,2) \notin L\) or wrongly answers False. Only the general bound \(\|v\| \ge \min_i \|\tilde{b}_i\|\) settles it.

Probability: about 0.03.

Variants:

  • 'The Gram-Schmidt vectors of a lattice basis lie in the lattice.' False: here \(\tilde{b}_2 = (0,2) \notin L\).
  • 'If \(b_1, \ldots, b_n\) is a reduced basis (as defined in class), then \(b_1\) is a shortest non-zero vector.' False: \((10,0), (5,8)\) is reduced (\(\mu_{2,1} = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\|b_2\|^2 = 89 \ge \frac{3}{4} \cdot 100\)), but \(\|b_2\|^2 = 89 < 100 = \|b_1\|^2\). LLL only guarantees \(\|b_1\| \le 2^{(n-1)/2} \lambda_1\).
  • The False sibling from the T/F analysis: the lattice spanned by \((2,1), (3,1)\), with \((2,1)\) claimed shortest (\((1,0) = (3,1) - (2,1)\) is shorter).
parts.sol:
True. Let \(b_1 = (2,0)\) and \(b_2 = (1,2)\). The Gram-Schmidt process gives \( ilde{b}_1 = b_1\) and

\[\mu_{2,1} = rac{\langle b_2, ilde{b}_1 angle}{\langle ilde{b}_1, ilde{b}_1 angle} = rac{2}{4} = rac{1}{2}, \qquad ilde{b}_2 = b_2 - rac{1}{2} ilde{b}_1 = (1,2) - (1,0) = (0,2).\]

As we have seen in class, every non-zero \(v \in L\) satisfies

\[\|v\| \ge \min_{1 \le i \le 2} \| ilde{b}_i\| = \min(2, 2) = 2 = \|b_1\|.\]

Hence \(b_1 = (2,0)\) is a shortest non-zero vector of \(L\).

Note that, unlike 2026B-1d, here \(\mu_{2,1} = rac{1}{2}\) is not an integer and \( ilde{b}_2 = (0,2) otin L\): every vector of \(L\) is \(a b_1 + b b_2 = (2a+b, 2b)\) with \(a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\), a second coordinate \(2\) forces \(b = 1\), and then the first coordinate \(2a+1\) is odd, not \(0\). So \( ilde{b}_1, ilde{b}_2\) is not a basis of \(L\), and the orthogonal-basis argument of 2026B-1d does not apply. The lower bound from class does not need it. A direct check also works: for \(v = (2a+b, 2b) e 0\), if \(b e 0\) then \(\|v\| \ge |2b| \ge 2\), and if \(b = 0\) then \(a e 0\) and \(\|v\| = |2a| \ge 2\).
parts.srcline: D. Micciancio, UCSD CSE206A (Winter 2012), Lecture 1 'Introduction to Lattices', Example 9: 'The Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization of the basis \(B = [(2,0)^T, (1,2)^T]\) is \(B^* = [(2,0)^T, (0,2)^T]\). However this is not a lattice basis for \(L(B)\) because the vector \((0,2)^T\) does not belong to the lattice.' Approximation deck, 'Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization' and 'Lower bound on shortest vector' slides (Approximation lecture deck). True twist of 2026B-1d.

parts.summary: True or false: a symmetric matrix whose leading principal minors are all non-negative is PSD.
parts.q: Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) be a symmetric matrix all of whose leading principal minors are non-negative, that is, \(\det(A_k) \ge 0\) for every \(1 \le k \le n\), where \(A_k\) is the top-left \(k \times k\) submatrix of \(A\). Then \(A\) is PSD.
parts.basis:
Source and lineage. The Approximation deck's 'PSD Matrices' slide lists four equivalent definitions, the fourth being 'All principal minors of \(A\) are non-negative'. Volk already made a T/F item from that line: 2024A-1b ('Let \(A\) be a symmetric matrix. If \(\det(A) \ge 0\), then \(A\) is PSD', False, counterexample \(-I\)). Replacing 'all principal minors' by 'leading principal minors' is the same move, and this is a well-known trap, because Sylvester's criterion only works with strict inequalities. Dropping a hypothesis is one of his most common T/F moves (2024A-1b, 2024C-1c, 2026A-1b).

Why 2026C. PSD matrices got more weight in 2026: hw2026 sheet 2 Q6 (the PSD equivalences: eigenvalues, \(A = B^T B\)), hw2026 sheet 4 Q4 (Goemans-Williamson rounding for Max-2-LIN) and 2026B-P5 (Max-Cut SDP dual, \(C - \mathrm{diag}(y)\) PSD). Slot (d) holds a linear-algebra fact from the Approximation or spectral material in about 65% of papers.

Probability: about 0.03.

Variant: 'The value of the Max-Cut SDP relaxation of \(K_3\) equals the size of its maximum cut.' False: three unit vectors at \(120^\circ\) give \(3 \cdot \frac{1 - (-1/2)}{2} = \frac{9}{4}\), while the maximum cut of \(K_3\) is \(2\).
parts.sol:
False. Take \(n = 2\) and

\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}.\]

Its leading principal minors are \(\det(A_1) = 0\) and \(\det(A_2) = 0 \cdot (-1) - 0 \cdot 0 = 0\), both non-negative. But for \(v = e_2 = (0,1)^T\) we get \(v^T A v = -1 < 0\), so \(A\) is not PSD (equivalently, it has the eigenvalue \(-1\)). The criterion we saw in class requires all principal minors to be non-negative, and the non-leading \(1 \times 1\) principal minor \(A_{22} = -1\) is negative.

Remark. The strict version is true (Sylvester's criterion): if all leading principal minors are strictly positive, then \(A\) is positive definite. The example shows that the criterion fails once zero minors are allowed.
parts.srcline: Approximation deck, 'PSD Matrices' slide (Approximation lecture deck): 'The following are equivalent definitions for PSD matrices:... 4. All principal minors of \(A\) are non-negative'. Re-skin of 2024A-1b ('If \(\det(A) \ge 0\), then \(A\) is PSD', False; 2024A official solution P1(b)).
